angle_summary: Domain swept: match score/goal models beyond basic Dixon-Coles (bivariate Poisson, Weibull counts, CMP, copulas, time-decay, hierarchical Bayes, state-space, Elo/SPI/xG hybrids) across academic benchmarks, betting-quant practice, and open-source implementations. Three headline conclusions for THIS odds-anchored engine. (1) The most verified, cheapest wins are on the odds-inversion side, not the count distribution: proportional de-vig + plain-Poisson inversion of 1X2 demonstrably under-recovers goal expectancy (practitioner validation shows -0.10 to -0.15 goals/team; Hegarty & Whelan's 80k-match IJF study confirms strong favourite-longshot bias in 1X2 but unbiased Asian-handicap probabilities) — this is a plausible mechanical cause of a chunk of the engine's -2.3 xPts-low audit gap, fixable via Shin de-vig plus fitting to the full free market ladder (AH, multiple totals lines, BTTS). (2) Scoreline-shape upgrades have real published wins over DC — Boshnakov et al.'s underdispersed Weibull-count + Frank-copula model beat Poisson/DC in and out of sample with positive Kelly returns; Karlis-Ntzoufras diagonal inflation fixes draw mass; McHale-Scarf show dependence turns increasingly negative in mismatched internationals — and these matter here even with 1X2 pinned to market, because they move clean-sheet, ceiling (P85), captain-EV and correct-score mass. (3) Standalone team-strength models almost never beat the market head-on (FiveThirtyEight SPI lost -6.2% ROI vs Pinnacle closing over 36k matches), so hierarchical-Bayes/state-space/xG ratings should enter as priors, learned convex blends (Egidi), and in-tournament conjugate updating (Koopman-Lit; Ridall 2025) — exactly the engine's missing Bayesian-updating stage — rather than replacing odds-implied lambdas.

methods.name: Full market-ladder calibration of the scoreline model (AH + totals ladder + BTTS + CS, not just 1X2+one total)
methods.what: Replace the exact 2-equation solve of (lambda_home, lambda_away) from 1X2+one totals line with a weighted least-squares / max-likelihood fit of the scoreline model to ALL free de-vigged prices from the book: Asian handicap line+price (supremacy), the totals ladder O/U 1.5/2.5/3.5 (distribution shape, not just mean), both-teams-to-score (joint dependence), team totals and correct-score grid when free. With 4+ constraints you can identify per-match dispersion and dependence parameters, not only the two means.
methods.evidence: Hegarty & Whelan (Int J Forecasting 41(2), 2025; 80k+ European matches) show 1X2 implied probabilities carry strong favourite-longshot bias while their Asian-handicap mapping yields probabilities that are statistically unbiased estimates of outcome rates — i.e., supremacy read from AH is cleaner than from 1X2. Practitioner validation of the engine's current approach (opisthokonta 'Expected goals from bookmaker odds') found plain-Poisson inversion of 1X2 under-recovers average goals by ~0.10-0.15 per team per match — a direct documented mechanism for the engine's -2.3 xPts-low audit. Fitting lambdas from odds is standard betting-quant practice (penaltyblog goal-expectancy post implements it with scipy minimization). That richer ladders identify dispersion/dependence per match is standard identification logic but not separately benchmarked in a paper — that specific step is informed practice, mildly speculative.
methods.apply: Stage 1-3. Extend the odds scraper/cache schema to keep AH line+price, every totals line offered, BTTS and CS grid. In the solver, minimize sum of w_m*(P_model(m) - P_devig(m))^2 over all cached markets m (weights by market liquidity/trust: AH/main total high, CS low), with parameters (lambda_h, lambda_a) always free and (dispersion nu, dependence rho/theta) free only when >=4 independent constraints exist, else pinned to tournament-level fits. Pure stdlib: reuse the existing lambda solver, generalize to N-constraint Nelder-Mead (already implementable offline). Backtest vs current solver on cached R1-R3 odds against realized goals and Rotowire gap.

methods.name: Shin de-vig replacing proportional normalization
methods.what: Invert the single book's overround with Shin's insider-trading model (solve for insider fraction z, then Shin probabilities) instead of proportional scaling. Corrects favourite-longshot bias: proportional de-vig systematically understates favourites and overstates longshots, so favourites' lambdas (and their star players' xPts) come out low.
methods.evidence: Strumbelj (Int J Forecasting 2014, 'On determining probability forecasts from betting odds') found Shin probabilities forecast better than basic normalization across large football samples; per Whelan's 2025 summary, Shin reduced forecast bias by about two-thirds vs normalized probabilities. Strumbelj (J Sports Economics 2016) caveat: Shin's advantage shrinks for large/sharp markets. Hegarty & Whelan (2025) confirm the favourite-longshot bias exists in 1X2 odds on 80k+ matches, i.e., the bias Shin corrects is real in exactly the market the engine consumes. World Cup group games with heavy favourites (France lambda 3.25-type fixtures) are where proportional de-vig bites hardest — consistent with the engine's under-projection of favourites.
methods.apply: Stage 2 only: swap the proportional de-vig function for a Shin solver (fixed-point/bisection on z, ~30 lines stdlib, no dependencies; penaltyblog's implied module is a reference implementation with shin() alongside power/logarithmic methods). Keep proportional as a config fallback; A/B the two through the existing lambda solve on cached rounds and measure the shift in favourites' lambdas and xPts vs the Rotowire audit gap. Apply Shin to 1X2 and AGS props (longshot-heavy, so bias is largest there); use power method for 2-way totals.

methods.name: Bivariate Weibull count model with Frank copula (Boshnakov-Kharrat-McHale) as the scoreline distribution
methods.what: Replace Poisson marginals + DC tau with Weibull inter-arrival count marginals (shape parameter captures football's under-dispersion; Poisson is the shape=1 special case) joined by a Frank copula for home-away dependence. Produces fatter/thinner tails where the data demand it — the whole scoreline grid, not just the 0-0/1-0/0-1/1-1 corner DC adjusts.
methods.evidence: Boshnakov, Kharrat & McHale (Int J Forecasting 33(2) 2017, 107+ citations): on English Premier League data the bivariate Weibull count model with Frank copula gave improved in- and out-of-sample fit vs independent Poisson, bivariate-independent Weibull and DC-type benchmarks, better calibration curves, and POSITIVE returns from a Kelly strategy on both 1X2 and O/U 2.5 markets (the standout published 'beats the market' result among count models). Shape estimates < 1 confirm under-dispersion of goals. Production-grade open-source implementation exists (penaltyblog WeibullCopulaGoalsModel, Cython, recently optimized in v1.11.0) as a correctness reference for a stdlib port. Caveat: single league/eras tested; returns are pre-limits/fees.
methods.apply: Stage 4: swap the DC pmf for Weibull-count marginals (pmf via the standard alpha-recursion series in lambda and shape; precompute/cache a (lambda, shape) -> pmf-vector table offline for reproducibility) + Frank copula applied to the discrete CDFs. Stage 3's solver then fits (lambda_h, lambda_a, shape, theta) to the market ladder (method 1); with only 1X2+total available, fix shape≈0.9 and theta from tournament-level fits. Downstream 50k MC sims sample from the new grid unchanged. Expected effects: less probability on freak totals for the same mean (cleaner P85 ceilings and captain EV), more accurate clean-sheet mass.

methods.name: Competitiveness-dependent dependence: copula theta as a function of supremacy (McHale-Scarf), market-calibrated per match
methods.what: Replace the constant DC rho with a dependence parameter that varies with match competitiveness: McHale & Scarf found dependence between opposing teams' goals is near zero for evenly matched internationals and becomes increasingly NEGATIVE as mismatch grows. Parameterize Frank-copula theta (or DC rho) as a function of odds-implied supremacy |log(lambda_h/lambda_a)|, and where BTTS/CS odds exist, calibrate theta per match directly from them.
methods.evidence: McHale & Scarf (Statistical Modelling 11(3) 2011) modelled international soccer with copula-joined marginals and found the negative-dependence-with-mismatch pattern (their Frank copula dependence estimate kappa ≈ -0.54 on international data); international matches are exactly this engine's regime. Petretta, Egidi et al. 'Mar-Co' (arXiv 2103.07272) propose an alternative dependence structure that 'outperforms the Dixon and Coles [model] in several betting scenarios'. Practitioner notes (DC model writeups) document that rho materially moves BTTS-No and 0-0/1-1 pricing. That per-match theta can be pinned from BTTS odds is informed practice, not a published benchmark — speculative but mechanically sound (BTTS is a direct functional of the joint distribution).
methods.apply: Stage 4 (with hooks in stage 3): theta_match = a + b*|log(lambda_h/lambda_a)|, with (a,b) fitted offline on cached international results (WC/Euro/qualifiers) by maximum likelihood, overridden per match by BTTS-implied theta when that market is cached. Biggest effect on blowout fixtures (the France-lambda-3.25 type the user must cover): correct joint mass on 4-0 vs 3-1 changes defender clean-sheet xPts and Malspillet X-0 vs X-1 pick EV.

methods.name: Diagonal-inflated bivariate Poisson (Karlis-Ntzoufras) for the draw diagonal
methods.what: Karlis & Ntzoufras' bivariate Poisson adds a shared component lambda_3 (covariance) and a diagonal-inflation mixture that adds mass to ALL draw scorelines (0-0, 1-1, 2-2, 3-3), where DC's tau only perturbs the four low-score cells. Gives a principled reshaping of where draw probability sits across scorelines.
methods.evidence: Karlis & Ntzoufras (JRSS-D 52(3) 2003) show bivariate Poisson improves fit and draw prediction vs independent Poisson, with diagonal inflation capturing excess draws including 2-2+. Ley, Van de Wiele & Van Eetvelde (Statistical Modelling 2019; arXiv 1705.09575) compared 10 models: bivariate Poisson had the LOWEST Rank Probability Score both for national teams (0.1651) and Premier League (0.1953), though only marginally better than independent Poisson (0.1653/0.1954) — so the win over DC-style models is real but small for 1X2; the value here is scoreline-shape, not 1X2. Open-source reference: penaltyblog BivariatePoissonGoalsModel (Karlis-Ntzoufras).
methods.apply: Stage 4 as a swap-in alternative to DC tau (cheaper than the Weibull-copula rebuild): pmf is a finite sum, trivially stdlib. Fit (lambda_3, diagonal inflation p, theta) at tournament level on cached WC results + odds; per match, solve (lambda_1, lambda_2) to the market ladder with the shared/diagonal parameters fixed. Directly improves: which draw the X lands on — the exact Malspillet X-0 vs X-1 decision the user already lost 2 pts to in R2 — and 1-1 vs 0-0 split for clean-sheet xPts.

methods.name: In-tournament Bayesian updating via conjugate Gamma-Poisson state-space filter (Koopman-Lit / Ridall-Titman-Pettitt)
methods.what: Treat each team's attack/defence strength as a latent state evolving between rounds; after each match, update the posterior with the observed goals (optionally xG-weighted) using a conjugate Gamma-Poisson mean-field step with a discount/forgetting factor, then blend updated strengths into next round's lambdas. This is the literature's answer to the engine's known 'no in-tournament Bayesian updating' weakness.
methods.evidence: Koopman & Lit (JRSS-A 178(1) 2015): dynamic bivariate Poisson with time-varying attack/defence produced a SIGNIFICANT POSITIVE RETURN betting against bookmaker odds on EPL 2010-11/2011-12 out of sample. Ridall, Titman & Pettitt (JRSS-C 74(3) 2025): a conjugate Bayesian state-space filter over the full EPL history is 'competitive, or superior, to weighted likelihood or score-driven' methods — and the conjugacy makes it cheap enough for pure stdlib. Macri-Demartino, Egidi et al. (arXiv 2508.05891): adaptive spike-and-slab weighting of ability evolution beat other discrete-time dynamic models across Bundesliga/EPL/La Liga (footBayes implementation). Caveat: all evidence is league football with 30+ matches/team; a World Cup gives 3-7 observations, so the filter's job is small posterior nudges on top of odds, not standalone strength estimation.
methods.apply: New stage between rounds: initialize each team's Gamma(alpha, beta) attack/defence posteriors from pre-tournament odds-implied lambdas (method 1) or the hierarchical prior (method 7); after each round, conjugate-update on goals-vs-opponent-adjusted expectation with discount delta≈0.8-0.9 per round; expose posterior mean/variance to the blend stage (method 8) and to the research overlay as an auto-computed form multiplier replacing part of the hand-set w. Fully offline: updates run from the cached stats_rN.json results already ingested.

methods.name: Hierarchical Bayesian national-team strength prior with Ley-style weighted likelihood (half-life + importance weights)
methods.what: Fit a Baio-Blangiardo-style hierarchical attack/defence Poisson (or bivariate Poisson) model on cached international results, with exponential time-decay weights w = (1/2)^(days/half-life) and match-importance weights (friendly=1 ... World Cup=4), giving every WC team a prior (lambda_attack, lambda_defence) WITH uncertainty. Hierarchy shrinks small-sample teams toward the confederation/global mean; Baio-Blangiardo's mixture variant prevents over-shrinkage of the elite tail.
methods.evidence: Ley, Van de Wiele & Van Eetvelde (2019): weighted-ML bivariate Poisson was the best of 10 models by RPS; the optimal half-life was ~3 years (1095 days) for NATIONAL TEAMS (vs 390 days for clubs) with importance weights 1-4 — directly transferable constants. Baio & Blangiardo (J Applied Statistics 37(2) 2010) established the hierarchical structure and documented the overshrinkage problem plus mixture fix. Egidi's footBayes (CRAN) is a maintained reference implementation of exactly these models (static + dynamic, Stan/MLE). Note: this class does NOT beat the market alone — its value here is priors for missing/soft markets, sanity flags on odd odds, and inputs to blending/updating.
methods.apply: New stage 0 module (offline, from a cached international-results file): MAP fit via stdlib gradient ascent (few thousand weighted matches, ~2N+2 params — minutes of compute); Laplace approximation for uncertainty. Consumers: (a) fixtures with missing/late odds get model lambdas instead of nothing; (b) |odds-implied lambda - prior lambda| z-score flags suspect feeds (the players.json-collision class of bug, but for odds); (c) prior for methods 6 and 8. Keeps the engine runnable offline even when the book hasn't priced a match yet.

methods.name: Learned convex blend of odds-implied and model-based scoring rates (Egidi-Pauli-Torelli)
methods.what: Formalize the engine's hand-set research-overlay weight w for team rates: each team's scoring rate becomes a convex combination of the odds-implied lambda and the historical-model lambda, with the mixing weight ESTIMATED from data (per match or globally) inside a Bayesian model, rather than hand-tuned in [0.05, 0.5].
methods.evidence: Egidi, Pauli & Torelli (Statistical Modelling 2018; arXiv 1802.08848): first model to fuse bookmaker odds (inverted to match-level scoring rates) with historical attack/defence estimates via a per-match convex combination with Bayesian-estimated mixing weight; on 9 seasons train / 1 season test of major European leagues it improved fit and predictive accuracy over historical-only models and supported a positive-return betting strategy in their evaluation. Implemented in footBayes (stan_foot). Interpretation for this engine: the market side is already primary, so the expected gain is smaller than in their paper — the win is replacing an arbitrary hand-set w with a fitted, uncertainty-aware weight, and it quantifies exactly how much soft research info should move lambdas. Effect size for an odds-primary engine: speculative.
methods.apply: Stage 3/8: lambda_final = w_m * lambda_odds + (1-w_m) * lambda_model(prior + in-tournament posterior), with w_m fitted by maximizing weighted predictive likelihood on the growing backtest cache (R1-R3 odds + results already stored; more each round). Start with a single global w and a logistic link on match covariates (odds staleness, market count, group vs knockout). This subsumes the soft-multiplier part of the markdown overlay for TEAM rates; hard facts (outs/suspensions) stay absolute at the player layer.

methods.name: Shots-based GAP ratings / xG-Dixon-Coles pseudo-scorelines as an auxiliary signal for team AND player rates
methods.what: Two related upgrades: (a) Wheatcroft's Generalised Attacking Performance (GAP) ratings — recursive ratings that predict a team's shots on target for/against rather than goals; (b) Torvaney's xG-DC — fit the scoreline model to Poisson-binomial pseudo-scorelines built from shot xG values instead of noisy goals. Use these to steer the engine's team SoT totals and player SoT/goal rates, and as a second opinion on lambdas.
methods.evidence: Wheatcroft (J Sports Analytics 7(2) 2021; arXiv 2001.09097): GAP ratings on shots/shots-on-target/corners contain information BEYOND the odds and yielded 'long-term and robust' profit in the over/under 2.5 market across 30 European leagues — one of the few published beat-the-market results using match statistics. Torvaney (statsandsnakeoil, regista R package): weighting DC fits by Poisson-binomial xG scoreline probabilities is validated qualitatively (more stable strengths; Leicester 15/16 rated 'average' not miraculous) but 'untested against vanilla DC in predictive accuracy' — speculative on effect size. Cautionary benchmark: FiveThirtyEight SPI (xG + non-shot-xG adjusted-goals ratings) lost -6.2% ROI against Pinnacle closing odds over 36,335 matches with systematic miscalibration (transferscience evaluation) — so shot-based ratings must OVERLAY odds, never replace them.
methods.apply: Stage 6 (player sim) + overlay: build GAP-style ratings from cached WC match SoT data (Holdet stats type 558 already decoded) to predict team SoT totals per fixture; reconcile player SoT rates to those totals exactly as goals are reconciled to team lambdas today — replacing the role-shaped guess with a fitted team-level SoT model. Optionally re-solve a second lambda set from xG pseudo-scorelines as a diagnostic column next to odds-implied lambdas. Requires a shots/xG cache per WC match (FBref/Understat-style scrape into the offline store) — the pipeline, not the math, is the work.

methods.name: Conway-Maxwell-Poisson marginals: the stdlib-cheap under-dispersion fix
methods.what: Swap Poisson marginals for Conway-Maxwell-Poisson (pmf ∝ lambda^x/(x!)^nu), whose second parameter nu captures football's under-dispersion with a trivially computable pmf (truncated normalizing sum). The pragmatic alternative to the Weibull-count rebuild: 90% of the dispersion benefit at 20% of the implementation cost.
methods.evidence: opisthokonta.net preliminary study (EPL + Bundesliga, 2010-11..2014-15, AIC): CMP and Double Poisson 'almost always better than the ordinary Poisson'; goals are UNDER-dispersed (see also the companion CMP goal-difference post) — though the author flags it as fit-based, not a full prediction backtest. Florez, Guindani & Vannucci (arXiv 2409.17129; J Quantitative Analysis in Sports 21(1) 2025): Bayesian bivariate CMP regression with random-effect correlation 'matches or outperforms' Poisson and negative binomial models on sports count data including football. No published head-to-head vs Weibull-count on betting returns — treat CMP-vs-Weibull ranking as open; CMP's forecasting edge over DC specifically is plausible-but-unproven (mark speculative).
methods.apply: Stage 4: implement CMP pmf (20 lines stdlib, truncate sum at ~25 goals), keep the DC-tau or copula dependence layer on top of CMP marginals. Identify nu per match from the totals ladder when method 1 lands (O1.5/2.5/3.5 pins the shape), else fit one tournament-level nu (<1 expected) on cached results. Decision rule: do EITHER this (fast) OR the Weibull-copula model (gold standard, method 3) — both together is redundant. Immediate payoffs: totals-ladder consistency, tighter team-total tails feeding player haul probabilities.

methods.name: Hybrid covariate model (random forest + ability parameters) as an odds bias-corrector for tournament football
methods.what: Groll-style hybrid: a covariate model (random forest or penalized regression over FIFA rank, squad market value, confederation, age, coach tenure, plus Ley-type ability parameters) trained on past World Cups to predict goals — used here NOT to replace odds but to model the RESIDUAL between odds-implied lambdas/xPts and realized outcomes, correcting systematic market biases at World Cups (the only published class of model that has beaten WC betting odds out of sample).
methods.evidence: Groll, Ley, Schauberger & Van Eetvelde (J Quantitative Analysis in Sports 15(4) 2019; arXiv 1806.03208): on FIFA World Cups 2002-2014 (leave-one-tournament-out), the hybrid random forest combining covariates with ranking-derived ability parameters improved substantially over either component and OUTPERFORMED the bookmaker-odds benchmark on the held-out World Cup matches; confirmed pattern in the Women's WC 2019 follow-up (arXiv 1906.01131) and later Euro papers. Big caveats: n≈64 matches per tournament so validation variance is high; 'beat the odds' is on match outcome probabilities, not player-level fantasy points; transfer to a residual-correction role is this report's proposal, not published — speculative.
methods.apply: Offline side-model, gated on the backtesting harness maturing: assemble a per-team covariate table for WC 2002-2022 (public: FIFA rank, Transfermarkt squad value, etc.), compute odds-implied lambdas for those matches from historical closing odds, fit a small tree ensemble / ridge model to log(realized-goal intensity) - log(odds-implied lambda), then apply the fitted correction to 2026 lambdas before stage 4. Pure-stdlib tree ensembles are writable but painful — this is the one method where the stdlib constraint genuinely hurts; consider a frozen coefficient table exported from an offline sklearn fit to stay reproducible.

angle_summary: Deep sweep of odds->probability extraction: de-vig theory (Shin 1992/93, Strumbelj 2014, Clarke/Kovalchik/Ingram 2017 power method, Buchdahl's 136k-match margin-model tests, penaltyblog 2025 benchmarks), multi-book aggregation (Kaunitz et al. 2017 consensus, Zeileis et al. bookmaker-consensus World Cup models 2010-2026, Pinnacle-as-sharp-anchor CLV evidence), tournament-specific efficiency (Santos IJSF 2020 on WC 1994-2014, Angelini & De Angelis IJF 2019, Winkelmann et al. 2024), and market-structure practice for pinning lambdas (opisthokonta's O/U and 1X2 inversion posts, Skellam/AH supremacy, BTTS, FPL Review's audit of anytime-goalscorer margins). Headline findings for this engine: (1) proportional de-vig is measurably the worst mainstream method — it leaves a favourite-longshot bias worth ~0.5-0.7% yield distortion that systematically deflates favourites' win probs and hence lambdas, one plausible contributor to the ~2.3-pt-low xPts audit; (2) inverting 1X2 with Poisson-family models underestimates lambdas by ~0.10-0.15 goals/team (measured by opisthokonta) — Asian-handicap supremacy + multi-line totals is the sharper, draw-bias-free identification; (3) single-book input is the highest-upside fix: de-vigged log-odds consensus across many books (with a sharp anchor) is close to the best available estimate of true probability; (4) AGS props carry 20-50% overrounds concentrated on longshots, so proportional prop de-vig materially distorts player goal rates — the single most fantasy-points-relevant bias. A caveat threaded through the evidence: on low-margin big-league 1X2 closing odds, de-vig method choice barely matters (RPS deltas ~1e-4); the payoff concentrates exactly where this engine lives — high-margin markets (props, outrights), mismatched international fixtures with extreme odds, and non-closing snapshots. Ten methods below, ordered roughly by (impact x realism), each mapped to a specific pipeline stage.

methods.name: Multi-book de-vigged log-odds consensus (replace SINGLE bookmaker input)
methods.what: Fetch 1X2/totals/AH from many bookmakers, de-vig each book's each market separately (Shin/power, see method 3), then average on the log-odds (logit) scale with reliability weights that up-weight sharp books (Pinnacle) and down-weight high-margin recreational books; snapshot as late before the fantasy deadline as feasible (closing-line efficiency). The consensus probabilities become the sole input to the lambda solver.
methods.evidence: Kaunitz, Zhong & Kreiner 2017 (arXiv 1710.02824): the mean of ~30+ books' closing odds is an 'extremely accurate proxy of the actual probability'; betting deviations from consensus was profitable in a 10-year historical simulation, a 6-month minute-level simulation, and 5 months of real money — i.e., consensus is better calibrated than any single soft book. Zeileis/Leitner/Hornik bookmaker consensus model: de-vig then logit-average across 26-28 books; correctly predicted the 2010 WC winner and 3/4 of 2014 semifinalists; reused for 2018/2022/2026 WCs. Buchdahl (Wisdom of the Crowd, 136,876 matches): fair probs derived from a sharp anchor identified +EV at other books whose realized returns matched expectation (+2.51% actual vs +2.27% expected over 36,395 bets), i.e., sharp-anchored fair probs are well calibrated. Practitioner analysis reports r^2=0.997 between Pinnacle closing odds and outcomes over 397,935 games (secondary source, not independently verified). The Odds API lists 25+ EU bookmakers including Pinnacle (delayed public-site prices) — a practical free-tier source; exact free limits not verified.
methods.apply: New fetch layer writes one cached JSON per book per snapshot (preserves offline reproducibility); de-vig module runs per book; a combine step takes precision-weighted mean of logit(p) per outcome; the existing single-book path becomes the fallback. Also log snapshot timestamps and keep an early+late pair per match so the backtest harness can measure how much line movement costs the projections. Replaces the 'free bookmaker odds (SINGLE bookmaker) -> proportional de-vig' stage wholesale; lambda solver is untouched but gets cleaner inputs.

methods.name: Pin lambdas from Asian-handicap supremacy + multi-line totals (Skellam inversion) instead of 1X2
methods.what: Identify (lambda_home, lambda_away) from the two sharpest, draw-free quantities: expected supremacy S from de-vigged AH lines (invert the Skellam/DC goal-difference CDF at each quoted quarter/half line, handling push/half-win settlement) and expected total T from de-vigged O/U at every quoted line (1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5...), then lambda_h=(T+S)/2, lambda_a=(T-S)/2 via weighted least squares across all lines with weights proportional to 1/margin. 1X2 is demoted to fitting the DC rho (draw mass) and to a residual diagnostic.
methods.evidence: opisthokonta (p=1760) measured that inverting 1X2 odds with a Poisson model 'underestimates both expected goals home and away' by roughly 0.10-0.15 goals per team across major leagues — a direct, quantified mechanism for this engine's xPts-running-low audit, because market draw pricing (plus margin loaded onto the draw under proportional de-vig) drags fitted lambdas down. His p=1835 post gives the exact ppois/uniroot recipe for totals inversion and notes a single O/U line cannot split home/away — hence the AH supremacy leg. AH markets are two-way and among the lowest-margin football markets, and academic work analyzes them as a distinct, sharper price structure (Whelan, 'Returns on Complex Bets: Evidence From Asian Handicap Betting on Soccer', using Pinnacle data across handicap values; a UK thesis models AH efficiency vs 1X2 with Skellam goal differences — text not extracted, so relative-sharpness magnitude is speculative). Using multiple totals lines instead of one adds CDF-shape constraints (over/under-dispersion vs Poisson) rather than just the mean.
methods.apply: Replaces the 'solve (lambda_home, lambda_away) to match implied 1X2+totals' stage. Stdlib implementation: Skellam pmf as a sum over Poisson products on the existing DC grid; bisection on S and T; quarter-line settlement = average of the two adjacent half-lines' EVs. Requires adding AH and extra O/U lines to the odds fetch (free at most books; The Odds API exposes spreads+totals). Expected first-order effect: lambdas rise ~0.1-0.2 for favourites in lopsided WC ties, lifting xPts toward the Rotowire benchmark; blowout-coverage picks (biggest-lambda fixture) get more reliable.

methods.name: Replace proportional de-vig with Shin / power method (favourite-longshot-bias-aware)
methods.what: Swap proportional normalization for Shin's insider-trading de-vig (iteratively solve insider fraction z; 2-outcome case is analytic and equals the additive method) on 1X2 and other 3+ outcome markets, and the power method (p_i^k normalized, solve k by Newton) on totals and props. Both strip more margin from longshots, matching how books actually load overround.
methods.evidence: Strumbelj 2014 (IJF): Shin probabilities beat basic normalization for ALL bookmaker/sport pairs tested and were the best method for 217/412 pairs; later work (Strumbelj 2016, via review) says Shin removes roughly two-thirds of the bias but not all. Clarke, Kovalchik & Ingram 2017: across three large datasets the multiplicative/normalization method 'performed badly on all predictive performance measures'; the power method universally beat it and matched-or-beat Shin, never produces probabilities outside [0,1], and is in commercial use. Buchdahl's 136,876-match Pinnacle-closing test: level-stakes yield from de-vigged 'true' odds = -0.56% for equal-margin (i.e., proportional) vs +0.10% margin-proportional-to-odds, +0.07% logarithmic, -0.20% odds-ratio — proportional is the clear laggard, biased exactly on longshots. Honest caveat (penaltyblog 2025, one EPL season of Bet365 closing odds): all seven methods land within ~0.00015 RPS of each other on low-margin big-league 1X2 — the win comes on high-margin, extreme-odds markets, which describes WC group mismatches, props, and outrights. Open-source reference implementations: mberk/shin (Python/Rust, Jullien & Salanie iteration) and the R 'implied' package (7 methods) — easy to port to pure stdlib.
methods.apply: Drop-in replacement inside the de-vig stage: ~50 lines of stdlib Python (Newton/bisection); add a per-market method flag so the new backtest harness can A/B proportional vs Shin vs power on cached snapshots. Downstream lambda solve, DC grid, and sims unchanged. Do this first — it is days of work and prerequisite plumbing for methods 1, 2 and 4.

methods.name: FLB-aware de-vig of anytime-goalscorer props with booksum reconciliation to team lambdas
methods.what: AGS books run 20-50% overround with the margin loaded onto longshots (defenders, subs). Instead of proportional shrinkage, de-vig the whole AGS book with a power exponent chosen so the de-vigged booksum equals the model-consistent target sum(1 - exp(-lambda_i)) implied by the team lambda and the minutes model; where multiple books are available, take longest-odds-per-player first (sharpest price) before de-vig. Then convert to per-90 scoring rates and reconcile to team totals as now.
methods.evidence: FPL Review's audit: goalscorer markets carry average margins around 45%, applied inconsistently across players and books; bookmaker-AGS-implied probabilities scored R^2=0.321 vs their model's 0.353 (two-way spread markets 0.331) on 2,021 player-gameweeks — informative but visibly distorted, and they explicitly recommend standardized margin cleaning (slightly better) or longest-available-odds before use. Player-prop tooling in the US market treats power/Shin de-vig of props as standard practice (PropsEdge and similar de-vig calculators; practitioner-level evidence). General FLB de-vig evidence from method 3 applies a fortiori here since AGS prices on fringe players are deep longshots. The booksum-target trick (tie the AGS book's total probability mass to the team-lambda-implied expected number of distinct scorers) is my synthesis of standard pieces — no published benchmark found, mark speculative — but it makes the prop layer internally consistent with the match layer by construction.
methods.apply: Modifies the 'goals from prop-derived rates' input to the per-player event simulation: replace the current prop de-vig with power-with-booksum-target; keep prior goal-shares as the no-props fallback. Direct effect: star forwards' scoring probs rise, deep longshots' fall — this compounds with the fixed realized-minutes priors to sharpen Holdet cheap-starter identification and captain EV. Days of work if single-book; add cross-book longest-odds when method 1 lands.

methods.name: Outright-market inverse abilities (bookmaker consensus model) for future-round lambdas and free in-tournament updating
methods.what: Each round, fetch tournament-winner (and group-winner/to-reach-X) odds, de-vig the 48-outcome book (power method — outright overrounds are enormous), logit-average across books, then invert via bracket simulation to per-team log-abilities such that simulating the remaining tournament reproduces the consensus winning probabilities (Leitner/Zeileis/Hornik's 'inverse' approach). Ability differences map to match lambdas (paired-comparison scale calibrated on this tournament's own match odds), giving principled lambdas for hypothetical future pairings where no match odds exist yet.
methods.evidence: Leitner, Zeileis & Hornik 2010 (IJF): bookmaker consensus forecast EURO 2008 better than Elo/FIFA-rating models; the framework correctly predicted the 2010 WC winner and 3/4 of 2014 semifinalists; refreshed versions ran for 2016/2018 (26 bookmakers) and inside the 2022/2026 'ML multiverse' (24 bookmakers), where odds-derived abilities are consistently among the strongest features (Groll et al. 2018-style hybrids: ability parameters + covariates beat single sources). Because bookmakers reprice outrights after every round, re-snapshotting and re-inverting is de facto Bayesian updating of team strength — it directly patches the engine's 'no in-tournament updating' weakness with market information rather than a hand-rolled filter. Accuracy for match-level lambdas of far-future hypothetical ties is necessarily softer than posted match odds (mark that use speculative).
methods.apply: New module upstream of the lambda solver: abilities feed (a) multi-round xPts horizons for wildcard/chip planning (the R32 rebuild decision needs exactly this), (b) a regularizer that shrinks noisy single-match lambdas toward ability-implied values, (c) sanity checks on the research overlay's soft multipliers. Bracket simulation reuses the existing Monte-Carlo machinery; the inversion is an outer optimization loop (stdlib, but genuinely weeks of careful work with the 2026 format's 32-team knockout).

methods.name: Tournament-calibrated residual FLB correction (historical recalibration layer)
methods.what: Even after Shin/power de-vig, residual favourite-longshot bias remains; fit a monotone recalibration g(p) (e.g., logit(g) = a + b*logit(p), or beta calibration) per market type on historical international-tournament odds+results (WC/Euro 2002-2022 archives), and apply it after de-vig, before the lambda solve.
methods.evidence: Strumbelj's follow-up work found Shin probabilities cut bias by about two-thirds but remained somewhat biased for European soccer. Angelini & De Angelis 2019 (IJF; 41 bookmakers, 11 leagues, 11 years) formally reject efficiency for longshots while favourites are priced near-efficiently — i.e., the residual bias is systematic and estimable. World-Cup-specific: Santos 2020 (IJSF; WC 1994-2014) shows a step-logit model over bookmaker odds picked the winner in 5/6 tournaments and generated consistent profits — WC prices are not fully efficient; Winkelmann, Ötting, Deutscher & Makarewicz 2024 report FLB, with search-level summaries indicating it is stronger in high-profile tournaments and later rounds (abstract not retrieved — treat that specific claim as reported, not verified). Net: a calibrated b>1-style shrink of mid/long odds at a World Cup is evidence-backed, but the exact coefficients must come from your own backtest data (speculative until fitted).
methods.apply: One pure function inserted between de-vig and lambda solve, with coefficients fitted offline by the backtesting harness now being built (calibration curves per odds bucket become a standing harness report). Historical international odds are the bottleneck: football-data.co.uk covers club leagues free; for internationals use OddsPortal/Kaggle WC odds dumps (data plumbing, not verified in this sweep). Also fixes the engine for the FPL/Holdet roadmap where multi-season club odds archives ARE freely available.

methods.name: Per-match Dixon-Coles rho and dispersion from BTTS / correct-score markets
methods.what: Stop using a global DC rho: per match, after (T,S) identification, fit rho (and optionally a dispersion tweak) so the model grid reproduces de-vigged BTTS probability — under independence P(BTTS)=(1-e^-lh)(1-e^-la), so the BTTS-vs-model gap isolates the low-score dependence — and/or weighted-KL fit (lh, la, rho) to the power-de-vigged correct-score grid.
methods.evidence: BTTS is a liquid, widely-quoted market analyzed academically (IJF 2022 'Forecasting football results and exploiting betting markets: the case of both teams to score': bookmakers are robust baselines, beatable only at the margins — i.e., BTTS prices are informative). Correct-score books embed the bookmaker's own scoreline dependence structure but carry strong per-scoreline favourite-longshot bias, so FLB-aware de-vig before fitting is mandatory (secondary references; no published benchmark of CS-fitted rho vs historically-fitted rho was found in this sweep — mark the CS-grid variant speculative; the BTTS variant is arithmetic on well-studied prices).
methods.apply: Extends the lambda-solver stage: add BTTS to the odds fetch; solve rho per match by bisection against de-vigged BTTS (stdlib, small). Payoff concentrates exactly where fantasy scoring is scoreline-sensitive: clean sheets, goals-conceded penalties, and the Malspillet per-match double-chance picks (X-1 vs X-0 calls hinge on the 0-0/1-1 mass you are currently setting with one global rho).

methods.name: Knockout markets: reconcile 90-minute 1X2 with to-advance odds to simulate extra time and penalties
methods.what: For knockout ties, fetch both the 90' 1X2 and the 2-way 'to advance/qualify' market. P(advance) - P(win in 90') = P(advance via ET/pens); combined with the DC draw probability this pins P(win in ET) and P(win on pens). Simulate a 30-minute ET mini-match with per-minute goal rates scaled from the regulation lambdas, then penalties.
methods.evidence: Market structure is standard and documented (knockout match bets settle on 90 minutes; separate to-advance markets exist — sportsbook/betstamp explainer level, not academic). Roughly a third of recent WC knockout ties have gone to extra time, so ignoring ET clips ~30 minutes of appearance/goal/save exposure in a material fraction of matches (proportion from general knowledge, not verified in this sweep). The ET goal-rate scaling factor (per-minute intensity slightly below regulation) is practitioner folklore — mark speculative; the decomposition P(advance)-P(win90) itself is an identity on de-vigged prices. No academic paper benchmarking this layer was found; classify the whole method as practice-grounded rather than literature-backed.
methods.apply: Extends the Monte-Carlo stage: on drawn 90' sims, branch into ET (scaled lambdas, same player goal-share machinery, +30 minutes to the minutes model — partially mitigating the crude 60+ assumption for knockouts) and a penalties coin-flip informed by the to-advance residual. Affects xMins, captain EV and P85 for every R32+ pick, and is required for the FIFA fantasy knockout rounds the engine is entering now.

methods.name: Betting-exchange (Betfair) prices as a near-vig-free second anchor, especially for outrights
methods.what: Exchange back/lay midpoints need no de-vig model — only a small commission adjustment — so they provide an assumption-free probability anchor to validate (or weight into) the consensus, most valuably on outright/winner markets where bookmaker overrounds are 30-100%+ and the de-vig model choice dominates the answer.
methods.evidence: IJF 2024, 'Forecasting soccer matches with betting odds: a tale of two markets', compares bookmaker vs exchange odds as forecasts (paper confirmed to exist; full findings not retrievable in this sweep — ScienceDirect 403 — so the direction/magnitude is unverified here). Zeileis et al. explicitly include betting exchanges among their 26 aggregated sources for WC forecasts. Buchdahl's framework treats commission-adjusted exchange prices as close to 'true' odds. Overall: mechanism is solid arithmetic, comparative-accuracy evidence is partially unverified — treat as medium-confidence.
methods.apply: Optional source in the new multi-book fetch layer (method 1): Betfair Exchange API (free key, needs account; cache snapshots for offline reruns). Use as (a) a validation column in the backtest harness, (b) the preferred de-vig-free input for outright odds feeding method 5's ability inversion. Skip if account/API friction is unacceptable — consensus alone captures most of the gain.

methods.name: Odds-implied Elo ratings as stale-odds gap-filler and overlay discipline
methods.what: Maintain an Elo-style team rating updated not by results but by each match's de-vigged pre-match probabilities (Wunderlich & Memmert's Betting Odds Rating System). Use it to synthesize lambdas when odds are missing/stale, and to convert the research overlay's hand-set soft multipliers (w in [0.05,0.5]) into a quantitatively anchored prior.
methods.evidence: Wunderlich & Memmert 2018 (PLOS ONE, ~15,000 matches across four leagues plus UCL/UEL): the betting-odds-based Elo outperformed classic result-based Elo, demonstrating pre-match odds contain more information than results themselves; the same authors compared odds vs FIFA ranking predictive power at the 2006/2010/2014 World Cups. This is a robustness/coverage method, not an accuracy-lift on matches where fresh odds already exist — impact on the current WC engine is small, larger for the FPL/Holdet roadmap (dense fixture lists, occasional missing markets, and a principled way to blend market with model — exactly what FPL Review's market-odds slider does commercially).
methods.apply: Small standalone module fed by the cached odds history (qualifiers + group stage already cached); exposes rating_diff -> (lambda_h, lambda_a) calibrated against this tournament's own match odds. Wire into the research-overlay stage as the default soft-multiplier prior so w stops being purely hand-set.

angle_summary: Minutes/lineup projection is where commercial systems beat open models: the OpenFPL benchmark paper explicitly attributes FPL Review's remaining edge (on zero/blank outcomes) to proprietary expected-minutes built from team news, congestion and odds — exactly the layer this engine handles with a crude 'starters get 60+' rule plus a hand-set markdown overlay. The literature and practice converge on a decomposition: P(start) x minutes-given-start + P(cameo) x sub-minutes, with each piece modellable — start probability via recency-weighted role security with hierarchical manager/team pooling (Caley shows persistent manager-level sub tendencies; La Liga ~10% of minutes from subs vs PL 6-7%), in-game exit times via survival/hazard models where score state is the dominant covariate (Del Corral 2008; tournament data shows losing teams sub at 55.3' vs 59.3-60.2' and 4.26 subs/match under the 5-sub rule), and per-minute event rates that are NOT flat — Dixon & Robinson (1998) show goal intensity rises through the match, so cameos are worth more than minutes/90 implies (subs score 13.2% of goals on ~10% of minutes). The single most engine-compatible architectural move: upgrade the 50k-sim Monte Carlo from scoreline-level to goal-TIME simulation (inhomogeneous Poisson, a sibling of the Dixon-Coles model already in place), which unlocks score-coupled substitution hazards, time-weighted player exposure, correct 60-minute appearance thresholds, and extra-time extension in knockouts (where 90-minute-settled AGS props and 90-minute lambdas currently understate fantasy exposure that includes ET) in one coherent change. Tournament-specific layers — qualification-scenario dead-rubber rotation (Portugal made 8 changes in their Euro 2024 third game; the 2026 format creates more dead rubbers) and structured news ingestion with per-source trust (transformer news features cut FPL prediction MSE 6.27->5.63) — sit on top. Methods below are ordered roughly by leverage.

methods.name: Decomposed appearance model: P(start) / P(cameo) / P(unused) with conditional minutes distributions
methods.what: Replace the binary 'starter = 60+ mins' with a mixture: per player estimate p_start, p_bench_cameo, p_unused; then draw minutes from empirical conditional distributions — minutes|start (mass at ~90, mean ~78-85, sub-off tail after ~55'), minutes|cameo (entry ~70.6' mean at tournaments, ~15-25 mins). This is the canonical structure of every serious xMins system.
methods.evidence: FPL Review's xMins docs state the metric is 'the average minutes a player might play across 1,000 simulations' and 'reflects mixed scenarios (e.g. 51 xMins = blend of starts and cameos)' with injury-proneness and role-security decay — i.e., exactly this decomposition run inside simulation. The OpenFPL paper (arXiv 2508.09992) benchmarks against FPL Review and finds the commercial edge concentrated on 'Zeros and Blanks', which it attributes to 'precise information on player availability and expected minutes'. AIrsenal (Alan Turing Institute) implements a poor-man's version: it resamples the player's last-3-match minutes as discrete scenarios and weights predictions by them. FPL Form likewise separates probability-of-appearing from if-appears points. Tournament sub-timing distributions to parameterize the conditionals are published: mean sub timing 70.6' under the 5-sub rule, 4.26 subs/match (PMC11167463).
methods.apply: New minutes module between the research overlay and the per-player event simulation. Per player: p_start from recency-weighted starts (the realized-minutes priors in core/realized.py are the seed), overlay hard facts force 0/1; p_cameo from bench-appearance history. Inside each of the 50k sims, draw appearance state, then minutes from the conditional distribution; gate the 60-minute appearance points on drawn minutes instead of assuming 60+. Goal/assist/SoT rates scale by drawn exposure (see time-weighting method). Clean-sheet eligibility (60' rules) also becomes correct per-draw.

methods.name: Goal-time simulation with score-coupled substitution hazards (survival model in the Monte Carlo)
methods.what: Upgrade the match simulator from drawing a Dixon-Coles scoreline to simulating goal TIMES as an inhomogeneous Poisson/birth process, then attach a piecewise substitution hazard to each starter that responds to the simulated score state: trailing teams make earlier attacking subs, big leads trigger star-resting, defensive subs come later. Minutes, goals, clean sheets and cards become jointly simulated and correlated with the scoreline within each iteration.
methods.evidence: Del Corral, Barros & Prieto-Rodriguez (2008, Journal of Sports Economics) fit an inverse Gaussian hazard to Spanish league first-sub times and find 'the most important factor explaining the timing of the first player substitutions is the score as it stands prior to the substitution', with defensive subs made later. Silva & Swartz (2016, JQAS) analyze substitution times via Bayesian logistic regression against Myers' 58'/73'/79' decision rule. Tournament-scale data under the 5-sub rule (PMC11167463): losing teams' first sub at 55.3' vs 59.3-60.2' for winning/drawing; first subs later in knockouts (59.8') than groups (57.2'); 4.26 +/- 1.07 subs/match. Dixon & Robinson (1998) established score- and time-dependent goal intensity on 4,000+ matches, giving the simulation backbone. A 2026 arXiv paper (2605.16066) shows a market-calibrated Weibull accelerated-failure-time match model calibrated to 1X2/totals odds — the same calibration this engine already does — reaching near-Betfair accuracy, evidence the goal-time layer can be market-calibrated rather than refit.
methods.apply: Replaces the scoreline-draw stage: keep the solved (lambda_home, lambda_away) and Dixon-Coles low-score correction as calibration targets, but generate each sim as timed goal arrivals (thin a time-varying intensity normalized to the 90' lambdas). Each starter gets a baseline exit hazard by position/role (parameterized from the published timing distributions, stdlib-implementable as piecewise-constant lookup tables), shifted by current simulated score margin. Player event exposure = integral of on-pitch time against the goal-intensity curve. This simultaneously fixes the crude minutes model, creates real player-scoreline correlation (the blowout-coverage weakness), and is the prerequisite for correct extra-time handling.

methods.name: Time-of-match goal-intensity weighting instead of linear minutes scaling
methods.what: Per-minute goal/assist/SoT rates are not flat: scoring intensity rises through a match. Weight a player's event exposure by the integral of a fitted intensity curve lambda(t) over his on-pitch window rather than minutes/90. A sub playing the final 25 minutes gets ~30-35% of a full-match goal expectation, not 28%; a starter subbed at 60' gets less than 67%.
methods.evidence: Dixon & Robinson (1998, JRSS-D, 144+ citations): 'clear evidence that the rate of scoring goals changes over the course of a match... tends to increase over the game', modeled as interacting birth processes; widely used in spread betting. Corroborating tournament fact: substitutes scored ~13.2% of goals at recent WCs/Euros (PMC11167463) while subs play ~10% of minutes in 5-sub leagues (Caley/Expecting Goals) — a per-minute rate premium for late-game minutes. Effect size on any single player is modest (5-15% of their cameo/early-hook xPts) but systematic across every bench player — one plausible contributor to the engine's audited ~2.3-pt-low bias vs Rotowire on rotation-risk players (that attribution is speculative).
methods.apply: Small change inside the per-player event simulation: precompute a normalized cumulative intensity table Lambda(t) for t=0..90 (fit offline once from cached goal-time data or lift the published Dixon-Robinson shape; store as a 90-entry array in the repo). Player rate multiplier = Lambda(t_off) - Lambda(t_on) instead of (t_off - t_on)/90. Fully stdlib, works even without the full goal-time simulator by applying it to drawn minutes from the appearance mixture.

methods.name: Extra-time exposure and 90-minute market-settlement correction for knockouts
methods.what: Knockout fantasy scoring includes extra time, but every input the engine calibrates to is a 90-minute object: 1X2 and totals define 90' lambdas, and anytime-goalscorer props settle on 90 minutes plus injury time at standard bookmaker rules (bet365 only extends player markets into ET via its 'More Time to Win' promo on selected competitions). So knockout xPts are systematically understated for players on teams likely to go to ET. Extend each sim with probability P(draw at 90') by 30 minutes of play with rescaled intensity, a 6th-sub hazard, and appearance/goal/CS/card accrual.
methods.evidence: bet365 sports rules: goalscorer bets 'settled on the result at the end of 90 minutes play; extra-time... do not count unless otherwise stated', with the ET extension only as a named enhancement on select fixtures — confirming the prop-to-fantasy mismatch. The engine already computes P(90' draw) from Dixon-Coles (typically ~20-30% for balanced knockout ties), so the correction multiplier on team goal exposure is roughly 1 + P(draw)*0.33*(ET intensity factor) — a 5-8% uplift on balanced ties, larger for players who stay on. Tournament data: substitute goalscorers enter later in knockouts (71.9' vs 61.4' in groups) and an additional substitution is permitted in ET (PMC11167463). Exact ET goal-intensity factor needs fitting from cached data (speculative until fit).
methods.apply: Two touch points: (1) in the lambda solver / prop de-vig stage, treat AGS-implied scoring rates as 90-minute rates (document which settlement rule the single book uses); (2) in the match simulator, on a drawn 90' draw, append an ET segment: extend on-pitch players' exposure, allow one more sub draw, keep accruing fantasy events, and re-settle 1X2-dependent outputs correctly. Captain EV and P85 ceilings for knockout fixtures change materially. This is immediately relevant to every remaining WC2026 match.

methods.name: Hierarchical manager/team rotation priors with partial pooling
methods.what: Managers have persistent, measurable substitution and rotation styles. Estimate per-manager parameters (starting-XI churn rate between matches, subs used per match, mean first-sub time, share of minutes to bench) with shrinkage toward league/tournament means (Beta-Binomial / normal hierarchical model, hand-rollable in stdlib), and feed them into the appearance mixture and sub hazards instead of one global rotation assumption.
methods.evidence: Michael Caley (Expecting Goals, top-5-leagues data since 2010-11): 'persistent tendencies' among clubs and managers — Lucien Favre and Sean Dyche flagged as consistently conservative sub users; league-level spread is large (La Liga/Serie A ~10% of minutes to subs vs Premier League ~6-7% historically; PL uses its 5th sub only about one-third of the time), and he argues the differences are cultural rather than tactical, i.e. stable and predictable. FPL Review's xMins docs list 'how securely players own their role' and modeled rotation events as explicit factors. Effect size on projection accuracy is not published anywhere (speculative), but the direction is unambiguous: a global sub-timing prior is wrong by 10-20 minutes across managers.
methods.apply: Offline estimation script over cached lineups/minutes (the stats_rN.json started/DNP event IDs already decoded per memory) produces per-team JSON: churn_rate, subs_per_match, first_sub_mean, bench_minute_share, shrunk toward pool means by sample size. The appearance-mixture module reads these instead of constants. For WC2026 fit on qualifiers + group stage; for FPL/Holdet next season fit on league history where manager identity is stable and the priors get strong.

methods.name: Qualification-scenario dead-rubber rotation model (tournament-aware start probabilities)
methods.what: Before final group rounds (and analogous low-stakes situations), classify each team's stakes state — locked top spot, qualified with seeding live, must-win, eliminated — and apply calibrated rotation shocks to p_start: heavy churn for locked/eliminated teams (veterans rested, backups start), near-zero churn for must-win. The engine can compute stakes states from its own simulated standings, making this almost free to condition on.
methods.evidence: Portugal made 8 changes to their starting XI for their third Euro 2024 group game once qualified (lost 0-2 to Georgia); France rotated most of the team vs Tunisia in 2022 and lost; Yahoo/ESPN coverage of the 2026 format notes head-to-head tiebreakers let teams lock a group or be eliminated after two games, creating MORE dead rubbers than before — a structural feature, not a one-off. No academic study quantifies P(rotation | stakes state) across tournaments (I could not find one — building the calibration table from 2018/2022 WC + Euro 2020/2024 third-round lineup-change counts is original but straightforward work; effect-size table is therefore speculative until built, though single-team datapoints of 8-9 changes bound it as huge).
methods.apply: New pre-processing pass for multi-match rounds: run the engine's existing group simulation to get each team's stakes distribution entering the final round, map stakes state to a churn multiplier on p_start (calibrated offline from cached historical tournament lineups), and let the research overlay override per-team when press conferences confirm intent. Knockout analog: yellow-card-accumulation suspension risk and semifinal-before-final rest. Directly addresses the class of error behind the R2 'blanket X-0 / 11 Spain, 0 France' concentration notes for future rounds and tournaments.

methods.name: Structured news ingestion with per-source reliability weights (replacing freeform overlay multipliers)
methods.what: Convert the markdown research overlay into a structured per-player feed: {status: confirmed_out | doubtful | rested_risk | confirmed_start, source_class, timestamp, trust}, where trust is a per-source-class prior (official team news > trusted beat reporter > aggregator/predicted-XI site), mapped to p_start via a calibrated table instead of the hand-set blend weight w. Optionally an LLM parses press conferences and news into this schema in a separate online step, keeping the engine itself offline-runnable.
methods.evidence: A 2025 IJCSS paper ('Players' Performance Prediction for FPL Using Transformer-based Sentiment Analysis on News and Statistical Data') added transformer-extracted news features from Google News to statistical FPL models and cut MSE from 6.27 to 5.63 — direct quantitative evidence that news features carry projection signal. OpenFPL's authors name 'crowd-sourced minutes forecasts and web-scraping AI agents' as the path to closing the gap to FPL Review, whose own pipeline includes press-conference reviews, hourly refresh and human validation. The user's own audit finding (SportsMole/predicted-XI aggregators unreliable; only confirmed team news should downgrade start-prob) is precisely the per-source-trust structure this formalizes.
methods.apply: Replaces the soft-multiplier half of the research overlay (hard facts stay absolute). Overlay files become structured entries; a small mapping table converts (status, trust, hours-to-kickoff) into p_start adjustments with calibration measured on past rounds (did 'doubtful from aggregator' actually predict DNP?). The blend weight w disappears in favor of per-source-class calibrated weights. The online collection step writes cached JSON so reproducibility is preserved.

methods.name: Two-stage deadline pipeline: prior projection -> confirmed-XI posterior snap
methods.what: Official team sheets drop ~60-75 minutes before kickoff. Add a re-run mode that ingests confirmed XIs, snaps p_start to 1/0, re-draws bench cameo probabilities, re-normalizes goal/assist shares to team totals, and republishes xPts and captain EV before the fantasy deadline for that match/round. Also log prior-vs-posterior deltas to quantify how much news is worth per round.
methods.evidence: This is how the benchmark systems actually win: Rotowire maintains predicted AND confirmed starting XIs per match with continuous updates; Fantasy Football Scout's core product is deadline-updated predicted lineups; FPL Review documents deadline re-runs and post-match validation. DFS practice universally waits for confirmed team sheets before lock (RotoGrinders lineup lessons). No effect size published, but OpenFPL's Zeros/Blanks gap is the indirect measurement: knowing who actually starts is the single largest error-remover on low scores.
methods.apply: Mostly plumbing on top of the appearance-mixture module: a confirmed_xi_rN.json cache format, a --confirmed flag that overrides p_start and re-runs only the player-simulation stage (lambdas unchanged), and a delta report. For Holdet/FPL where deadlines precede first kickoff this becomes a per-match refresh for later matches in the round where rules allow.

methods.name: Market-implied availability signals from the props already ingested
methods.what: The single book's anytime-goalscorer sheet encodes its own lineup expectations: books reprice or pull player props when lineups leak. Use (a) presence/absence of an AGS quote for squad players, and (b) the deviation of a player's AGS-implied goal probability from his rolling baseline, as a soft rotation-risk signal feeding p_start — an odds-derived early-warning that requires zero new data sources.
methods.evidence: Practitioner-documented: bookmakers 'quickly reprice odds after squad news leaks — Germany's odds were adjusted within hours of team information becoming public' (FanDuel Research, WC2026 coverage), and goalscorer pricing explicitly bakes in 'minutes-played reliability' (betscorenow market guide). SPECULATIVE: no published quantification of AGS-drift as a start-probability predictor, and a single soft book adds noise (limits, slow updates); treat as a weak prior with a small calibrated weight, validated against confirmed XIs over a few rounds before trusting.
methods.apply: In the odds-ingestion stage, snapshot AGS quotes with timestamps (multiple snapshots per match where possible); compute implied-prob drift vs the player's tournament baseline after de-vig; emit flags (quote_missing, sharp_lengthening, sharp_shortening) consumed by the appearance-mixture module as small p_start adjustments. Costs almost nothing since props are already parsed.

methods.name: Team-level minutes conservation (reconciliation constraint)
methods.what: Enforce accounting identities the current independent per-player minutes ignore: exactly 11 players on pitch, total team player-minutes = 11 x (90 + stoppage) (+ET), exactly one GK x full match, bench share ~10% of outfield minutes under the 5-sub rule. After per-player xMins are set, rescale within team/position groups to satisfy the constraints — mirroring the engine's existing goal-share-to-team-total reconciliation.
methods.evidence: Standard practice in NBA DFS, the most mature minutes-projection culture: projections are built and audited against the fixed 240 team-minute budget, and 'minutes are king' models redistribute the budget on injury news (RotoGrinders lessons). Soccer budget analog is exact (11 x match length); the sub-share target is measured: ~10% of minutes to subs in 5-sub leagues vs 6-7% under 3 subs (Caley). Transfer of the reconciliation practice to soccer is my inference (speculative as to accuracy gain), but the constraint itself is arithmetic, and it mechanically catches projection bugs — e.g., two players simultaneously projected full minutes in one slot, the same failure family as the players.json name-collision corruption already hit.
methods.apply: Post-processing pass after the appearance-mixture module (or as a per-sim invariant in the goal-time simulator, where it holds by construction): scale outfield xMins within each team to the 990+stoppage budget with position-group sanity bounds, assert one GK at 90', and emit warnings when pre-reconciliation sums deviate >5% (bug detector). Cheap, pure arithmetic, stdlib.

methods.name: Workload/congestion covariates for start and sub-off probabilities (2026-specific: heat, altitude, travel)
methods.what: Add fatigue-state features to p_start and exit hazards: days since last match, cumulative tournament minutes, age, plus WC2026 venue factors — extreme heat kickoffs, Mexico City/Guadalajara altitude, and long inter-venue travel across North America. High cumulative load + short rest raises rotation and early-hook probability for older starters.
methods.evidence: FPL Review's xMins explicitly derive from 'team news, fixture congestion, and betting odds' (per the OpenFPL paper's description of commercial inputs). The 5-sub rule itself was introduced to manage congestion — Catapult's report documents load/RPE reductions as the rationale, and the WC/Euros substitution study frames sub usage as congestion mitigation (PMC11167463). SPECULATIVE: no public model quantifies heat/altitude/travel effects on tournament rotation; effect sizes would need fitting on this tournament's own group-stage data, and the sample is small — implement as small, capped multipliers.
methods.apply: Feature additions to the appearance-mixture and hazard modules: per-player rest-days and cumulative-minutes counters maintained from cached round stats; per-fixture venue flags (heat index band, altitude, travel km from previous match) in the fixtures cache. Multipliers start hand-capped (e.g. max +/-10% on p_start) and get calibrated as the backtesting harness comes online. Grows in value deep in the tournament and transfers directly to FPL's congestion weeks.

angle_summary: Per-player event-rate modelling sweep across academic literature (JRSS A/C/D, KDD, arXiv 2024-25), practitioner methodology (FPL Review docs, Opta Analyst, StatsBomb, American Soccer Analysis) and open source (OpenFPL, socceraction, soccerdata, AIrsenal). The highest-upside, most-real findings: (1) the engine's proportional de-vig is provably wrong for anytime-goalscorer props — margins run 20-40%+ with documented longshot skew, and Shin-style margin removal plus minutes-deconvolved Poisson inversion is a first-order fix; (2) hierarchical shot-generation-times-conversion priors (McHale-Szczepanski line of work) demonstrably beat naive goal-rates AND bookmaker-implied probabilities (FPL Review measured R2 0.353 vs 0.321), so a fitted prior layer should replace ad-hoc goal-shares and the hand-set blend weight; (3) the new defensive-contribution threshold categories are highly predictable from negative-binomial count models (top players hit thresholds in 55-73% of starts) and should be simulated, not role-estimated; (4) within-match birth-process simulation (Dixon-Robinson) unlocks minute-level scorer/DC allocation and fixes the crude 60+ minutes treatment at the event level; (5) a category-stratified calibration harness (OpenFPL/FPL Review protocol) directly attacks the audited -2.3 xPts bias. All methods respect the stdlib/offline constraint via an offline-fit, cached-coefficients pattern.

methods.name: Shin-style de-vig + coherent minutes-aware inversion of anytime-goalscorer props
methods.what: Replace proportional de-vig on AGS markets with Shin's method (or the power method), which allocates more of the overround to longshots, then invert p_anytime = 1 - exp(-theta_i) where theta_i is the player's full-match expected goals AS PRICED (i.e. including the bookmaker's embedded expected-minutes assumption). Deconvolve: lambda90_i = theta_i / (E[minutes_book]/90), so the engine's own start/sub expectations can be re-applied instead of silently inheriting the book's. Haircut team lambda by the own-goal share (~3-4% of all goals; speculative, measure from cached data) before reconciling the sum of player thetas to team lambda, and allocate the residual to non-priced players.
methods.evidence: Strumbelj (2014, Int. J. Forecasting) showed Shin probabilities beat basic (proportional) normalization and regression approaches across bookmakers/sports (best in 217 of 412 cases); the advantage grows as the number of outcomes rises — AGS markets have 25-40 runners. Goalscorer-market margins are documented at 20-40% (some props >50%) vs 2.5-12% for 1X2, with margin concentrated on longshots (favourite-longshot bias confirmed for UK football betting, Cain/Law/Peel 2000). FPL Review's public comparison found bookmaker AGS-implied goal probabilities carry 'inconsistent margin treatment across scorer markets' and were beaten by their stats model (R2 0.321 vs 0.353, RMSE 0.218 vs 0.213 over 2,021 player-samples) — i.e. raw prop-implied rates are exactly where the engine is most exposed. Speculative: the exact margin skew at the engine's single bookmaker must be measured from its own cached AGS boards (fit Shin z per market and inspect).
methods.apply: At the odds-ingest stage, keep proportional de-vig for 2-way totals/1X2 but switch AGS to Shin (Newton solve for z per market — pure stdlib). At the prop-to-rate stage, replace the current p->rate mapping with the exp-inversion above, using the engine's expected-minutes to deconvolve. In the reconciliation step, subtract the own-goal haircut from team lambda, then scale prior-based players to the residual. Log per-round Shin-z and margin-by-runner diagnostics into the backtest harness to quantify the correction.

methods.name: Hierarchical shot-generation x conversion prior model (McHale-Szczepanski / Whitaker line)
methods.what: Replace static prior goal-shares with a fitted hierarchical Bayesian model that decomposes each player's scoring intensity into shot generation per 90 x conversion, with partial pooling (random effects) over player, position, club, league strength, and a club-vs-international-tournament effect. Outputs shrunk per-90 npxG/goal intensities and assist intensities with posterior variances; the variance drives principled blending with prop-implied rates (inverse-variance weighting), replacing much of the hand-set w in [0.05,0.5].
methods.evidence: McHale & Szczepanski (JRSS-A 2014) showed exactly this decomposition predicts next-season goals better than the naive goals-per-minute rate, attributing the gain to separating ability from chance. Whitaker, Silva & Edwards (JRSS-C 2021) extended Baio-Blangiardo to player-level Poisson event occurrences with variational inference and validated on out-of-sample over/under 2.5 predictions. Practitioner confirmation: FPL Review's 'Massive Data' stats model outperformed bookmaker-odds implications for goalscoring (R2 0.353 vs 0.321), and OpenFPL (arXiv 2508.09992) matched/beat FPL Review on high-return players using ONLY public FPL+Understat data — public per-90 xG data carries enough signal to rival commercial and odds-implied numbers. Directly attacks the engine's weakest players: the many WC squad members with no prop coverage.
methods.apply: Offline fitting script (may use numpy/scipy or hand-coded EM/empirical-Bayes; runs outside the engine) trained on Understat/FBref club per-90s plus StatsBomb open-data internationals; engine consumes a cached JSON of posterior means + variances per player (keyed by fifaId per the collision lesson). This replaces the 'prior goal-shares' input to the reconciliation stage, and the research-overlay w becomes a computed precision weight per player (props-rich players lean on odds, props-poor lean on priors) with the hand-set w kept only as an override.

methods.name: Defensive-contribution simulation via negative-binomial count models coupled to game state
methods.what: Replace the role-shaped midfield defensive-action estimate with per-player simulated counts: tackles+interceptions+blocks+clearances (+recoveries where the table needs them) drawn from a negative binomial with player-specific per-90 mean and dispersion, where the mean is modulated inside each Monte-Carlo sim by opponent possession proxy (from the lambda ratio) and simulated score state (leading teams defend deeper -> more clearances/blocks; the team without the ball accrues defensive actions). Threshold points (e.g. FPL's 10 CBIT for DEF / 12 CBIRT for MID = 2 pts) are then P(X >= T) per sim, which is dispersion-sensitive — a mean-based estimate is structurally wrong near the threshold.
methods.evidence: FPL introduced defensive-contribution points in 2025/26 (premierleague.com), and the category proved highly predictable from prior-season counts: Opta Analyst's preseason analysis showed Tarkowski would have hit 10+ CBIT in 22 matches of 2024/25 (+44 pts, lifting him from joint-26th to 8th among defenders), with start-level hit rates of 73.1% (Huijsen), and for midfielders Caicedo hit 12+ CBIRT in 21 matches (55.3% hit rate), Casemiro 66.7%; early 25/26, three defenders (Tarkowski, Senesi, van den Berg) hit max DC in every game. Interceptions are more tactics/opponent-dependent than tackles (The Football Analyst), motivating the opponent-possession conditioning. Free data: FBref (Opta) publishes all CBIT components per 90. Speculative: exact elasticity of CBIT to possession share must be fitted; no public paper quantifies it.
methods.apply: In the per-player event simulation stage: add cached NB(mu, k) parameters per player (fitted offline from FBref per-90s with position shrinkage); inside each of the 50k sims, scale mu by f(opponent lambda share, simulated score path) and draw counts; score thresholds per the FIFA/FPL/Holdet tables. This directly replaces the 'role-shaped estimate' and is a prerequisite for the FPL port where DC is a live 2-pt category.

methods.name: Category-stratified calibration harness + residual recalibration layer (kill the -2.3 bias)
methods.what: Adopt the OpenFPL/FPL Review evaluation protocol in the new backtesting harness: stratify realized-vs-projected error by return category (zeros / blanks / mid / haulers) and by points component (minutes, goals, assists, CS, DC, SoT, saves), then fit a small per-position recalibration (linear or isotonic) mapping simulated component means to realized component means. This converts the observed ~2.3-pt shortfall vs Rotowire from a mystery into an attributed, corrected decomposition — and guards against over-correcting toward a possibly-miscalibrated third party.
methods.evidence: OpenFPL (arXiv 2508.09992) established the reference protocol: RMSE stratified into Haulers/Tickers/Blanks/Zeros, where it beat FPL Review's commercial model on high-return players (RMSE 5.142 vs 5.172; up to 5% better) while losing on zeros/blanks where proprietary expected-minutes data dominates — evidence that (a) stratified evaluation localizes model weaknesses and (b) minutes drive the low-end error. Its second key finding: directly regressing points outperformed intermediate event-decomposition models, which argues for a learned residual correction ON TOP of a simulation engine rather than trusting raw sim sums. FPL Review's 'Ultimate Truth' study shows top models sit at RMSE ~2.80 vs a simulated perfect-model ceiling of ~2.7-2.9 (R2 ~0.15) — so calibration, not exotic new signal, is where remaining bias lives.
methods.apply: Extend the in-progress backtest harness: for each completed round, store per-player simulated component means and realized official-table components (Holdet stats event IDs already decoded per memory); fit per-position additive/multiplicative corrections offline and cache them; apply as a final post-scoring adjustment with a flag to disable. Report stratified RMSE/MAE per round so regressions are visible immediately.

methods.name: Within-match time-inhomogeneous goal process with minute-level scorer allocation (Dixon-Robinson)
methods.what: Upgrade the Monte-Carlo from drawing final scorelines to simulating goal TIMES from interacting birth processes whose intensities ramp up over the match and depend on the current score (Dixon-Robinson), then allocate each goal to the players actually on the pitch at that minute (starters until a sub-off hazard, subs after sub-on). Player scoring/assist/SoT/DC intensities become per-minute rates integrated over their simulated on-pitch window, replacing the 'starters treated as 60+ mins' shortcut at the event-allocation level and correctly valuing supersubs and late-game accumulation.
methods.evidence: Dixon & Robinson (JRSS-D 1998), fitted on 4,000+ English matches, found clear evidence scoring rates increase over the course of the match and shift with the current score — i.e. uniform-in-time goal allocation is empirically wrong (a disproportionate share of goals arrive after minute 60, when subs are on). The birth-process form is the standard in-play pricing model used by spread-betting practitioners. Fantasy relevance: OpenFPL/FPL Review both show expected minutes is THE dominant driver of low-return error, and minute-level allocation is the mechanism that couples any improved minutes model to event rates. Speculative: the size of the xPts gain for this engine specifically is untested, but the current 60+ treatment plus late-goal clustering means sub-heavy WC squads (rotation at 48 teams) are systematically mis-rated.
methods.apply: Replace the Dixon-Coles scoreline draw inside each sim with sequential goal-time generation (piecewise-constant intensity calibrated so match-level totals still match the solved lambdas and DC correlation — keep the DC low-score adjustment as a dependence tweak on early segments). Per-player: draw sub-off/sub-on times from simple hazard tables (cached), maintain the on-pitch set per minute, and allocate goals/assists/SoT by per-minute shares. Downstream scoring (appearance thresholds, 60-min bonuses) reads simulated minutes directly.

methods.name: Explicit penalty and set-piece decomposition with taker registry
methods.what: Split each team's solved lambda into components: penalties, direct free kicks, corner/indirect set-piece goals, and open play. Penalties: team pen-award rate x P(taker on pitch) x ~0.76-0.78 conversion assigned to a cached taker hierarchy; corner goals allocated by aerial-threat shares (boosting CBs/target men); only the残 open-play pool is then divided by the goal-share priors. Prevents double-counting pens inside AGS-implied rates (bookmakers price takers' pen equity in) when blending props with priors.
methods.evidence: Magnitude is large and rising: WC2018 saw a record 29 in-game penalties awarded, 22 scored (~0.45/match, VAR-driven — conversion 76%); EPL 2025/26 produced 269 non-penalty dead-ball goals, +25% YoY and +43% vs five years prior, with Arsenal scoring ~35% of league goals from set pieces — set-piece share of total goals is now roughly a quarter to a third for strong set-piece teams. For a designated taker, ~0.23 pens/team-match x 0.77 adds ~0.18 xG/start — often the difference in captain EV rankings. Practitioner adoption: FPL Review explicitly lists 'penalty responsibilities' among its model's contextual features; RotoWire and Covers publish full 2026 WC set-piece/penalty taker lists per team (cacheable). Speculative: corner-goal allocation shares by player require event-data fitting (StatsBomb open data headers/set-piece xG) rather than a published table.
methods.apply: New cached registry file (taker hierarchies per team, source: RotoWire/Covers lists + research overlay corrections) and a decomposition step between the lambda solve and player allocation: lambda_team = lambda_pen + lambda_sp + lambda_open. Pen goals simulated as separate Bernoulli(award) x Bernoulli(convert | taker on pitch) events inside each sim so cards/misses/saves stay coherent; set-piece pool allocated by aerial shares fitted offline from StatsBomb open data.

methods.name: Coherent shots -> SoT -> goals hierarchical chain with shrunk finishing
methods.what: Simulate each player's attacking events as a chain: shot count (negative binomial per-90, opponent-scaled) -> shots on target (beta-binomial accuracy) -> goals (shrunk conversion / post-shot xG), reconciled so player goals still sum to team goals. Guarantees internal coherence (no goal without a SoT; SoT and goals correlated), which matters because Holdet pays per SoT (event 558) and saves must equal opponents' non-goal SoT. Finishing skill enters only as a heavily-shrunk conversion multiplier.
