methods.evidence: American Soccer Analysis's Replication Project: G-minus-xG is poorly self-predictive season-over-season — the signal is in shot/xG VOLUME, so conversion must be shrunk hard toward position means. Davis et al. (arXiv 2401.09940) show standard xG models systematically understate elite finishers (Messi's goals-above-expected underestimated by ~17%), i.e. small positive finishing adjustments for proven elite finishers are justified but only for extreme cases. StatsBomb's post-shot xG work ('Quantifying Finishing Skill') is the practitioner standard for separating shot placement from chance quality. New: Pipping-Gamon et al. (arXiv 2512.00203) show possession-level joint modelling of shot occurrence + quality yields MORE persistent player skill signals than shot-only xG — supporting the count-then-quality decomposition. McHale-Szczepanski's predictive gain also came precisely from this decomposition.
methods.apply: In the per-player event sim, replace independent goals/SoT draws with the chained draw (NB shots -> binomial SoT -> binomial goals), with a final reconciliation pass thinning/boosting to match the simulated team scoreline. Parameters (shot/90, accuracy, conversion with shrinkage constants) fitted offline from Understat/FBref and cached. Also fixes the saves channel: opposing GK saves = sum of opponent SoT minus goals within the same sim.

methods.name: xT/VAEP-based creation rates for assist shares and involvement priors
methods.what: Compute possession-value metrics — xT (Karun Singh grid model) and/or VAEP (Decroos et al.) — per player from free event data using the open-source socceraction library, and use per-90 creation value (pass-based xT, xA, VAEP-offense) as the prior for assist shares and any 'goal involvement'-type fantasy categories, replacing ad-hoc assist priors derived from raw assists.
methods.evidence: VAEP (KDD 2019, 'Actions Speak Louder than Goals') values all on-ball actions by their effect on scoring probability and is fully implemented in socceraction (supports StatsBomb/Wyscout/Opta feeds, including the FREE public Wyscout dataset via PublicWyscoutLoader). xT was introduced by Karun Singh (2018) and is now industry-standard for possession value (Hudl/Statsbomb ecosystem); a KU Leuven working paper critically compares xT and VAEP for player rating. On predictiveness: Opta/Stats Perform document that xA is a more stable predictor of future assists than raw assists, since it strips receiver finishing noise. Speculative: no public benchmark quantifies xT->fantasy-assist-points lift specifically; the mechanism (assists are goal-dependent and finisher-noisy, so upstream creation volume is the stabler prior) is well supported but the effect size on this engine must come from its own backtest.
methods.apply: Offline pipeline: socceraction over StatsBomb open data (WC2018/WC2022, Euros) + public Wyscout (WC2018, big-5 2017/18) + Understat xA for current club form -> cached per-90 creation values per squad player. In the engine, assist-share priors and the assists-per-goal allocation draw from these values (reconciled so assists <= goals per sim); the research overlay's soft form multipliers can then act on a defensible base instead of raw assist counts.

methods.name: ToS-clean free data layer: StatsBomb open data + public Wyscout + FBref/Understat via rate-limited cached scrapes
methods.what: A one-time-fetch, cache-forever ingestion layer covering: StatsBomb open data (full event + lineup JSON for WC2018, WC2022, Euros and more; free with attribution requirement), the Pappalardo/Wyscout public dataset (all events for 7 competitions incl. WC2018, CC BY 4.0 on figshare), FBref (Opta-sourced per-90 CBIT/xG/xA tables; limited scraping tolerated with rate limits), Understat (shot-level xG for big-5 leagues since 2014), and football-data.co.uk odds CSVs — all via the maintained soccerdata package or thin stdlib scrapers writing to the engine's cached-data directory.
methods.evidence: StatsBomb open-data licence: free for research/genuine football-analytics interest, mandatory attribution + logo, no auth needed; the WC2022 release was announced publicly. Wyscout public dataset is peer-reviewed (Pappalardo et al., Nature Scientific Data 6:236, 2019) and explicitly CC BY 4.0 — the safest large event corpus. soccerdata (probberechts) implements caching and per-request pauses specifically because FBref rate-limits and temp-bans aggressive scrapers; it also wraps Understat and Sofascore (note: Sofascore/WhoScored scraping is ToS-grey — flag before relying on it). OpenFPL is existence proof that FPL+Understat public data alone reaches commercial-grade accuracy on high-return players.
methods.apply: New fetch scripts outside the runtime engine (network allowed at build time only), writing normalized JSON keyed by fifaId (per the players.json collision lesson) into the cached-data tree; the engine stays offline-runnable. This layer is the prerequisite feeding methods on hierarchical priors, DC counts, shot chains, set-piece shares and xT/VAEP — build it first.

angle_summary: Correlation/joint-simulation sweep for the wc2026/evmax engine. The literature and practice split into four families: (a) STRUCTURAL simulation that generates correlation as a by-product of simulating the game itself (SaberSim's play-by-play sims; Dixon-Robinson minute-level birth processes) — the gold standard because correlations are 'baked in' rather than imposed; (b) PARAMETRIC dependence — copulas and bivariate Poisson over team goals (Boshnakov/Kharrat/McHale Frank copula beat Dixon-Coles with positive betting returns; Karlis-Ntzoufras common-shock; Mar-Co), and Gaussian copulas over player outcomes as used by sportsbooks to price same-game parlays; (c) PORTFOLIO/GAME-THEORY layers that CONSUME joint sims — Hunter-Vielma-Zaman's stacking + variance IP (top-10 finishes in thousand-entry contests), Mlčoch-Hubáček's mean-variance-covariance MIQP (34% ROI live), Haugh-Singal's Dirichlet-multinomial opponent field model (Management Science, real-money NFL validation) — all showing the edge from correlation is realized at the LINEUP/CAPTAIN decision layer, not in per-player means; (d) CALIBRATION of tails — quantile coverage/PIT/CRPS discipline plus market-implied joint prices (SGP/scorecast) as ground truth for dependence. Key insight for THIS engine: conditioning player events on simulated team goals already gives first-order within-team correlation, so the highest-leverage gaps are (1) scorer-assister jointness per goal, (2) a joint minutes model with substitution coupling (also the likeliest culprit for the -2.3 xPts audit gap alongside the 60+ minutes crudeness), (3) market-calibrated team-goal dependence, and (4) actually using the 50k joint draws for lineup/captain/rank decisions instead of collapsing to xPts means. Per-player mean accuracy is mostly untouched by correlation work — its payoff shows up in P85/ceiling accuracy, captain EV, and contest rank EV, so the coverage-backtest harness (method 9) is the enabling investment that proves the rest.

methods.name: Joint scorer-assister assignment per simulated goal
methods.what: Replace independent assist simulation with a per-goal joint draw: for each simulated team goal, draw scorer from goal-share multinomial, then assister from an assist-share distribution conditioned on the scorer (self-assist excluded, explicit 'unassisted' outcome ~25-35% of goals, optional pair-chemistry weights for known combos e.g. wing-striker). Produces exact within-team goal-assist correlation and hard accounting constraints (assists <= goals, no self-assist) that independent draws violate.
methods.evidence: Architecture precedent: AIrsenal (Alan Turing Institute) predicts 'player goal involvements' conditional on team scoreline — same conditional structure. Market evidence that scorer/teammate/result dependencies are real and priced: sportsbooks price same-game parlays with correlation matrices and Gaussian copulas (shutterb.org; Wizard of Odds SGP mathematics article; LSports on prop-vs-total correlation risk). DFS evidence: PFF reports QB performance positively correlated with EVERY same-team skill position and that 17.4% of high-stakes lineups still ignored stacking; SaberSim's whole pitch is that correlations must emerge from the sim, not be layered on. Soccer-specific goal-assist correlation magnitudes: not published openly (RotoViz matrix is paywalled, NFL-based) — SPECULATIVE, estimate from your own cached Holdet/FPL event data (stats_rN.json has goal/assist event types already decoded).
methods.apply: Stage: per-player event simulation. Keep team-goal conditioning as is; replace the independent assist draw with the conditional (scorer, assister) categorical draw per goal event. Assist shares already exist as priors; add a scorer-exclusion renormalization plus an unassisted-goal probability calibrated from tournament data. Per-player marginal xPts barely move; joint outputs (lineup P85, captain-vs-stack EV, Holdet pair values) become correct.

methods.name: Minute-level match simulation (Dixon-Robinson birth process)
methods.what: Replace scoreline-level sampling with an event-time simulation: goals arrive via two interacting inhomogeneous Poisson processes whose intensities rise over the match and depend on current score (trailing teams attack more) and time remaining. Each 50k-sim then has goal TIMES, enabling: clean-sheet credit for players subbed off before a late goal, goals-while-on-pitch exposure, red-card and game-state effects, late-goal clustering, and correlated defensive-action volume by game state.
methods.evidence: Dixon & Robinson (JRSS-D 1998) fitted 4000+ English matches: clear evidence scoring rate increases over the match and is influenced by current score; model built for in-play/spread markets and remains the canonical reference. Soccermetrics discussion confirms score-state multipliers and time profile. Newer treatment: 'Stochastic modelling of football matches' (arXiv 2312.04338) and market-calibrated in-play AFT models (arXiv 2605.16066) show the approach is current practice in betting quant work. Direct fantasy-accuracy effect size: not published — SPECULATIVE, but it structurally fixes the known CS-vs-substitution and minutes-exposure biases.
methods.apply: Stage: replaces Dixon-Coles scoreline sampling + flat per-match player sim. Keep the odds-implied (lambda_h, lambda_a) solve as the aggregate constraint; distribute intensity over minutes with the DR time profile and score-state multipliers, renormalized so the aggregate scoreline distribution still matches implied 1X2/totals (important: calibration constraint, or you silently drift from the market). Player events then attach only to minutes the player is on pitch (couples with the minutes model). Pure-stdlib feasible: it is just thinning/inversion sampling.

methods.name: Hierarchical joint minutes model with substitution coupling
methods.what: Replace 'starters get 60+' with a per-player stochastic minutes model sampled JOINTLY per sim: P(start) x sub-off hazard for starters, P(sub-on) x entry-time distribution for bench, with team-level constraints (11 on pitch, sub windows, positional replacement matrix) so backup minutes are structurally negatively correlated with starter minutes. Each sim yields a coherent team minutes vector; all rate-based events scale by simulated minutes and CS points follow the >=60 rule per sim.
methods.evidence: FPL Review — the commercial state of the art the audit implicitly benchmarks against via Rotowire-class services — defines xMins as 'the average game-time a player would receive if a match were played out 1,000 times' with rotation-event modeling and role-security decay (docs.fplreview.com). OpenFPL (arXiv 2508.09992) shows open-source position-specific models can rival FPL Review accuracy, and treats minutes as first-class. Attribution of your -2.3 xPts audit gap partly to the crude 60+ rule is SPECULATIVE but mechanically plausible: flat 60+ understates star starters' ~85-90 expected minutes, deflating goal/assist/appearance expectations exactly in the direction observed.
methods.apply: Stage: per-player event simulation, upstream of event draws. Estimate start probs from your realized-minutes priors (core/realized.py already exists for Holdet) plus research-overlay hard facts; sub-off hazards by position archetype from cached tournament data. Per sim: draw lineup state, then minutes, then scale player event rates by minutes-on-pitch and evaluate CS eligibility. This is the single biggest mean-accuracy fix available and is a prerequisite for method 2's full value.

methods.name: Market-calibrated copula/bivariate dependence between team goals
methods.what: Replace the single Dixon-Coles low-score tau with an explicit dependence parameter: either a Frank/Gaussian copula joining the two marginal goal counts, or a Karlis-Ntzoufras common-shock bivariate Poisson (G_home = X_h + X_c, G_away = X_a + X_c). Solve (lambda_h, lambda_a, theta) jointly so the scoreline distribution reproduces the book's 1X2 AND totals simultaneously — with fixed tau these two markets are generally not exactly co-satisfiable, and the residual lands in draw/clean-sheet probabilities.
methods.evidence: Boshnakov, Kharrat & McHale (Int. J. Forecasting 2017): Weibull-count marginals joined by a Frank copula beat Dixon-Coles in- and out-of-sample, with calibration curves and POSITIVE Kelly returns on win/draw/loss and over/under 2.5 markets. Karlis & Ntzoufras (JRSS-D 2003): even a small dependence parameter materially improves draw prediction. Mar-Co model (arXiv 2103.07272) outperforms Dixon-Coles in several betting scenarios. Open-source reference implementation: penaltyblog's Cython bivariate Poisson (port to stdlib is straightforward).
methods.apply: Stage: lambda solve + scoreline distribution. Extend the 2-parameter solver to 3 parameters (lambda_h, lambda_a, theta) fitted to de-vigged 1X2 + totals (and BTTS when the book lists it free — BTTS is the single most theta-informative market). Downstream Monte Carlo just samples the new joint pmf; everything else unchanged. Matters most for Malspillet scoreline picks, clean-sheet probabilities, and knockout draw probabilities.

methods.name: Simulation-consuming lineup portfolio optimizer (stacking + variance + covariance)
methods.what: Stop collapsing the 50k joint sims to per-player means for team selection. Persist the players-x-sims points matrix; evaluate any candidate lineup's FULL distribution by summing member rows per sim (matches are independent, so within-match correlation is preserved and cross-match convolution is free). Optimize for the contest objective: P(top-k) or expected payout, via Hunter-Vielma-Zaman-style constraints (max mean s.t. variance lower bound + stacking constraints + max-overlap across multiple entries) or Mlcoch-Hubacek MIQP on mean + variance + covariance, or plain greedy/swap hill-climbing scored directly on sims (pure-stdlib friendly).
methods.evidence: Hunter, Vielma & Zaman (arXiv 1604.01455): submodular P(at least one entry wins) objective + stacking/variance constraints produced multiple top-10 finishes in hockey/baseball contests with thousands of entries; documents strong positive same-team fantasy-point correlation as the mechanism. Mlcoch & Hubacek (Int. Trans. in Op. Research 2024): generative-model point distributions + MIQP over mean/variance/covariance earned EUR 2,439 profit on EUR 7,133 (34% ROI) over 8 live weeks. Commercial validation: SaberSim and Stokastic both rank lineups by first-place frequency across tens of thousands of contest sims rather than by mean points.
methods.apply: Stage: new post-scoring module. Serialize per-sim player point vectors (int16 array per match is ~players x 50k x 2 bytes — cacheable, reproducible offline). Lineup EV/quantiles = row sums. Directly implements your memory-noted 'blowout coverage' rule as an emergent property (covering the biggest-lambda fixture maximizes lineup ceiling), replaces hand rules. Also the substrate for methods 6 and 7.

methods.name: Opponent-field model + rank objective (Haugh-Singal Dirichlet-multinomial)
methods.what: Model the FIELD's team selections as a Dirichlet-multinomial over players (parameterized from published ownership percentages, captain shares where visible), sample opponent portfolios, and pick your squad/captain to maximize P(finishing above rank X) instead of expected points. Your score and the field's score are computed on the SAME match sims, so the you-vs-field correlation (the quantity that actually drives rank movement) is captured automatically — owning the chalk player hedges, fading him is leverage.
methods.evidence: Haugh & Singal, 'How to Play Fantasy Sports Strategically (and Win)', Management Science 67(1) 2021: Dirichlet-regression opponent model + mean-variance optimization WITH opponent-portfolio correlation; real-money 2017 NFL DFS experiments show the opponent-aware strategy substantially outperforms points-maximization benchmarks, with the edge largest in top-heavy contests; framework also quantifies value of insider info. FPL practitioner corroboration: effective-ownership (EO) analytics are the standard rank-management tool; one practitioner analysis claims the captain multiplier alone is ~15-20% of score variance among similar squads (SPECULATIVE, community figure, not peer-reviewed).
methods.apply: Stage: new module consuming method 5's sim matrix + scraped ownership (FIFA fantasy publishes ownership; Holdet popularity is scrapeable). Start simple: independent Bernoulli field sampling from ownership + captain shares (days of work), upgrade to Dirichlet regression later. Directly fills the engine's admitted 'no ownership/rank game theory' hole and formalizes the R32 'contrarian YOLO build' as a solvable optimization.

methods.name: Captaincy as a distributional option (per-sim captain evaluation)
methods.what: Choose captain on the joint distribution, not 2x mean xPts: for each candidate, form lineup-with-doubled-player per sim and compare full distributions — P85 lineup points, P(beat rival captain choice), rank-EV under effective ownership. Captures two effects means miss: (a) right-tail leverage — the best captain is the highest-covariance-with-your-stack, highest-ceiling player, not highest-mean; (b) EO hedging — doubling the chalk is insurance, doubling a differential is a rank option.
methods.evidence: Stokastic's showdown methodology: rank captain-vs-flex assignments by first-place frequency across tens of thousands of contest sims, explicitly advising highest-CEILING (not highest-mean) at captain because the multiplier magnifies the tail; their boom/bust tooling is built on 25th/75th-percentile ranges. Mechanically implied by the Hunter-Vielma-Zaman objective (multiplier slots increase lineup variance, which the top-heavy objective rewards). Rigorous academic treatment of fantasy captaincy specifically: none found — evidence is practitioner-grade, effect direction robust, magnitude SPECULATIVE.
methods.apply: Stage: outputs. Replace 'captain EV = 2 x xPts' with per-sim evaluation over the stored sim matrix (method 5's substrate; near-zero extra compute). Report per candidate: mean, P85, P(best captain among candidates), and EO-adjusted rank delta when ownership is loaded. Days of work once sims are persisted.

methods.name: Parameter-uncertainty and overdispersion layering (mixture-of-lambdas sims)
methods.what: Current sims treat the solved (lambda_h, lambda_a) and player rates as exact, so 50k draws only capture Poisson noise and systematically understate tails (P85 too low, busts and blowups too rare). Fix: per sim, first draw parameters from an uncertainty distribution — Gamma mixing on team lambdas (giving negative-binomial-like overdispersed margins), Beta on start/appearance probabilities, Dirichlet on goal/assist shares — then run the event sim. Means are preserved; variance and joint tails widen honestly.
methods.evidence: Standard probabilistic-forecasting doctrine: predictive distributions must integrate over parameter uncertainty, and miscalibration shows up as quantile-coverage failure (AWS quantile-coverage definitions; Fantasy Projection Lab's benchmarking guidance that floor/ceiling accuracy is a separate skill from mean accuracy). Boshnakov et al. validate football models with calibration curves — the same test this method targets. Count-mixture overdispersion is standard in sports statistics. Direct published effect size on fantasy P85 accuracy: none found — SPECULATIVE until measured with method 9; the sign of the bias (independent point-parameter sims are overconfident) is not in doubt.
methods.apply: Stage: Monte Carlo loop, one extra draw layer before each sim. Set mixing spreads from observable proxies: odds-vs-solve residuals across the 1X2/totals margins, line-move history in your cached snapshots, prior-strength counts on player shares. Pure stdlib (random.gammavariate/betavariate). Directly targets the ceiling/P85 output the engine already ships.

methods.name: Joint-calibration backtest harness (quantile coverage, PIT, pair-event frequencies)
methods.what: Extend the nascent backtesting harness from mean-error audits to DISTRIBUTIONAL and JOINT audits: (a) per-round quantile coverage — 85% of realized player/lineup scores should fall below predicted P85 (pool rounds for power); (b) PIT/CRPS on team goals and player points to tune dispersion and copula parameters; (c) the correlation-specific test almost nobody runs: predicted vs realized frequency of PAIR events (both attackers of a stack returning, GK+2 DEF clean-sheet combos, scorer+assister same play) — the direct measurement of whether the joint sim beats an independence baseline.
methods.evidence: Coverage/PIT/CRPS is the standard evaluation stack for probabilistic forecasts (AWS Forecast docs define quantile coverage exactly; Fantasy Projection Lab documents fantasy-specific backtest protocol — snapshot projections at lineup lock, score against the exact fantasy table, evaluate floor/ceiling separately). Boshnakov et al. use calibration curves as their headline model-comparison evidence. Public benchmarks for JOINT fantasy calibration do not exist — building one is novel practice (SPECULATIVE payoff, but it is the only way to prove methods 1,2,4,8 and to re-run the Rotowire-gap audit distributionally).
methods.apply: Stage: backtest harness (already in progress) — log predicted quantiles and the full per-sim matrix at prediction time (engine is already reproducible/offline, so this is just persistence); after each round, join with cached Holdet stats_rN.json / FIFA results and emit coverage + pair-event report. Fit theta (method 4) and mixing spreads (method 8) by minimizing CRPS on past rounds.

methods.name: Market-implied joint calibration from combo prices (scorecast/wincast/BTTS/SGP)
methods.what: Use the one book you already scrape as ground truth for DEPENDENCE, not just marginals: combo markets — scorecast (player scores + exact score), wincast (player scores + team wins), BTTS, team-total doubles, SGP builder quotes — embed the book's own correlation model. De-vig them, invert for implied joint probabilities, and tune the engine's dependence knobs (scorer-result linkage, theta from method 4, assist-goal jointness) so simulated joint frequencies reproduce the implied joints, exactly as the lambda solve already does for 1X2/totals.
methods.evidence: Sportsbooks price SGPs with correlation matrices, Gaussian copulas, and empirical-frequency hybrids (shutterb.org technical writeup; Wizard of Odds 'Same-Game Parlays: The Mathematics of Correlation'; LSports on player-prop vs team-total correlation risk). The same construction is priced 20-40% apart across books because correlation models differ (practitioner claim) — meaning combo prices are informative about dependence, and also noisy: single-book calibration inherits that book's correlation model plus its typically larger combo vig (LIMITATION, flag in de-vig). Effect size on fantasy accuracy: SPECULATIVE, but it converts the engine's most hand-wavy quantities into market-anchored ones using infrastructure you already have.
methods.apply: Stage: odds ingestion + a new calibration step between the lambda solve and player sim. Scrape wincast/scorecast/BTTS for a subset of star players per match (coverage at World Cups is good); add a dependence-residual term to the existing solver's objective. Works with the single-bookmaker constraint — no new data vendor.

methods.name: Empirical joint resampling benchmark (ffsimulator-style team-block bootstrap)
methods.what: Build the cheap non-parametric competitor to the structural sim: resample entire historical team-match blocks of player fantasy-point vectors (drawing a whole team's realized round as one block preserves empirical within-team correlation exactly — goal+assist pairs, CS cascades, blowout clustering), rescale blocks to current match lambdas/xPts. Use it as (a) a correlation-structure sanity check on the structural sim and (b) a fallback joint sampler for markets where the structural model is weakest.
methods.evidence: ffsimulator (ffverse, CRAN) does precisely this for NFL fantasy: bootstrap resampling of week-level nflfastR scoring populations to simulate seasons, widely used in the fantasy R community; its design rationale is that empirical joint resampling captures correlation without any parametric model. Applicability to soccer with small tournament samples is the weak point — needs pooling across seasons/leagues (SPECULATIVE how well WC-specific structure survives pooling).
methods.apply: Stage: validation harness (pairs with method 9). You already cache per-round Holdet stats (stats_rN.json event IDs decoded) — build the block library from those plus historical FPL/club data for the Holdet/FPL expansions. Compare pair-event frequencies: structural sim vs bootstrap vs independence.

methods.name: Gaussian copula over player marginals (fallback joint sampler)
methods.what: If the structural upgrades (methods 1-3) stall or for sports/markets without a team-goal backbone: keep each player's marginal points distribution from the current engine, and induce dependence at the sampling layer via a Gaussian copula with a position-archetype correlation matrix (same-team attacker pairs +, GK-DEF within team strongly + via CS, attacker vs opposing defender/GK -, estimated per pair-type from historical fantasy data). Draw correlated normals -> uniforms -> invert each marginal CDF per sim.
methods.evidence: This is the sportsbook-standard construction for pricing correlated player props/SGPs (Gaussian copulas + correlation matrices per shutterb.org and Wizard of Odds). DFS industry equivalents: FantasyLabs/optimizer 'correlation settings' impose pairwise correlation on static projections; PFF documents positive same-team skill-position correlation as the stacking rationale. Known weakness acknowledged by SaberSim's critique: copulas over static marginals are 'guesses layered on guesses' vs structural sims — and for THIS engine the copula breaks exact team-goal reconciliation (player goals no longer sum to simulated team goals), so it is strictly a fallback or a layer for outcomes OUTSIDE the goal chain (cards, saves, defensive actions). Correlation magnitudes for soccer fantasy: not publicly published — estimate from own data (SPECULATIVE).
methods.apply: Stage: per-player simulation sampling layer. Pure stdlib: Cholesky on a small per-match correlation matrix (~30 players), random.gauss draws, empirical-CDF inversion against the engine's existing marginal distributions. Best first use: correlate the non-goal event streams (defensive actions, saves, cards) with game state, which the goal-chain conditioning currently leaves independent.

angle_summary: Squad optimization + rank game theory for the wc2026/evmax engine. Today the engine stops at per-player xPts/P85/captain EV and a human picks the squad; every serious competitor (FPL solver community, DFS pros, and Management Science-grade research) closes the loop with (a) exact MILP squad/transfer/chip optimization, (b) multi-round planning weighted by tournament-advancement probability, and (c) ownership-aware rank objectives — maximizing P(high rank), not E[points]. The single biggest structural unlock is nearly free: the engine already runs 50k Monte-Carlo worlds with player-level events, which is exactly the joint scenario matrix that DFS papers (Hunter/Vielma/Zaman; Haugh/Singal) had to approximate with Gaussian copulas — persist it, align sim indices across a round's matches, and every downstream method (portfolio variance, field simulation, P(rank) optimization, chip option value, mini-league match-racing) becomes a sum over columns. Evidence quality varies by layer: MILP squad/transfer optimization has strong replicated practice evidence (sertalpbilal's open toolkit, FPL Review, Bonomo et al. reported ~top 0.2% in Gran DT, Matthews et al. ~top 1% of 2.5M in FPL); ownership-aware rank play has rigorous evidence in adjacent formats (Haugh-Singal MS 2021 real-money DFS; Clair-Letscher OR 2007 pools outperforming max-score strategies by orders of magnitude) but its transfer to classic fantasy is quantitatively speculative and marked as such. Note on the impact ratings: these methods mostly do NOT improve projection accuracy (xPts stays the same) — impact is rated on realized outcomes (points captured and final rank), which is the stated goal of this domain; the two exceptions that touch scoring realism are bench/autosub valuation and advancement-weighted horizons.

methods.name: Joint scenario matrix export (common random numbers across a round)
methods.what: Turn the engine's existing 50k per-match sims into 50k round-level 'worlds': use a shared sim index (or shared RNG seed schedule) across all matches in a round, and persist the per-sim, per-player fantasy-point vectors as a players x 50k integer matrix per round. Any squad's full score distribution, variance, covariance with any other squad, and rank statistics then become exact column sums over the matrix — with all player correlation (shared team goals, clean-sheet coupling) preserved for free.
methods.evidence: This is the substrate every rank-aware system runs on. Hunter/Vielma/Zaman (arXiv 1604.01455) and Haugh/Singal (Management Science 67(1) 2021) both needed joint player-score distributions and had to APPROXIMATE them with jointly-Gaussian/copula models because they lacked a simulator; this engine already has the simulator, which is strictly better. Commercial DFS tools (SaberSim) explicitly build both lineups and ownership from play-by-play simulations of full slates. No standalone benchmark — it is an enabler, and rated high because methods 2-11 all consume it (marked: enabler, not a direct accuracy gain).
methods.apply: Modify the per-player event-simulation stage: instead of aggregating to means (xPts/P85) and discarding draws, write scenarios_rN (gzip'd struct/array binary, pure stdlib) of per-sim points per player, with sim index i meaning 'world i' across all fixtures in round N. Keep the existing outputs unchanged — this is additive. Also store per-world team results (scorelines) so advancement simulation (method 3) can reuse the same worlds. ~50k x 400 players x 2 bytes ≈ 40MB/round, fine for cached offline runs.

methods.name: MILP squad/captain/bench optimizer with per-game constraint packs
methods.what: Exact optimization of the 15-man squad, starting XI, captain, and bench order maximizing xPts subject to budget, formation, max-N-per-country/club, and transfer costs — replacing eyeballing the xPts table. Constraint packs per game: FIFA WC 2026 (100m budget, +5m at knockouts, 3-per-nation, 1 free transfer carried, -3/extra), Holdet (1% trade fee on purchase price, limited 'contracts' per game on Basic teams, free captain change, captain value-growth bonus), FPL later (1FT, -4 hits, 3-per-club).
methods.evidence: The most replicated result in the field. sertalpbilal's open-source FPL-Optimization-Tools (MILP via HiGHS, multi_period.py) is the de-facto community standard with a full tutorial series; FPL Review ran a commercial MILP planner (docs still live); Bonomo/Duran/Marenco (ITOR 2014) built MILP 'virtual coaches' for Argentina's Gran DT — secondary summaries report it placing ~top 0.2%; a 2025/26 arXiv framework (2505.02170) formulates squad+chips+rolling transfers as deterministic and robust MILPs; Matthews/Ramchurn/Chalkiadakis (AAAI 2012) framed FPL as multi-dimensional knapsack inside an MDP and reached ~top percentile of 2.5M managers (secondary reports: best variant ~top 500). Gains come from decision quality, not projections.
methods.apply: New module (e.g. optimize/squad.py) consuming the existing per-player output table. Pure-stdlib constraint: don't hand-roll simplex — implement DP-knapsack-plus-local-search (greedy build, then 1-swap/2-swap hill climb with random restarts; AIrsenal similarly ships a heuristic optimizer), and add an OPTIONAL HiGHS/CBC subprocess backend when installed, asserting the heuristic matches on small instances. Deterministic seed keeps it reproducible/offline. This becomes the chassis methods 3, 4, 6, 9, 10 plug into.

methods.name: Advancement-weighted multi-round transfer planning (rolling horizon + decay)
methods.what: Plan transfers over the remaining tournament, not one round: a player's future value in round r = xPts_r x P(his team is still alive and playing in round r). Get alive-probabilities from a tournament-progression Monte Carlo that chains the engine's own Dixon-Coles scoreline distributions through group standings (with tie-breakers) and the knockout bracket. Optimize the transfer sequence with a rolling-horizon objective with exponential decay, respecting WC 2026 boundary rules (unlimited transfers into R32 so plans should NOT hoard value across that boundary; no wildcard in R32).
methods.evidence: sertalpbilal's multi-period solver uses exactly this decayed multi-week objective (decay_base default 0.84) and is standard practice among top FPL solver users; the 2505.02170 framework implements multi-week rolling-horizon transfer planning + dynamic captaincy; an NTNU forecast-based optimization thesis backtested 35 gameweeks of 2017/18 against real participants; Bergman & Imbrogno (Operations Research 65(5) 2017, NFL survivor pools) found planning PARTWAY ahead yields the highest win probabilities and dominated millions of randomly generated strategies — direct evidence that horizon choice itself is a first-order decision. Advancement-weighting specifically is standard WC-fantasy practice (guides plan around the group->KO unlimited-transfer boundary); its point value in this exact game is unquantified (speculative).
methods.apply: New tournament simulator: reuse per-world match results from method 1 for played/next fixtures and the engine's odds-implied lambdas for future hypothetical ties (fall back to a simple Elo/market prior where odds don't exist yet) -> table P(team plays in round r) per team -> multi-round xPts matrix -> feed method 2's solver run per horizon window. Directly serves the stored R32 plan (memory): it turns 'Wildcard at R32, rebuild for knockout ties' into a solved plan instead of a heuristic.

methods.name: Projected ownership + effective ownership model (Dirichlet-multinomial regression)
methods.what: Model the FIELD: predict each player's next-round selection %, captaincy %, and thus Effective Ownership (EO = started% + captained% (+ triple-captained%)), plus transfer flows. Features: price, xPts/value, last-round returns, team advancement odds, brand/popularity priors, price trend. Haugh-Singal's Dirichlet-multinomial regression is the canonical form: it gives a full joint distribution over opponent squads, not just marginal percentages, which method 6 needs for sampling realistic opponent teams.
methods.evidence: Core innovation of Haugh & Singal, Management Science 67(1):72-92 (2021): Dirichlet-multinomial data-generating process for opponents' team selections, parameters via Dirichlet regressions, validated in real-money DFS contests during the 2017 NFL season; the framework also priced insider info and collusion. Commercially: SaberSim projects ownership by simulating how fields react to news/salary/projections; RotoGrinders has published ownership-prediction methodology for years. In classic fantasy, EO tables for the top-10k (LiveFPL, Fantasy Football Pundit) are the standard rank-management tool. Training data exists for THIS engine: FIFA's fantasy UI exposes per-player selection %, and Holdet publishes player popularity — snapshot both each round. Prediction accuracy achievable on WC data is unproven (speculative), but Haugh-Singal showed usable accuracy with one season of NFL data.
methods.apply: New cached data feed (ownership_rN.json snapshotted at each round lock, next to the odds cache — keeps offline reproducibility) + a stdlib-implementable multinomial-logit/Dirichlet regression fit by gradient descent. Output columns own%, capt%, EO join the existing per-player output table. Zero effect on xPts accuracy — it is the missing input for every rank-aware decision (methods 6-8, 11) and the audit says nothing about it today.

methods.name: Field-simulation rank engine: optimize P(rank target), not E[points]
methods.what: Sample N (~10-50k) budget-feasible opponent squads from the ownership model (method 5), score ALL of them plus your candidate squads across the SAME 50k worlds (method 1), and read off your full round-rank distribution: P(top 1% round rank), P(gaining X places), expected rank percentile. Then pick squad+captain maximizing the rank objective rather than E[points]. This formalizes the two lessons already in memory (blowout coverage; no blanket X-0): the field's concentration is what makes an omission catastrophic, and only a field model can price that.
methods.evidence: Haugh & Singal (MS 2021) prove and demonstrate that top-heavy (rank-payoff) optimal teams systematically deviate from mean-optimal ones — toward higher variance and lower correlation with opponents — reducing to binary quadratic programs, and validated with real-money 2017 NFL contests; Hunter/Vielma/Zaman maximize P(an entry clears a threshold) and report multiple top-ten finishes in hockey/baseball contests with thousands of entries; Mlcoch et al. (ITOR 2024) generate opponent lineups with generative models to compete in DFS (paywalled; details from abstract/secondary summaries). Commercial practice: SaberSim/ETR run contest sims with field lineups as the default GPP workflow. No published classic-fantasy backtest of P(rank) optimization — effect size for WC fantasy is speculative, mechanism is not.
methods.apply: New module field_sim.py: (1) draw opponent squads from Dirichlet-multinomial + budget/formation repair; (2) matrix-multiply against the scenario matrix (pure-Python loops are fine at this scale with array module; ~minutes); (3) evaluate candidate squads produced by method 2 run along a frontier (vary risk weight λ and ownership-penalty γ); (4) report per-candidate P(top-x%) and pick argmax. Replaces the current captain-EV single number with a rank-aware captain pick, and replaces gut-feel differential decisions.

methods.name: Leverage frontier + captain leverage (closed-form lite version)
methods.what: The cheap 80/20 of method 6, shippable now: score any squad by xPts + λ·σ(squad points, from scenario matrix) − γ·(EO-weighted overlap with field), and score captain options by rank-equity — captaining a 60%-EO player is nearly rank-neutral (you move with the field), while an equal-EV low-EO captain is pure rank upside. λ,γ > 0 when chasing (tournament/round prizes), λ,γ ≈ 0 or negative when protecting a lead.
methods.evidence: Hunter et al. formalize exactly this: maximize mean subject to a variance LOWER bound and correlation caps, plus stacking — their entries hit top-10s in thousand-entry contests. Haugh-Singal show double-up vs top-heavy optimal portfolios differ exactly in this variance/field-correlation direction. Pool theory quantifies the payoff of field-aware deviation: Clair & Letscher (Operations Research 55(6) 2007) find strategies maximizing expected return beat max-expected-score strategies 'often by orders of magnitude', driven by crowd overconcentration on favorites (e.g. >80% on one team in a 2004 NCAA pool); Kaplan & Garstka (Management Science 2001) similar. Classic-fantasy EO practice (Fantasy Football Scout, LiveFPL) applies the same logic weekly. Effect size in WC fantasy specifically: unmeasured (speculative).
methods.apply: Three new columns in the existing outputs stage: squad-σ contribution (from scenario matrix), EO, and leverage-adjusted captain EV (extends the existing captain-EV output). Add the λ/γ terms as options in method 2's objective. Needs only methods 1 and 5's ownership snapshot (even manually-entered ownership for ~50 relevant players works on day one).

methods.name: Booster/chip timing via simulation EV + option value
methods.what: Compute each remaining booster's per-round EV DISTRIBUTION from the scenario matrix (captain-boost chips scale the captain's simulated distribution; bench chips add simulated bench sums; wildcard = re-solve squad with method 2 and value the delta), then choose timing by backward induction over remaining rounds where holding a chip has option value driven by advancement uncertainty — under WC 2026 rules: wildcard unusable in R32, unlimited transfers at the group->KO boundary (so wildcard EV right before/after that boundary is heavily discounted), +5m knockout budget.
methods.evidence: Rules grounded in the 2026 game guides (Never Manage Alone, AllAboutFPL booster strategy guide, RotoWire booster guide; and FIFA's own FAQ). Practice: chip decisions are first-class binaries in sertalpbilal's multi-period MILP, and FPL Review built a dedicated 'literal evaluation' mode to compare chip plans objectively — the two most battle-tested planners both treat chip timing as an optimization variable, not a vibe. Academic evidence for chip-timing value in classic fantasy: none found (speculative); community consensus is chips are worth tens of points over a season if timed by EV rather than sentiment.
methods.apply: Extend method 3's planner with chip binaries per round and a per-round 'chip EV report' (mean + P85 of each chip's added points, from the scenario matrix + advancement probs). Output a recommended chip schedule with sensitivity (how much EV is lost by burning it one round early/late).

methods.name: Multi-entry portfolio construction (Holdet main + YOLO teams)
methods.what: When running K entries (the user already runs a main + a 'YOLO' Holdet team), stop optimizing them independently: maximize P(the BEST of K entries clears a rank target). Greedy submodular construction: solve entry 1 as the max-EV/rank team, then re-solve each next entry with overlap caps vs previous entries, a variance floor, forced differential captain, and within-entry team-stacking to create correlated ceilings (decorrelated ACROSS entries).
methods.evidence: Hunter/Vielma/Zaman's central contribution: portfolio of lineups with submodular P(at least one wins) objective, mean-variance + correlation-cap heuristic, multiple top-ten finishes in contests with thousands of entries; Haugh-Singal give a multi-entry algorithm motivated by submodularity + parimutuel results (MS 2021); a 2024 arXiv paper on March Madness multi-entry portfolios reports their best 100-entry portfolio had a 2.2% chance at a $1M pool prize via exact DP + heuristics. Transfers cleanly to Holdet where multiple teams per user are normal; effect size for K=2-3 entries is smaller than K=100 (obvious but worth stating; speculative for Holdet specifically).
methods.apply: Loop method 2's solver with cross-entry constraints (max shared players, min pairwise scenario-matrix distance, distinct captains); evaluate the portfolio's P(best-of-K) on the scenario matrix + field model. Directly implements the deferred 'differentiate YOLO into a contrarian build' item from the R32 plan in memory — as a solved artifact instead of a manual differentiation pass.

methods.name: Mini-league match-race optimizer (exact rival squads, not ownership approximations)
methods.what: For the leagues actually being contested (Holdet mini-leagues, FIFA private leagues), rivals' full squads are visible in-game — so skip ownership approximation entirely: scrape rivals' squads each round, score them over the SAME 50k worlds, and get the EXACT joint distribution of your score minus each rival's. Then optimize transfers/captain to maximize P(overtaking the leader by the final round) given the current points gap and rounds remaining — mathematically a match race: when trailing, deliberately hold differentials and captain off-template; when leading, mirror the chaser's squad to freeze the gap.
methods.evidence: This is the exact-opponent setting where the pools literature shows the largest gains: Clair-Letscher's orders-of-magnitude result comes precisely from optimizing against known/modeled opponent picks; Bergman-Imbrogno's survivor-pool IP plans against the field week-by-week; in Haugh-Singal terms it is the double-up/H2H case where you optimize against an order statistic of known opponents — with visible squads the opponent model is exact, removing the noisiest component. No published classic-fantasy mini-league backtest exists (speculative quantitatively), but the mechanism is exact given the engine's scenario matrix — covariance between your squad and a rival sharing 9 players is computed, not estimated.
methods.apply: Small per-game scraper caching rival squads per round (rival_squads_rN.json, offline-reproducible like the odds cache); new report: per-rival P(overtake), gap distribution, and the single transfer/captain change maximizing P(win league). Feeds Målspillet-style side games too. Builds entirely on methods 1-2; no ownership model needed, so it can ship before methods 5-6.

methods.name: Rank-state-dependent risk policy (dynamic variance dial across rounds)
methods.what: Make the λ (variance) and γ (leverage) knobs from methods 6-7 functions of STATE: points gap to target rank/league leader, rounds remaining, chips left. Approximate dynamic programming: simulate gap-closure probabilities per round from the scenario matrix + field model, and pick tonight's risk posture to maximize P(final target), not this round's EV — trailing with 2 rounds left forces high-variance/contrarian builds even at material EV cost; leading flips to field-mirroring.
methods.evidence: State-dependent contrarian planning demonstrably dominates static strategies in the nearest solved formats: Bergman-Imbrogno (OR 2017) show week-state-aware survivor planning dominates millions of random strategies; Clair-Letscher derive pick distributions that shift with pool size/state; Haugh-Singal's double-up vs top-heavy contrast is the static two-point version of this dial. Application to a multi-round classic-fantasy tournament is a straightforward Bellman recursion but has NO published benchmark — the most speculative item here, and also the one that turns all the other machinery into an actual title-chasing policy.
methods.apply: Thin policy layer over methods 6/7/11: a lookup table (state -> λ, γ, chip-aggressiveness) computed by backward simulation over remaining rounds using advancement probs from method 3. Surfaces as a one-line recommendation in the round report: 'trailing by 31 pts, 3 rounds left -> P(catch) 11% on template play vs 19% with 2 differentials + off-template captain'.

methods.name: Scenario-based stochastic transfer planning (SAA with recourse)
methods.what: Replace expected-value transfer planning (method 3) with sample-average approximation over scenario bundles: this round's transfers are first-stage decisions; next rounds' transfers are recourse decisions inside each scenario (who qualified, who got suspended/rotated, price/value moves in Holdet). Optimize E[points] or a quantile over bundles — captures option value of flexible squads (players whose teams have wide advancement distributions) that deterministic planning systematically misprices.
methods.evidence: Directionally supported, thin on published effect sizes: sertalpbilal's tutorial series explicitly covers stochastic optimization and simulation extensions of the FPL MILP; FPL Review's 'full evaluation' abandoned pure linear EV for probability-based nonlinear plan scoring (autosubs, xMins) because linear-optimal plans were not globally optimal (their docs state this trade-off outright); NTNU thesis line formulates forecast-based multi-week FPL optimization; 2505.02170 adds robust (worst-case) MILP variants. No paper cleanly quantifies stochastic-vs-deterministic planning gains in fantasy (speculative); in a knockout tournament the qualification branching is far more violent than FPL fixtures, so the recourse value should be LARGER here than in the FPL evidence base.
methods.apply: Wrap method 2's heuristic solver in an SAA loop: draw ~200 scenario bundles (round outcomes + advancement + a simple availability shock model from the research overlay's soft multipliers), solve recourse greedily inside each, score first-stage candidates across bundles, pick the best. Computationally the heaviest item; only worth building after methods 1-3 exist and the backtesting harness can measure whether it beats decayed-EV planning.

methods.name: Probability-weighted bench/autosub valuation
methods.what: Value bench slots and formation choice by simulated substitution probability instead of ignoring them: for each world, if a starter records DNP, the autosub fires in bench order — so bench value = P(sub fires) x sub's conditional points, computed exactly from the scenario matrix's existing DNP events. Changes optimal budget allocation (cheap 4.0 enablers vs playing-bench) and bench ordering, and puts direct pressure on the known-crude minutes model where it actually costs points.
methods.evidence: FPL Review's full evaluation 'carries out full probability based calculations (determined by xMins, availability and usage characteristics) to determine expected contribution from each sub, rather than using fixed factors for each sub slot' (their docs) — they considered this worth the loss of optimality guarantees; sertalpbilal's solver exposes bench-weight parameters for the same reason; the 2505.02170 MILP models bench and captaincy jointly. Effect is real but bounded — a few points per round at most, concentrated in rotation-heavy rounds (final group games with dead rubbers, exactly where WC rotation is worst).
methods.apply: The engine already simulates DNP (stats event 342 analog) per world — add autosub resolution inside the scoring stage per candidate squad (needs method 1's matrix plus per-world DNP flags), and include probability-weighted bench value in method 2's objective. Small, honest scoring-realism gain (this one DOES touch effective projection accuracy at squad level) and a synergy forcing-function for the minutes-model workstream.

angle_summary: Deep sweep of in-tournament Bayesian updating with tiny samples (4-8 matches), covering academic state-space/score-driven football models (Koopman-Lit, Rue-Salvesen lineage, 2025 adaptive-shrinkage work in JRSS-C/footBayes), weighted-likelihood ranking literature (Ley et al.: optimal half-period ~3 YEARS for national teams — i.e., 1-3 tournament matches should move team strength only ~5-10%), the bookmaker-consensus/ability-inversion school (Leitner/Zeileis, used live for WC2026 right now), player-level empirical-Bayes evidence (finishing skill is essentially non-updatable in-tournament: year-over-year correlation ~0; role/minutes ARE fast-updatable), and squad-level fatigue/travel/altitude evidence (Scoppa: rest-day effects vanished in modern tournaments; McSharry BMJ: ~0.5 goals per 1000m altitude gap; heat degrades running but not outcomes). The central architectural insight for THIS odds-driven engine: for priced matches the market already performs near-optimal Bayesian updating, so the highest-upside updating layers are (a) rounds/pairings with NO odds yet (outright-odds ability inversion + a dynamic ratings backbone — exactly what the R32 Wildcard planning needs), (b) player quantities the market never prices (start probability, substitution minutes, goal-shares — the likely main driver of the -2.3 xPts low bias), (c) squad-shock propagation (injuries/dead-rubber rotation should move TEAM lambda, not just zero a player), and (d) replacing the hand-set overlay weight w with estimated mixing (Egidi-style convex combination). Methods below are ordered by expected value to the engine.

methods.name: Bayesian expected-minutes model: beta-binomial start probability + substitution-hazard minutes (replaces 'starters = 60+')
methods.what: Two-part xMins model. Part 1: P(start) per player via beta-binomial updated after every team sheet (recency-weighted evidence from qualifiers/friendlies/tournament so far), with manager-level rotation priors and a dead-rubber prior for group game 3. Part 2: conditional minutes via empirical substitution hazards by position and score-state (5-sub era: outfield starters average ~70-80 mins, defenders more, attackers less; bench players cluster 15-30 mins), plus an extra-time branch for knockouts (P(draw at 90) from the engine's own Dixon-Coles distribution -> extend player minutes and team lambda by ~30/90). xPts becomes an expectation over the joint (start, minutes) distribution, not a point assumption. This is the fastest-updating quantity in a tournament: 1-3 team sheets legitimately move P(start) a lot because the prior is weak, unlike team strength.
methods.evidence: FPL Review — the commercial benchmark this engine was audited against Rotowire for — makes xMins the centerpiece: minutes simulated across 1,000 scenarios with rotation/injury decay (https://docs.fplreview.com/the-model/projections/xmins/), and their own 'Ultimate Truth' benchmarking shows model accuracy is dominated by availability/minutes information (https://fplreview.com/ultimate-truth-how-fpl-models-perform-relative-to-a-perfect-model/). OpenFPL (arXiv 2508.09992) reproduces near-state-of-the-art accuracy and attributes low-return (blanks/zeros) accuracy chiefly to minutes/availability features (https://arxiv.org/html/2508.09992v1). AIrsenal (Alan Turing Institute) is an open-source reference implementing team+player models with explicit minutes heuristics (https://github.com/alan-turing-institute/AIrsenal). For 2026 dead rubbers: the 48-team format produces more dead rubbers than any prior WC and betting/pricing assumptions break down there (https://www.msn.com/en-gb/sport/football/group-stage-dead-rubbers-at-the-2026-world-cup-the-hidden-betting-market-nobody-is-talking-about-yet/ar-AA25aHdw); Germany/USMNT round-3 rotation coverage shows manager heterogeneity, so a per-manager prior beats a blanket rule (https://www.espn.com/soccer/story/_/id/49140112/usmnt-faces-world-cup-dilemma-vs-turkiye-rotate-squad-keep-same-xi). SPECULATIVE: exact share of the engine's -2.3 xPts-low audit gap attributable to the 60+ truncation is unmeasured, but truncating sub minutes to zero-band and ignoring extra-time minutes/goals mechanically biases xPts down, in the observed direction.
methods.apply: Replaces the CRUDE minutes stage inside per-player event simulation. New core/minutes.py: (1) beta-binomial start posteriors updated from cached team sheets (stats_rN.json started/DNP event IDs 224/562/342 already decoded per memory); (2) a small hazard table of sub-on/sub-off minute distributions by position estimated once from cached tournament data, applied per MC draw; (3) knockout sims draw an ET branch using the already-computed P(draw at 90) and extend lambdas by 1/3 with a mild fatigue haircut. Research overlay keeps hard out/suspended -> P(start)=0; soft 'rotation risk' multipliers become explicit beta-binomial prior downgrades instead of hand-set w-blended rate multipliers. Downstream, the 60+ appearance-points threshold in the FIFA scoring table is evaluated per-draw rather than assumed.

methods.name: Outright-odds ability inversion (bookmaker consensus model) for rounds with no match odds yet
methods.what: Fetch tournament-winner (and/or group-winner, reach-QF) outright odds from your single book, de-vig, convert to log-abilities via the Leitner/Zeileis 'inverse simulation' procedure: find per-team abilities such that simulating the full remaining bracket reproduces the market's outright probabilities. Those abilities give a pairwise 1X2/lambda estimate for EVERY possible future pairing (R32/R16 hypotheticals) BEFORE match odds are posted. Re-running after each round harvests the market's own in-tournament Bayesian updating — outright books reprice within hours of results — into forward-round projections.
methods.evidence: Leitner, Zeileis & Hornik (2010, EJOR lineage) introduced the model and showed bookmaker consensus beat Elo and FIFA-ranking-based forecasts at Euro 2008; the approach correctly predicted the 2010 FIFA and Euro 2012 winners and 3/4 of 2014 WC semifinalists (https://ideas.repec.org/p/inn/wpaper/2016-15.html, https://ideas.repec.org/p/inn/wpaper/2018-09.html). The ability-inversion mechanics (log-odds averaging, overround removal, inverse tournament simulation to get all pairwise probabilities) are documented in the WC2018 working paper and the 2022 'multiverse' methodology I fetched (https://www.zeileis.org/news/fifa2022/). It is being used for WC2026 right now, combined with a random forest over abilities + market values + plus-minus player ratings, simulating the tournament 100,000 times (https://www.r-bloggers.com/2026/06/football-meets-machine-learning-forecasting-the-2026-fifa-world-cup/). Note their published versions are pre-tournament snapshots without stated mid-tournament refits — re-fetching odds each round to refresh abilities is your straightforward extension, and Zeileis-group tournament reports have historically been re-issued at knockout stages.
methods.apply: New fetcher (outright winner odds, single book is fine — consensus averaging degrades gracefully to one book) + core/outright.py implementing inverse simulation on top of the EXISTING Dixon-Coles + Monte-Carlo machinery (abilities -> per-pairing lambdas -> existing 50k sim path). Slots in upstream of the lambda-solve stage as the fallback lambda source whenever 1X2/totals odds are missing or stale; primary consumer is the R32 Wildcard planner (scenario xPts for all possible ties, probability-weighted by bracket odds). Keep cached odds snapshots per round for offline reproducibility.

methods.name: Gamma-Poisson conjugate shrinkage: opponent-adjusted tournament xG vs market prior, with published-magnitude discipline
methods.what: The core tiny-sample updater. Treat each team's attack (and defence) rate as Gamma-distributed with prior mean = market-implied strength (from the last solved lambdas, opponent-adjusted) and prior effective sample size n0 calibrated on past tournaments (n0 ~ 15-30 matches, consistent with a 3-year half-life). Observation = opponent-adjusted non-penalty xG for/against per tournament match. Posterior mean is a precision-weighted blend; 3 group games with npxG 30% above prior moves the rate only ~5-8% (e.g., prior lambda 1.5, n0=15, three matches at 2.0 adjusted-npxG -> (22.5+6)/(15+3)=1.58). Direction of evidence: use xG, not goals — at team level xG is more predictive of future performance than goal difference or shot counts in small samples.
methods.evidence: Update-size evidence is the strongest-published part: Ley, Van de Wiele & Van Eetvelde (2019, Statistical Modelling) tested half-periods from 0.5 to 6 years for NATIONAL teams and found 3 years (1095.75 days) optimal by Rank Probability Score, i.e., a match today should carry roughly the same weight as two matches from 3 years ago — tournament evidence must be shrunk hard (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1471082X18817650, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.09575); the same literature finds ~390 days optimal for club leagues, so international priors are ~3x stickier. Foundational tiny-sample shrinkage: Efron-Morris/James-Stein-style empirical Bayes is standard (applied in soccer by ASA, see method 8). xG > goals for future prediction at team level is the consistent industry finding (e.g., xG more predictive than goal difference and shot ratios: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expected_goals). FiveThirtyEight's WC model operationalized exactly this blend: match ratings from adjusted goals + shot xG + non-shot xG, with pre-tournament ratings 75% match-based / 25% roster-based, updated after every WC match (https://github.com/fivethirtyeight/data/blob/master/world-cup-predictions/README.md). SPECULATIVE: the exact n0 for this engine must be fit on cached 2022/2024 tournament data; 15-30 is my translation of the 3-year half-life into effective matches.
methods.apply: New core/bayes_update.py maintaining per-team (attack, defence) Gamma posteriors, updated after each round from cached match xG (needs an xG-per-match feed cached per round — FotMob/FBref numbers pasted into the research overlay pipeline would do). Consumed in three places: (1) multiplier on lambdas for matches WITHOUT fresh odds (with fresh odds, weight ~0 — the market already updated); (2) divergence flag when posterior disagrees with the single book's implied lambdas by >X% (catches one-book pricing errors given proportional de-vig); (3) prior-strength input to the outright-inversion module (method 2). Keeps stdlib-only: conjugate closed forms, no sampling.

methods.name: Roster-adjusted lambda corrections: propagate injuries/suspensions/rotation into TEAM strength, not just player rates
methods.what: Currently a hard 'out' zeroes the player's rate but the team lambda (solved from possibly-stale odds) is untouched, and mass dead-rubber rotation isn't reflected in team strength at all. Build a player-value layer (market values and/or plus-minus style ratings aggregated to expected-XI quality) so that swapping an expected XI recomputes a team-quality delta, converted to a lambda multiplier. This is the 538 'roster-based SPI' idea and the Zeileis-2026 player-rating covariate, repurposed as an in-tournament shock adjuster: star striker out -> attack lambda down x%; B-team in a dead rubber -> both lambdas shift toward the bench-quality estimate.
methods.evidence: FiveThirtyEight's WC ratings were explicitly 25% roster-based (club-data player quality mapped to national teams) precisely because national-team match samples are tiny (https://github.com/fivethirtyeight/data/blob/master/world-cup-predictions/README.md). The 2026 Zeileis-group forecast adds per-player plus-minus ratings aggregated over club+national matches and Transfermarkt market values as covariates, and the Groll et al. hybrid random-forest papers (WC2018 arXiv 1806.03208, Euro 2020 arXiv 2106.05799) consistently find team ability + market-value covariates dominate predictive importance and 'improve the predictive power substantially' when combined (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.03208, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.05799, https://www.r-bloggers.com/2026/06/football-meets-machine-learning-forecasting-the-2026-fifa-world-cup/). Nate Silver's current PELE system likewise adjusts an Elo-style rating with player market values and ages and will drive Silver Bulletin's WC2026 forecast (https://www.natesilver.net/p/pele-international-football-rankings-soccer-ratings-projections). SPECULATIVE: the elasticity (XI market-value delta -> lambda multiplier) must be fit on cached data; no paper publishes a direct conversion, though 538's red-card analogue (one-player advantage ~1.1 goals/match) bounds the extreme case.
methods.apply: Extend players.json (reconciled by fifaId per memory note) with market value; new core/roster.py computes expected-XI value from the minutes model (method 1) posteriors and a fitted value->lambda elasticity (regress solved lambdas on XI values across cached rounds). Applied as a multiplicative correction at the lambda stage whenever the expected XI at projection time differs from the XI the odds were priced on (late injury news, confirmed rotation) — exactly the case where the single stale book is wrong. Also powers dead-rubber scenarios: overlay marks 'B-team likely', engine now moves BOTH the player rates and the team lambdas coherently (fixes the R2-style blowout/coverage misreads).

methods.name: Egidi-Pauli-Torelli convex combination: replace the hand-set overlay weight w with an estimated market/data mixing parameter
methods.what: Hierarchical Bayesian Poisson model where each match's scoring rate is a convex combination of (a) historical-data team abilities and (b) bookmaker-odds-implied rates (they invert 1X2 odds via the Skellam distribution to recover per-match Poisson means — directly analogous to this engine's 1X2+totals lambda solve). The mixing weight is estimated, not hand-set, and can vary by information regime (fresh odds vs stale, big market vs obscure). This is the principled version of the engine's research-overlay blend weight w in [0.05, 0.5], and of any market-vs-model reconciliation.
methods.evidence: Egidi, Pauli & Torelli (2018, Statistical Modelling; arXiv 1802.08848): first model to formally fuse bookmaker odds into a hierarchical goals model; on 9 seasons of top European leagues predicting the 10th, the odds-augmented model improved fit and out-of-sample predictive accuracy vs historical-data-only models (https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.08848, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1471082X18798414). Implemented and maintained in the footBayes R package (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/footBayes/footBayes.pdf), so there is a working reference implementation to port from. The Skellam-inversion trick also gives a cleaner way to solve lambdas from 1X2 when totals odds are missing. SPECULATIVE: magnitude of accuracy gain for national-team tournaments is not separately benchmarked in the paper (their data are club leagues).
methods.apply: Two plug points. (1) Overlay engine: soft form/rotation signals stop being 'multiplier x, blended by hand-set w' — instead each source (market lambdas, xG posterior from method 3, overlay soft signals treated as noisy pseudo-observations with declared variance) enters an inverse-variance convex combination; fit the source variances once on cached rounds by minimizing RPS/log-loss of resulting 1X2 vs outcomes. (2) Lambda solver: when totals odds are missing/stale, use Skellam inversion of 1X2 plus the method-6 ratings as the second mixture component. Pure-stdlib: closed-form precision weighting after a one-off offline calibration script.

methods.name: Time-decayed weighted-likelihood bivariate Poisson ratings backbone (Ley et al.), fit offline on cached internationals
methods.what: An odds-independent national-team rating layer: bivariate Poisson attack/defence fit by weighted maximum likelihood over ~8 years of internationals, weights = exp(-t * ln2/half-period) x match-importance factor (WC/qualifier/friendly). Ley et al.'s model comparison says bivariate/independent Poisson with ~3-year half-period is the best current-strength estimator for national teams. During the tournament, each new WC match enters with weight 1 and top importance, giving a fully reproducible, offline 'what the ratings say' counterpart to the market — and quantifying exactly how much 1-3 matches move strength (a few percent).
methods.evidence: Ley, Van de Wiele & Van Eetvelde (2019): 10 ranking models compared by Rank Probability Score on domestic leagues AND national teams; bivariate Poisson with time depreciation + importance weighting wins; half-period grid search selected 3 years for national teams (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1471082X18817650, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.09575). This exact ability layer is the input Groll et al. found 'improves predictive power substantially' inside their WC2018/Euro2020 hybrid models (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1806.03208, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.05799). Club-side corroboration of exponential weighting: Dixon-Coles' own xi=0.0065 per half-week and the widely replicated optimal xi~0.0018-0.0033/day (https://opisthokonta.net/?p=1013, https://dashee87.github.io/football/python/predicting-football-results-with-statistical-modelling-dixon-coles-and-time-weighting/). Zeileis' 2022/2026 pipelines use the same construct ('8 years of data, exponential weighting') as one of their core components (https://www.zeileis.org/news/fifa2022/). Importance weights: eloratings.net's K=60 WC vs K=20 friendlies gives the conventional 3x importance ratio (https://www.eloratings.net/about).
methods.apply: New core/ratings.py + a cached international-results dataset (one-off download, then offline forever — fits the reproducibility constraint). Weighted Poisson MLE is doable in pure stdlib with Newton/coordinate ascent (penaltyblog and AIrsenal are reference implementations of the likelihood: https://github.com/martineastwood/penaltyblog). Feeds: prior means for method 3's Gamma posteriors, the second mixture component in method 5, seed abilities for method 2's inversion, and a standing market-vs-model divergence report per round. This is the foundation most other methods sit on.

methods.name: Score-driven (GAS) update rule for time-varying attack/defence — a principled 'how much per match' learning rate
methods.what: Koopman-Lit score-driven models: team attack/defence states update after each match by (learning rate) x (scaled score, i.e., gradient of the predictive log-likelihood). For Poisson goals the score is (observed - expected)/expected-scaled — so the update is automatic, observation-driven (no simulation needed, unlike parameter-driven state-space models), and the estimated learning rates ARE the published answer to 'how much should one match move strength'. Run it on xG-adjusted goals to reduce noise. Strictly more principled than ad-hoc Elo-style bumps, and estimable by maximum likelihood on cached data.
methods.evidence: Koopman & Lit (2019, International Journal of Forecasting 35(2):797-809): score-driven bivariate Poisson / Skellam / ordered-probit models on national-league panels; dynamic score-driven versions outperform static and rival benchmarks in out-of-sample forecasting (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0169207018302048, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3004605). Predecessor parameter-driven version (Koopman & Lit 2015, JRSS-A): dynamic bivariate Poisson via importance sampling produced 'a significant positive return over the bookmaker's odds' out-of-sample on EPL 2010/11-2011/12 (https://ideas.repec.org/p/tin/wpaper/20120099.html) — one of the few published market-beating results. Caveat marked speculative: both papers are club leagues with long panels; transfer of the estimated learning rates to 4-8-match international tournaments is plausible (it nests the 3-year-half-life world) but not directly benchmarked.
methods.apply: Extension of core/ratings.py (method 6): after each round's cached results/xG land, apply the closed-form GAS update to each team's attack/defence states; learning rates fitted once, offline, on 2018/2022 WCs + Euros + qualifiers by maximizing predictive likelihood. Because updates are closed-form (a few lines of arithmetic per match), it stays pure-stdlib and instant. Replaces nothing in the odds path; upgrades the no-odds/scenario path and the divergence flag with a defensible, literature-backed update magnitude.

methods.name: Dirichlet-multinomial goal-share updating with a hard 'never update finishing' rule
methods.what: Within-team player goal-shares (used where AGS props are missing) treated as Dirichlet priors over the team's goals; tournament evidence updates shares conjugately — but the evidence vector is shots/xG share, set-piece and penalty duty observations (role signals), NOT goals-vs-xG (finishing). Concentration parameter set high enough that 1-3 matches shift shares meaningfully only via role changes (new striker, new penalty taker), a few percent otherwise. Assist shares analogous via key-pass/secondary-share priors.
methods.evidence: The 'don't update finishing on tournament samples' half is strongly evidenced: American Soccer Analysis' Replication Project found essentially ZERO year-over-year correlation in empirical-Bayes-adjusted G/xG at player level (their example: 30 shots at raw G/xG 3.0 shrinks to 1.37, and even adjusted values don't repeat season-to-season) (https://www.americansocceranalysis.com/home/2023/8/28/the-replication-project-measuring-shooting-overperformance); StatsBomb's finishing-skill work requires multi-season shot volumes for detectability (https://blogarchive.statsbomb.com/articles/soccer/quantifying-finishing-skill/); Davis & Robberechts show xG-model biases masquerade as finishing skill, further arguing against small-sample finishing updates (https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.09940). The 'do update roles quickly' half is practitioner-standard (AIrsenal's player model conditions goal involvement on appearances/role: https://github.com/alan-turing-institute/AIrsenal) but the precise stabilization speed of shot-share in 1-3 matches is SPECULATIVE — set the Dirichlet concentration by backtest on cached 2022 WC rounds.
methods.apply: Modifies the per-player event-sim stage: prior goal-shares (currently static, reconciled to team totals) become Dirichlet posteriors updated per round from cached per-player shots/SoT (SoT event ID 558 already decoded per memory) and set-piece duty flags from the research overlay. Where AGS props exist they remain the primary rate source (market prices roles already); posterior shares fill the gaps and sanity-check props from the single book. Explicit code-level guard: G-minus-xG never enters the update. Cheap: conjugate arithmetic only.

methods.name: Full state-space smoothing with adaptive shrinkage (particle/importance-sampling filter) + posterior-uncertainty propagation into the 50k sims
methods.what: The 'most real' heavyweight option: parameter-driven dynamic bivariate Poisson where attack/defence follow random walks; estimate by particle filter or importance sampling; the 2025 JRSS-C advance (footBayes lineage) adds commensurate spike-and-slab priors so the filter LEARNS when to shrink hard toward the past and when to allow rapid moves (manager change, key injury) — adaptive updating instead of a fixed learning rate. Crucially, it yields full posterior uncertainty on each team's strength, which the engine can propagate by drawing lambda from the posterior per Monte-Carlo replicate instead of using a point lambda — widening scoreline distributions honestly and materially changing P85 ceilings and captain-EV tails (currently understated because parameter uncertainty is ignored).
methods.evidence: Koopman & Lit (2015 JRSS-A): non-Gaussian state-space bivariate Poisson with importance sampling; out-of-sample betting returns significantly positive vs bookmaker odds (https://ideas.repec.org/p/tin/wpaper/20120099.html). Crowder, Dixon, Ledford & Robinson (2002) established the non-Gaussian state-space formulation with approximating filters (surveyed with the rest of the lineage in https://arxiv.org/html/2508.05891v1). Macri-Demartino, Egidi et al. (2025, JRSS-C qlag032 / arXiv 2508.05891): commensurate priors with spike-and-slab time-varying precisions 'yield better predictive performance' than fixed-dynamics baselines on 5 seasons x 3 top leagues, implemented in open-source footBayes (https://academic.oup.com/jrsssc/advance-article/doi/10.1093/jrsssc/qlag032/8704597, https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05891). Also Bayesian state-space EPL modelling in JRSS-C 2025 (https://academic.oup.com/jrsssc/article/74/3/717/7929974). SPECULATIVE: effect sizes on international tournaments unbenchmarked; the uncertainty-propagation benefit to P85/captain-EV is a modelling argument (variance decomposition), not a published fantasy result.
methods.apply: core/dynamic.py: bootstrap particle filter (500-1000 particles/team, stdlib random is fine at this scale — ~50 teams x 8 obs) over the method-6 backbone, observations = xG-adjusted goals; run as an offline nightly job from cached data. Wire the posterior draws into the existing 50k-sim loop: replicate i uses lambda_i ~ posterior (or a 3-point quadrature to stay cheap) — a one-line change at the sim stage with outsized effect on ceiling metrics. Also emits credible intervals for the divergence dashboard (flag only when market lambda falls outside the 80% CI). Do AFTER methods 3/6/7 — it subsumes them but is weeks of careful work and needs their plumbing anyway.

methods.name: Elo-anchored update-magnitude guardrail (K=60) for all in-tournament strength moves
methods.what: Use the century-tested World Football Elo convention as a calibration guardrail: WC finals matches carry K=60 (friendlies 20, qualifiers 40), with goal-difference multipliers. Convert any proposed in-tournament strength update (from methods 3/7/9 or ad-hoc overlay judgment) into Elo-equivalent points; cap or flag moves exceeding what K=60 would allow (a maximal shock result ~ 60-90 Elo points; a routine expected win ~ 10-20). Elo-to-lambda conversion fit once by regressing solved lambdas on cached Elo differences. Cheap, transparent, prevents both over-reaction (the classic tiny-sample failure) and silent under-reaction.
methods.evidence: eloratings.net methodology: K=60 for all WC finals matches, 50 continental finals, 40 qualifiers, 30 others, 20 friendlies, with 1.5x/1.75x goal-diff multipliers (https://www.eloratings.net/about, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Football_Elo_Ratings). Elo-family ratings are repeatedly the strongest simple baseline in the tournament-forecasting literature (used as covariates in the Groll/Zeileis hybrids: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.05799, https://www.r-bloggers.com/2026/06/football-meets-machine-learning-forecasting-the-2026-fifa-world-cup/), and FIFA's own post-2018 SUM formula uses I=50 group / 60 knockout — independent convergence on the same per-match update scale. SPECULATIVE: the Elo-points-to-lambda-multiplier mapping is a fit, not published; treat as internal calibration.
methods.apply: Small utility in core/bayes_update.py: elo_equiv(delta_lambda) and a clamp applied wherever team strength is moved outside the odds path (methods 3/4/7/9 outputs and any manual overlay team-strength multiplier). Also add cached eloratings.net snapshots as a prior covariate for method 6. Days of work; mostly a safety rail that makes every other updater trustworthy enough to ship.

methods.name: Rest-differential and extra-time carryover adjustments (evidence says: mostly DON'T adjust)
methods.what: Codify fatigue effects with the published magnitudes — which are close to zero under modern schedules: no lambda penalty for ordinary rest differences; small penalty ONLY when a team has <=3 days rest and the opponent more (the one condition Scoppa finds relevant), and a watch-flag (not an automatic penalty) after 120-minute matches. The 2026 wrinkle: the 104-match calendar plus summer heat creates more <=4-day turnarounds deep in the bracket, so the trigger condition actually fires sometimes, unlike 2018/2022. Equally important is the negative result: this stops the research overlay from hand-applying folk 'tired legs' multipliers the data don't support.
