methods.evidence: Scoppa (2015, Journal of Sports Economics 16(5):482-507; IZA DP 7519): all WC matches 1930-2010 + Euros 1960-2012 — under modern schedules rest-day differentials have NO significant effect on points/goals; effects existed pre-1990s; the advantage is 'quite relevant' only when one team's rest is <=3 days (https://www.iza.org/publications/dp/7519, https://newsroom.iza.org/en/archive/research/new-evidence-from-soccer-tournaments-three-days-of-rest-are-enough/). Extra-time carryover: BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil (2025) analysis of 2022 WC + 2023 WWC found running performance MAINTAINED in the following match given 4-5 days between matches; Croatia 2018 case study (3 consecutive 120-min matches) also showed no measurable next-match physical drop (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11883913/). Physiology shows real acute fatigue and injury-risk elevation from 120-min matches (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00421-017-3561-9), so the carryover channel is injury/rotation probability (feed method 1), not team-strength decline. SPECULATIVE: behavior under 2026's 3-day turnarounds + heat is extrapolation — hence flag-not-penalty design.
methods.apply: Schedule-metadata module computing per-match rest days and prior-match-went-to-ET flags from the fixtures cache; applies (a) a small fitted lambda penalty only when rest<=3 days AND differential>=2 (magnitude fit on cached Scoppa-style regression over historical WCs, default ~2-4% if fit is null), (b) bumps sub-early hazard and rotation priors in the minutes model (method 1) after ET matches. Explicitly documents 'no adjustment' as the default so overlay authors stop freelancing fatigue multipliers.

methods.name: Venue covariates for 2026: altitude (Azteca/Guadalajara) and extreme-heat kickoffs
methods.what: Static per-stadium covariate table (altitude, roof/AC, expected WBGT by kickoff slot) driving two small adjustments: (1) altitude adjustment ONLY for acclimatization asymmetries — Mexico and altitude-based CONMEBOL squads at Estadio Azteca (2,240m) / Guadalajara (1,566m) vs sea-level opponents; (2) extreme-heat afternoon kickoffs at unroofed venues (Monterrey, Miami, Kansas City afternoon slots) shade BOTH lambdas slightly down and raise late-substitution probabilities (more bench minutes — feeds the minutes model), since heat suppresses high-intensity output but not technical quality.
methods.evidence: Altitude: McSharry (BMJ 2007), 1,460 international matches: each 1,000m of altitude DIFFERENCE shifts expected goal difference ~0.5 goals (high-altitude side scores more, concedes fewer; p<0.001) (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18156225/, https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2007/12/071221094837.htm) — SPECULATIVE TRANSFER: that estimate is from South American home fixtures with fully acclimatized home sides; at a neutral WC with 1-2 week acclimatization camps the realistic effect is a fraction of 0.5, hence asymmetry-only application. Heat: Nassis et al. (2014 WC Brazil): WBGT>28C cut sprint counts ~10% and high-intensity distance ~25 m/min/player while pass accuracy ROSE 3.2% — physical not technical degradation, no established outcome effect (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/272416570_The_association_of_environmental_heat_stress_with_performance_Analysis_of_the_2014_FIFA_World_Cup_Brazil); Int J Biometeorology (2025) maps extreme-heat risk across 2026 venues/kickoff slots (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11947059/); 2025 Club World Cup heat case study documents same pattern at these exact venues (https://doi.org/10.1080/23328940.2026.2623745); systematic review of weather/altitude effects (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12980601/). Travel/jet-lag within-tournament: best recent evidence says NO measurable performance effect for football (randomization-inference study: https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2023.10.19.23296960v1) — recommend NOT adjusting for travel, another supported negative. SPECULATIVE: heat->totals magnitude unquantified; start at -2 to -3% on both lambdas for WBGT>28C afternoon games and backtest.
methods.apply: Static venues.py table (16 stadiums: altitude, roof, typical kickoff WBGT) + hook at the lambda stage applying the asymmetric altitude multiplier and heat totals-shade BEFORE the DC/sim stages; heat flag also raises substitution hazards in method 1. Note the market largely prices altitude for Mexico matches already — so like all team-level adjustments here, weight goes to ~0 when fresh odds exist and full when projecting future rounds (e.g., 'winner group A plays at Azteca'). Days of work, fully offline.

angle_summary: Honest headline from the ML-vs-statistics literature: at MATCH level, model class barely matters and the market is nearly unbeatable. The 2017 Soccer Prediction Challenge was won by XGBoost+pi-ratings (RPS 0.2063, odds banned); the 2023 edition was won by a bookmaker-consensus-type model (RPS 0.2063) with the best published pure-ML entries at 0.2085-0.2195, and deep learning (0.2098) LOST to CatBoost+pi-ratings (0.2085). Hubacek's 'Forty years' review and a 2024 ML-vs-Poisson study both conclude top methods are near-indistinguishable and feature/market information dominates model choice. The few peer-reviewed market-beaters are instructive exceptions: Koopman-Lit's dynamic bivariate Poisson (positive EPL betting returns), Kaunitz's multi-book consensus-deviation strategy (+3.5-9.9% ROI over 479k matches), and Hubacek's decorrelation-trained models. So for evmax the high-upside ML plays are NOT replacing Dixon-Coles with a neural net; they are (1) PLAYER-level ML rate models, where evidence shows models demonstrably beat bookmaker anytime-goalscorer implications (FPL Review's Massive Data: R2 0.353 vs 0.321 for AGS odds; OpenFPL replicates commercial accuracy with free data and open XGBoost+RF ensembles), (2) an expected-minutes model (OpenFPL explicitly attributes the remaining commercial edge to xMins; engine's crude 60+ assumption is its weakest link), (3) better market extraction: Shin/power de-vig (Strumbelj: bias cut ~2/3 vs proportional) and logit-averaged multi-book consensus, which plausibly explains part of the -2.3 xPts audit gap via longshot-bias-distorted prop rates, (4) exploiting the joint simulation distribution with DFS portfolio math (Hunter-Vielma-Zaman; Mlcoch's soccer-DFS generative ensemble made +34% ROI real-money), and (5) the XL frontier: Large Events Models — LLM-style autoregressive event simulators (62.2% next-event accuracy, public code) that could eventually replace the per-player event sim with natively correlated rollouts, though no published evidence yet ties LEMs to better fantasy-point projections. A log-loss (ignorance) backtest scored against the de-vigged odds baseline is the S-difficulty enabler that makes all of these selectable honestly — Wheatcroft shows RPS is the wrong yardstick and whole model classes are separated by ~0.002-0.013, so proper scoring plus recalibration is where the audited level bias gets found and fixed.

methods.name: Player-level ML scoring-rate model (FPL-Review-style, replaces single-book AGS props as primary source)
methods.what: Position-aware gradient-boosted ensemble predicting per-player per-90 goal/assist/SoT rates from cached per-90 xG, xA, shots, penalty duty, opponent strength and venue, hierarchically shrunk (Gamma-Poisson) toward position/price priors for thin-history players, then reconciled to odds-implied team lambdas. AGS props demote to one feature/fallback instead of the primary rate source.
methods.evidence: Strongest player-level evidence found anywhere: FPL Review's 'Massive Data' benchmark on 2,021 player-matches (GW9-26, 2019/20) — their ML goalscoring model hit R2 0.353 vs quality-adjusted xG, beating spread-market implications (0.331), bookmaker AGS odds implications (0.321), recent xG5 (0.288) and goals/90 (0.081); their conclusion: market-implied scorer probabilities are 'comfortably beaten' by a model using positional changes, penalty ownership, injury context. OpenFPL (arXiv 2508.09992) proves open replication: position-specific XGBoost+RandomForest ensembles on public FPL+Understat data (4 seasons, ~200 features/position, team-based CV folds) match FPL Review overall and beat it on high-return categories (Haulers/Tickers, up to ~5% RMSE gain) in prospective 2024-25 testing. Finishing-regresses-to-xG is analytics consensus, supporting shrinkage priors for prop-less players.
methods.apply: Per-player event-simulation stage: replace 'prior goal-shares + prop-derived rates' with model-predicted per-90 rates, still proportionally reconciled to the solved (lambda_home, lambda_away) so market anchoring at team level is preserved. Requires one new cached feed (FBref/Understat-style per-90 tables per squad, snapshotted per round to stay offline-reproducible). Train offline in any stack, export as flat JSON coefficient/leaf tables the stdlib engine evaluates. Directly fixes the Holdet cheap-boomer blindness (rates for prop-less players) and star-rate suppression from high-margin single-book props.

methods.name: Expected-minutes model: P(start) x sub-timing survival curves, scoreline-coupled
methods.what: Two-part minutes model replacing 'starters = 60+': a start-probability classifier (rotation history, competition state, confirmed news via the existing overlay) times a minutes-if-start survival/hazard curve (sub probability rising after 60'/70', varying by position and role) plus a sub-on minutes distribution; minutes drawn per simulation and coupled to the simulated scoreline state (big leads trigger earlier star subs).
methods.evidence: OpenFPL's authors explicitly attribute FPL Review's remaining accuracy edge on Zeros/Blanks categories to 'precise information on player availability and expected minutes' unavailable from public tags — i.e., xMins is the identified differentiator between open and commercial-grade projections. FPL Review's own docs list xMins (from team news, fixture congestion, odds) as a core hourly-updated input to their EV model. Academic literature on pre-match minutes prediction is thin (in-match physical-performance RF studies exist at 0.91 accuracy but do not answer the pre-match xMins question) — the sizing of the accuracy gain is practitioner-evidenced rather than peer-reviewed [that part speculative]. Mechanically every event rate scales ~linearly in minutes, so this multiplies all xPts and plausibly contributes to the -2.3 audit gap; blowout-driven early subs are exactly the high-lambda fixtures the engine's coverage rule cares about.
methods.apply: Player event-sim stage: per sim draw start indicator, sub-off time from a hazard table (position x role x current scoreline from the DC/MC state), or sub-on window; weight goal/assist/SoT/card/save rates by drawn minutes; apply the 60-minute appearance-points threshold exactly. Calibrate hazard tables from cached historical minutes (the Holdet stats event IDs already decode started/DNP; add club-season minutes for priors — consistent with the realized-minutes priors already built). Pure stdlib.

methods.name: Shin / power / odds-ratio de-vig replacing proportional normalization (biggest effect on AGS props)
methods.what: Replace proportional de-vig with margin-removal methods that model the favourite-longshot bias: Shin's insider-trading model (closed-form iterative solution), power/logarithmic normalization, or Buchdahl's margin-proportional-to-odds. Applied per market family; most important for the ~120%+ overround anytime-goalscorer books where proportional de-vig systematically shaves favorites (star scorers) and inflates longshots.
methods.evidence: Strumbelj (Int. J. Forecasting 2014): Shin probabilities beat basic normalization across large European soccer samples, reducing forecast bias by roughly two thirds; also beat regression-based inversion. Buchdahl's 'Wisdom of the Crowd' study (football-data.co.uk): margin-proportional-to-odds, odds-ratio and logarithmic models handle the favourite-longshot bias far better than equal-margin removal; validated over ~18,000 real value bets (predicted +4.0% vs realized +3.7% ROI). The R 'implied' package vignette documents all methods (reference implementation to port). Mechanism directly matches the audited symptom: understated star goal rates from proportionally de-vigged longshot-heavy prop books push xPts low — a concrete candidate for part of the -2.3 vs Rotowire gap.
methods.apply: De-vig stage: implement shin() and power() in pure stdlib (few dozen lines, Newton iteration); select method per market (1X2, totals, AGS) by backtested log loss; downstream lambda solve and prop-rate derivation unchanged. Days of work, immediately testable against the existing Rotowire audit.

methods.name: Market-anchored residual GBM for match lambdas (hybrid model+market, replaces hand-set soft multipliers)
methods.what: Keep de-vigged odds-implied lambdas as the anchor and train a small gradient-boosted-tree or regularized-linear corrector on features (time-decayed team ratings/pi-ratings, aggregate xG, squad market value, rest days, stage, travel) predicting multiplicative residuals: lambda_final = lambda_market * exp(f(x)). This is the learned, validated version of the current hand-tuned research-overlay blend weight w.
methods.evidence: The hybrid family is the only match-level approach with evidence of matching/beating books at tournaments: Groll et al. random-forest hybrids combining bookmaker-consensus abilities + ranking abilities + covariates were 'close to or even outperforming' bookmakers across WC 2018 / Women's WC 2019 / EURO 2020 backtests. Hubacek-Sourek-Zelezny won the 2017 challenge with XGBoost+pi-ratings (RPS 0.2063, odds banned). Wheatcroft (arXiv 2001.09097): shot-based GAP ratings are 'informative beyond that reflected in the odds' — residual signal exists. Egidi-Pauli-Torelli model scoring rates as convex combinations of historical and odds-implied parameters (the same blend, Bayesian form). Counterweight, be honest: the 2023 challenge winner was a bookmaker-consensus-type model (RPS 0.2063 vs best ML 0.2085+), and both the 'Forty years' review and the 2024 ML-vs-Poisson study find model choice has minor influence — so expect small, single-digit-percent log-loss gains concentrated where a single free book is noisy or slow.
methods.apply: New stage between lambda solve and Dixon-Coles grid: compute features from cached results/ratings, apply exp(f(x)) correction with f trained on the backtest harness (log-loss objective vs realized goals), shrink f toward 0 with tournament-size regularization; hard overlay facts (outs/suspensions) stay absolute, but the soft form/rotation multipliers and the hand-set w get retired in favor of the fitted corrector. Train offline, ship coefficients as JSON for the stdlib engine.

methods.name: Multi-book consensus odds layer (logit-averaged) with single-book deviation flags
methods.what: Ingest 2-3 free bookmakers (or a free aggregated average line), de-vig each, average implied probabilities on the log-odds scale into a consensus used for the lambda solve; flag fixtures where the primary book deviates materially from consensus as low-trust inputs.
methods.evidence: Kaunitz-Zhong-Kreiner (arXiv 1710.02824; 479,440 matches): individual books' deviations from the consensus probability are systematic mispricings — betting deviations returned +3.5% (10-yr closing-odds sim) to +9.9%, confirmed with 5 months of real money; corollary: any single book (the engine's current input) is measurably noisier than consensus. Zeileis et al.'s bookmaker-consensus World Cup models (logit-scale averaging of de-margined odds from ~20+ books) are the benchmark tournament forecaster family and the ability source in Groll's hybrids. Strumbelj (2014) likewise found averaging across books improves implied-probability accuracy.
methods.apply: Odds-ingest stage: add fetchers for 1-2 more free books (cache all raw books per round for reproducibility), insert consensus step before de-vig/lambda solve; player props stay single-book but get rescaled so prop-implied team totals match consensus lambdas. Also gives a data-quality alarm the research overlay can surface ('book X is off consensus by >5% on this match').

methods.name: Log-loss (ignorance) backtest against the de-vigged odds baseline + level recalibration of player rates
methods.what: Make the nascent backtesting harness score every output (1X2, totals, clean sheets, scorer probabilities, realized fantasy points vs xPts) with the ignorance/log-loss score, always alongside the de-vigged (Shin) closing-odds baseline, then fit a low-parameter recalibration layer (global multiplicative level on goal/assist/appearance rates, or isotonic on probabilities) from accumulated rounds.
methods.evidence: Wheatcroft (J. Quant. Anal. Sports 2021; arXiv 1908.08980): the ignorance score outperforms both RPS and Brier at selecting the better football forecast — he 'strongly recommends' it; RPS's non-locality is a liability. Challenge history shows whole model classes separated by RPS 0.002-0.013 (0.2063 vs 0.2085 vs 0.2195), i.e., without proper scoring and hundreds of matches you cannot tell improvements from noise. FPL Review's 'Ultimate Truth' post benchmarks FPL projection models against a 'perfect model' upper bound the same way — the practitioner standard. The audited -2.3 xPts-vs-Rotowire gap is precisely a level bias this layer detects against REALIZED points (settling whether the engine or Rotowire is miscalibrated).
methods.apply: Backtest harness (already being built): freeze per-round inputs (already cached), score all probabilistic outputs with log loss vs realized outcomes and vs the odds baseline; add calibration module fitting a 1-3 parameter multiplicative correction on player event rates per position; every subsequent engine change (methods above) gates on log-loss delta. Pure stdlib, days of work, and it is the enabler that makes the other methods' gains measurable.

methods.name: Joint-simulation portfolio optimization (DFS correlation math on the existing 50k sims)
methods.what: Stop collapsing the Monte-Carlo output to per-player means: persist per-sim joint player-point vectors and pick captains/lineups/differentials by optimizing functionals of the joint distribution — P85 of squad total, P(beat a reference field team), mean-variance-covariance — with stacking and blowout coverage emerging endogenously instead of via hand rules.
methods.evidence: Hunter-Vielma-Zaman 'Picking Winners' (arXiv 1604.01455): canonical top-heavy-contest result — construct entry portfolios maximizing P(at least one wins) via greedy submodular optimization with expected-score maximization, variance lower bounds and inter-entry correlation caps; widely deployed in DFS with public implementations. Mlcoch et al. (Int. Trans. Operational Research 2024): soccer DFS pipeline estimating the JOINT fantasy-point distribution with an ensemble of generative models plus a mixed-integer quadratic program over mean/variance/covariance — +34% ROI (EUR 2,439 profit on EUR 7,133) over 8 real-money weeks [small sample, single period — treat ROI as speculative, the methodology as solid]. The engine already produces the joint distribution (player correlation via shared team goals) and currently throws it away; the user's R2 blowout-coverage lesson is a correlation-exploitation failure this fixes structurally.
methods.apply: Output stage: dump a 5-10k subsample of per-sim player score vectors to a compact cached file; add a stdlib optimizer (greedy submodular for portfolios; exhaustive/branch-and-bound over the shortlisted pool for a single Holdet XI and captain) maximizing chosen joint-distribution objectives; expose 'coverage' and 'stack' diagnostics. Improves realized rank/contest EV rather than per-player xPts accuracy — impact is on decisions, not projections.

methods.name: Weibull-count + copula scoreline layer (replace Dixon-Coles tau)
methods.what: Swap independent-Poisson-with-DC-tau for Weibull inter-arrival count marginals (shape parameter captures under/over-dispersion in goals) joined by a copula (e.g., Frank) for flexible home-away dependence, still moment-matched to de-vigged 1X2 + totals constraints.
methods.evidence: Boshnakov, Kharrat, McHale (Int. J. Forecasting 2017): the bivariate Weibull count model gave improved fit and better-calibrated forecasts than Poisson-based models (including DC-type) on EPL data, and positive returns in an out-of-sample Kelly betting exercise against published odds. Generalised joint regression for football counts (arXiv 1908.00823) confirms flexible dependence structures beat DC's single-tau adjustment. Effect sizes at 1X2 level are small; gains concentrate in exact-score cells (0-0/1-1), draw structure and totals tails — exactly what prices clean sheets, Malspillet scoreline picks and over-concentration risk.
methods.apply: Scoreline-distribution stage: replace the DC pmf with Weibull-count pmf (the required series expansion is computable in pure stdlib; cache per-lambda tables for speed) plus copula; the solver fits (lambda_h, lambda_a, shape, dependence) to 1X2+O/U instead of (lambda_h, lambda_a, rho); the 50k MC sampler then draws from the new grid unchanged. Backtest on cached rounds vs DC using the log-loss harness before adopting.

methods.name: Time-decayed dynamic strength layer + in-tournament Bayesian player-share updating
methods.what: Weighted-maximum-likelihood bivariate Poisson team strengths with exponential time decay (Ley-style; full Koopman-Lit state space as stretch), refit after every round and blended with odds-implied lambdas; plus conjugate Gamma-Poisson updating of per-player goal/assist shares from observed tournament events and xG.
methods.evidence: Koopman & Lit (JRSS-A 2015): dynamic bivariate Poisson with stochastically time-varying attack/defence strengths produced a significant positive out-of-sample betting return vs bookmaker odds on EPL 2010/11-2011/12 — one of the few peer-reviewed market-beating statistical models. Ley, Van de Wiele, Van Eetvelde (Statistical Modelling 2019): across ten model classes, time-decayed bivariate/independent Poisson with match-importance weights gave the best RPS for both leagues and NATIONAL TEAMS (directly the WC use case). Honest caveat: the engine re-fetches odds each round, so team-level updating is partly redundant with the market's own updating — the durable value is (a) a sanity check when the single book is stale/noisy and (b) the player-share posterior updating, which nothing in the market feed provides for prop-less players mid-tournament.
methods.apply: New module refit from cached results after each round (Newton solver, pure stdlib): outputs blend into the lambda stage with a backtest-chosen weight (expect small, e.g. 0.1-0.2, per the hybrid literature); player goal/assist shares become Gamma-Poisson posteriors updated with tournament goals/xG, replacing static priors between rounds — addresses the 'no in-tournament Bayesian updating' weakness at the level where it actually binds (players, not teams).

methods.name: Decorrelation-trained edge model routed to contrarian/YOLO builds
methods.what: Train the residual/player models not only for accuracy but with a decorrelation objective that rewards confident, historically-profitable DISAGREEMENT with market-implied probabilities; route flagged disagreements to the differential/YOLO build rather than the main projection, with portfolio-theory-style exposure sizing.
methods.evidence: Hubacek, Sourek, Zelezny (Int. J. Forecasting 2019, 'Exploiting sports-betting market using machine learning'): with identical features, a model trained to decorrelate from the bookmaker beat both accuracy-trained and profit-trained variants, yielding systematically positive cumulative profit on NBA 2007-2014; they combine convolutional nets with modern portfolio theory for stake distribution. Core insight transfers: predictions that mirror the market have zero edge after margin — for fantasy, zero rank-gain vs an odds-following field. The translation from betting profit to fantasy rank EV is analogous but unproven [speculative], and overlaps game-theory/ownership territory.
methods.apply: Overlay/output stage: add an 'edge report' ranking spots where model-estimated player rates diverge from prop-implied rates, weighted by backtested reliability of such divergences; the deferred R32 plan's differentiated YOLO build consumes this list; main xPts stay market-anchored. Requires methods 1/6 (backtest + player model) first.

methods.name: Large Events Model (LEM): autoregressive event-sequence simulator as the player-event engine
methods.what: LLM-style next-event models trained on event-stream data (WyScout/StatsBomb): autoregressively generate full-match event rollouts (event type, location, time, success, goal flag), conditioned or importance-reweighted to match the engine's odds-implied lambdas; player attribution via share models or player-conditioned LEM variants. Would replace the per-player event simulation with natively correlated goals/assists/SoT/cards and realistic within-match dynamics (red cards, game state, momentum).
methods.evidence: Mendes-Neves et al., 'Towards a foundation Large Events Model for soccer' (Machine Learning 113, 2024; arXiv 2402.06820): MLP-based LEM on public WyScout reaches 62.2% next-event-type accuracy (vs 40.8% frequency baseline, 55.7% prior LEM), 24-28% lower coordinate MAE, supports win-probability, over/under forecasting, VAEP valuation, and 'parallel simulation of millions of matches'; code public (github.com/nvsclub/LargeEventsModel). Seq2Event (KDD 2022) established transformer next-event prediction; a unified tabular-autoregressive LEM (Springer MLSA 2025) improves scalability/context; HIGFormer (arXiv 2507.10626) adds player-team interaction graph transformers claiming outcome-prediction gains [no bookmaker comparison published]. CRITICAL HONESTY: no published result yet shows LEM-simulated FANTASY POINTS beating prop/rate-based simulation, and current public LEMs drop player identity entirely — player conditioning is open research. This is the highest-ceiling, highest-risk item; ceiling high, floor near zero.
methods.apply: Long-horizon replacement of the DC-grid + per-player event sim: train/fine-tune a LEM offline (GPU, outside the stdlib constraint), pre-generate N conditioned rollouts per fixture, reduce them to per-player event-count distributions and cache as JSON so the stdlib engine remains offline-reproducible (heavy compute outside, cached artifacts inside — same pattern as the odds cache). Phase 1: team-level LEM replacing the scoreline grid; Phase 2: player-conditioned rollouts. Only attempt after the log-loss harness exists to prove/disprove gains.

angle_summary: Validation methodology for an odds-driven fantasy projection engine. The sweep covered proper scoring rules for 1X2/scoreline forecasts (Constantinou & Fenton's RPS canon vs Wheatcroft's ignorance-score rebuttal), distributional calibration for count models (PIT histograms, reliability diagrams, FiveThirtyEight's public calibration practice), de-vig method validation (Štrumbelj/Shin), closing-line-value as a fast ground-truth proxy (Kaunitz et al., betting-quant practice), leakage-free point-in-time backtest design, small-sample inference for ~104-match tournaments (Diebold-Mariano small-sample corrections, betting significance rules-of-thumb), fantasy-layer scoring practice (FantasyPros accuracy-gap methodology, Fantasy Football Analytics R²/MASE work, FPL Review's "perfect model" noise-ceiling study), and pooled-corpus validation as used in the World Cup forecasting literature (Groll et al.). Core theme: the engine can't be validated on one tournament's match-level outcomes — it needs (a) market-relative skill scores and CLV for fast feedback, (b) distribution-level calibration tests on the DC core, (c) player-match-level pooling (~2,700 obs/tournament) with honest paired tests, and (d) a point-in-time data store so the research overlay and blend weight w can be tuned without hindsight. Several methods double as direct accuracy fixes (Shin de-vig, beta recalibration) because the validation literature is where their effect sizes are established.

methods.name: Proper-scoring harness: ignorance/log-loss primary, RPS+Brier secondary, always reported as skill vs the de-vigged odds baseline
methods.what: Per-match scoring of the engine's 1X2 (and scoreline) probabilities with the ignorance score (log loss), plus RPS and Brier for comparability with the football literature. Every metric is reported as a skill delta vs the de-vigged bookmaker baseline, never in isolation, because odds-based forecasts are the strongest known benchmark.
methods.evidence: Constantinou & Fenton (JQAS 2012) established RPS as the football-forecasting standard because outcomes are ordinal. Wheatcroft (JQAS 2021, arXiv:1908.08980, fetched) ran simulation experiments showing the ignorance score outperforms both RPS and Brier at identifying the better forecaster — recommends ignorance as primary. Hvattum & Arntzen (IJF 2010, ~8,000 matches) found odds-based benchmarks significantly beat every statistical model tested, so skill-vs-market is the informative framing. Note: publishing both scores hedges the ongoing RPS-vs-ignorance dispute.
methods.apply: New eval module in the backtesting harness (stdlib math only). Score the Dixon-Coles-derived 1X2 probs at stage 'scoreline distribution' against cached results. Because the engine solves lambdas TO match implied 1X2+totals, raw scores are near-tautological vs the same book — the informative quantities are (a) delta log-loss of final engine probs (after DC tau reshaping + research overlay) vs the pure de-vigged odds, which directly measures whether the overlay and w add or destroy information, and (b) drift between early-fetch odds and closing. Wire into per-round reports.

methods.name: PIT-histogram calibration testing of the Dixon-Coles goal/scoreline distributions (Czado-Gneiting-Held non-randomized PIT for counts)
methods.what: For every match, evaluate the predictive CDF at the observed home/away/total goal counts using the non-randomized probability integral transform for discrete distributions; aggregate into PIT histograms (U-shape = underdispersed/overconfident, hump = overdispersed). Add reliability diagrams for derived binary events: clean sheet, over 2.5, BTTS, anytime-scorer.
methods.evidence: Czado, Gneiting & Held (Biometrics 2009) is the canonical method for count-forecast calibration; implemented in R 'surveillance' and epiforecasts 'scoringutils' (both fetched/found — logic is ~50 lines, portable to pure Python). Practitioner precedent: FiveThirtyEight's public 'Checking our work' calibration pages found their soccer model overconfident on heavy favorites (predicted 80% won only 72% in 2020, Brier 0.161) — exactly the failure mode a WC group stage with extreme favorites would hit. Dixon-Coles' own tau adjustment exists because raw Poisson miscalibrates low-scoring draws; PIT tests whether the engine's version actually fixes it on new data.
methods.apply: Plugs at the scoreline-distribution stage output. Compute PIT values from the DC pmf per match (home goals, away goals, totals), pool per round and per tournament, chi-square test against uniformity. Clean-sheet reliability diagram directly audits the probabilities feeding defender/GK fantasy points — the crude 60+ minutes model means CS points are the most leveraged calibration risk in the whole player pipeline. Output: one calibration page per round in the harness report.

methods.name: De-vig bake-off validated by proper scores: Shin's method vs power vs proportional (replace proportional if it loses)
methods.what: Implement Shin's insider-trading margin model, the power/exponential method, and additive de-vig alongside current proportional normalization; run each through the lambda solver and compare downstream log-loss/RPS and PIT calibration on historical odds. Adopt the winner as the default de-vig at the odds-ingestion stage.
methods.evidence: Štrumbelj (International Journal of Forecasting 2014): Shin-implied probabilities are significantly more accurate forecasts than basic normalization across bookmakers and Betfair; advantage shrinks with market size (WC 1X2 is liquid, but totals and especially anytime-goalscorer props are NOT — where the engine's single-book proportional de-vig is weakest). Favourite-longshot bias is documented in UK football 1X2 and is strong in correct-score markets (Cain et al., Whelan 2024 Economica). Open-source reference implementations: R 'implied' package vignette (lists Shin, power, additive, OR methods) and penaltyblog (MIT, Python — fetched README). WC2026 group games have extreme favorites where proportional de-vig most distorts solved lambdas.
methods.apply: Replaces the proportional de-vig stage. Shin's z solves via a ~20-line fixed-point iteration (pure stdlib). Crucially, apply Shin to the AGS prop de-vig too — longshot goalscorer props (big overrounds, 20-40%) are where proportional de-vig systematically inflates low-probability scorers' rates, which propagates straight into xPts. The bake-off itself runs inside the harness from methods 1-2; adopt per-market-type winners.

methods.name: Closing-line-value benchmark loop: score every model probability against de-vigged closing odds, not just outcomes
methods.what: Snapshot odds twice (at model-run time and just before kickoff); treat de-vigged closing consensus as a ground-truth probability proxy and score the engine's team AND player probabilities against it (mean delta log-odds / KL per market). CLV converges orders of magnitude faster than outcome-based scoring because it removes outcome noise.
methods.evidence: Kaunitz, Zhong & Kreiner (arXiv:1710.02824, fetched): consensus closing odds are accurate enough that systematic deviations from them were profitably exploitable in a 10-year closing-odds simulation, a minute-by-minute simulation, and 5 months of real-money betting (paper-reported figures ~3.5% ROI over ~56k simulated bets and ~+8.5% over 265 real bets — from the paper's reported results, verify against PDF). Practitioner canon (Pinnacle betting resources; boydsbets; rebelbetting): consistently beating the close over ~1000 bets is treated as near-proof of +EV, while raw P/L needs thousands of bets — e.g., 5% yield at odds 2.0 still has ~1/3 luck probability after 100 bets, needs ~1,100 for p<0.05. Speculative extension: using closing AGS props as truth for player goal rates is my transfer of the team-level result; player prop markets are softer so the proxy is noisier.
methods.apply: Add a second timestamped odds snapshot to the fetch pipeline (kickoff-minus-1h), cached like everything else so offline reproducibility holds. Eval: for each market (1X2, totals, AGS) compute model-vs-close divergence per round. This gives round-by-round feedback on whether the research overlay moved probabilities TOWARD the close (information) or away (noise) — a direct, fast test of the hand-set w weight, and of lineup-news handling (memory: SportsMole-style predicted XIs are unreliable; CLV quantifies that damage).

methods.name: Distributional player-points scoring: sample-based CRPS + pinball loss at tau=0.85, benchmarked against a simulated noise ceiling (FPL Review 'perfect model' replica)
methods.what: Score each player's FULL Monte-Carlo points distribution against realized points with sample-based CRPS (E|X−y| − 0.5·E|X−X'| computed directly from the 50k sims), pinball/quantile loss at 0.85 to validate the P85 ceiling claim, plus per-position MAE/RMSE/R²/Spearman on the mean. Then compute the achievable ceiling by simulating outcomes from the engine's own distributions and scoring the engine against those synthetic outcomes.
methods.evidence: CRPS is a strictly proper scoring rule generalizing MAE to distributions (Gneiting & Raftery; skforecast docs). The ceiling idea is proven practice: FPL Review's 'Ultimate Truth' (fetched) simulated a perfect model (1,000 sims/player) and found on N=3,730 player-GWs a PERFECT model scores RMSE ~2.7-2.9, MAE ~1.9-2.0, R² only ~0.12-0.17; real models clustered just behind (best RMSE 2.803/MAE 1.973/R² 0.151, worst 2.884/2.115/0.102). Implication: raw MAE without a ceiling is uninterpretable, and the engine's −2.3 xPts gap vs Rotowire must be split into bias (fixable) vs irreducible variance (not).
methods.apply: Plugs at the fantasy-scoring output stage: persist per-player sim samples (or a 100-quantile sketch) per round, score vs realized FIFA-fantasy and Holdet points. The noise-ceiling run reuses the existing 50k-sim machinery unchanged — score engine means against sim-drawn synthetic outcomes to get the WC-fantasy equivalent of FPL Review's ceiling numbers. Systematic mean shortfall vs realized (but not vs synthetic) = bias in rates/minutes, isolating the −2.3 audit finding.

methods.name: Component-level bias decomposition audit: reconcile the xPts gap by scoring each simulated event stream separately
methods.what: Decompose projected points into components (minutes, goals, assists, SoT, clean sheets, cards, saves, defensive-action estimate, bonus) and score each against realized per-position totals (mean error = bias, not just MAE) and against prop-implied rates where markets exist. Produces a per-round table: 'defenders: −0.4 pts from minutes, −0.3 from CS, +0.1 from cards', pinpointing where the known −2.3 vs Rotowire lives.
methods.evidence: This is how mature fantasy evaluators work: FantasyPros scores position-by-position with value weighting (methodology fetched); Fantasy Football Analytics evaluates per-source, per-position with R²/MASE and found aggregation beats single sources (R² ~0.57-0.67 season-level). Mean-error vs absolute-error decomposition is standard forecast-audit practice (Hyndman). Effect size on THIS engine is speculative until run, but the audit target is concrete: the crude 'starters=60+min' model and the role-shaped midfield defensive-action estimate are the two components with no market anchor, hence the prime bias suspects.
methods.apply: Extends the backtest harness. Realized component data already exists in the cached Holdet stats feeds (decoded event-type IDs: 224/562 started, 218 goal, 220 assist, 558 SoT, 559 save) and FIFA fantasy scoring tables. Run after each round; feed the per-component biases into (a) the recalibration layer (method 7) and (b) targeted model fixes (minutes model first). Also score goal-rate projections vs de-vigged AGS closing props as a market cross-check.

methods.name: Post-hoc recalibration layer: beta calibration of derived event probabilities, refit walk-forward each round
methods.what: Fit beta calibration (Kull-Silva Filho-Flach; 3-parameter map on log(s) and log(1−s), contains identity, works on small samples) to historical (predicted prob, outcome) pairs for each event family — clean sheets, anytime scorer, 2+ goals, assist — and apply the fitted transform to new predictions before fantasy scoring. Coefficients checked into the repo with data vintage for reproducibility.
methods.evidence: Kull et al. (AISTATS 2017): beta calibration was never significantly worse than any competitor and significantly better than all others across their benchmark suite; parametric so it tolerates small calibration sets, unlike isotonic regression which overfits below ~1000 samples (sklearn calibration docs). Sample budget: ~104 matches × ~26 relevant players ≈ 2,700 player-match event pairs per tournament, comfortably enough for a 3-parameter fit per event family, marginal for isotonic. Domain-specific precedent: recent work infers 'true' football probabilities with explicit favourite-longshot-aware calibration achieving best log-loss/calibration (MDPI Mathematics 2025, found in search).
methods.apply: New stage between per-player event simulation and fantasy-table scoring: transform event probabilities (or equivalently rescale per-player event rates so simulated frequencies hit calibrated targets). Fit via stdlib Newton/L-BFGS-free logistic regression on the two log features (~80 lines). Strict walk-forward: round k uses fits from rounds 1..k−1 plus (once built) the pooled club-football corpus from method 11. Directly attacks the −2.3 systematic under-projection if it is calibration-shaped.

methods.name: Leakage-free point-in-time backtest protocol: append-only timestamped snapshots, dated overlay facts, pre-registered metrics
methods.what: Restructure the cache as an append-only point-in-time store: every odds fetch, price list, lineup, and research-overlay entry carries the timestamp it became public; backtests replay strictly as-of decision time; the markdown overlay gets per-fact dates so hindsight can't leak (memory notes research files are currently not round-scoped — that IS a leakage bug for backtesting). Pre-register the metric set per round (delta log-loss vs market, CRPS, per-position bias, CLV) to prevent metric shopping.
methods.evidence: Standard quant practice: look-ahead bias is the dominant failure of backtests (Marketcalls look-ahead-bias writeup; MachineLearningMastery walk-forward for time series; sports-specific 'time cuts' in the nxtbets NFL model guide — no feature may postdate the decision). Sports odds add a subtle trap the finance literature flags: evaluating with CLOSING odds while pretending decisions were made days earlier silently imports team news. Evidence is practice-based, not experimental (marked as such), but the failure mode is deterministic, not speculative.
methods.apply: Schema change to the cached-data layer (stays offline-runnable — snapshots are just more files with timestamps in names). Harness gains a replay clock. Payoff: the hand-set blend weight w in [0.05, 0.5] becomes legitimately TUNABLE — grid-search w on rounds 1..k−1, evaluate on round k, instead of hand-setting; same for the DC tau and minutes thresholds. This is the prerequisite that makes methods 1-7 trustworthy rather than in-sample stories.

methods.name: Small-sample honesty kit: paired permutation/bootstrap tests, small-sample Diebold-Mariano, and minimum-detectable-effect reporting for ~104-match tournaments
methods.what: Every model-A-vs-B comparison ships with a paired test on per-match (or per-player-match) score differentials — permutation test or moving-block bootstrap, plus Diebold-Mariano with Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold correction or fixed-smoothing asymptotics — and a minimum-detectable-effect statement. Player-level tests use cluster bootstrap by match, since teammates' points are correlated through shared team goals (which the engine explicitly models).
methods.evidence: DM test has known size distortions in small samples; Coroneo & Iacone (J. Applied Econometrics 2020) fixed-smoothing asymptotics and HLN (1997) correction are the standard remedies (both found; R forecast::dm.test documents HLN). Magnitude context from betting practice: 5% yield at odds 2.0 is indistinguishable from luck after 100 bets (~1/3 luck probability), needs ~1,100 bets for p<0.05 (rebelbetting FAQ; Buchdahl's football-data t-test article covers the same approximation). FPL Review's comparison needed N=3,730 player-GWs to separate six models spanning just 0.08 RMSE. Conclusion: 104 matches can only resolve LARGE match-level differences; player-match pooling (~2,700/tournament) and cross-tournament pooling are mandatory for finer claims — e.g. the '−2.3 vs Rotowire' audit needs a CI before it drives changes.
methods.apply: Small stdlib stats module in the harness (permutation and block bootstrap are ~100 lines, no scipy). Every harness report prints metric, CI, and MDE; comparisons that don't clear the bar are labeled 'insufficient evidence' instead of driving engine changes. Also sets the pooling requirement that motivates method 11.

methods.name: Decision-level fantasy metrics: FantasyPros-style value-weighted rank accuracy, top-K capture, captain regret, optimal-lineup regret
methods.what: Score what the game rewards, not just per-player error: (a) FantasyPros-style accuracy gap — map each model rank to a rank-slot point baseline, compare to actual points, weight by player relevance; (b) top-K capture — share of the round's actual top-10 scorers inside the model's top-20; (c) captain regret — model captain's points vs best-possible captain (validates captain EV); (d) full-lineup regret vs the ex-post optimal squad under game constraints; (e) for Målspillet, log loss on the per-match pick distribution.
methods.evidence: FantasyPros' published in-season methodology (fetched): rank-slot historical point baselines → accuracy gap → z-scored across experts, value-weighted player pool (top-N by consensus AND by actual points), worst week dropped — the de-facto public standard for scoring ranking accuracy. Fantasy Football Analytics found rankings-vs-projections and source-vs-source differences are small and that averaging sources wins — motivating a standing Rotowire-blend benchmark inside the harness. Decision-level regret metrics are standard DFS practice but I found no rigorous published effect sizes (speculative as to how much they change model choice vs plain MAE; memory shows past losses were decision-shaped: blowout coverage, blanket X-0 picks).
methods.apply: Pure post-processing on existing outputs (xPts ranks, captain EV, sim distributions) plus realized points — no engine changes. Add to per-round report for FIFA fantasy and Holdet; captain regret and top-K capture also become the acceptance tests for the R32 wildcard/differentiation plans. Rank metrics (Spearman/Kendall per position) sidestep the level-bias problem that plagues the Rotowire comparison: a uniformly-2.3-low model can still rank perfectly.

methods.name: Pooled cross-competition validation corpus: backfill the match-layer pipeline over thousands of archived-odds matches
methods.what: Build a historical corpus from football-data.co.uk's free CSV archive (20+ seasons, 1X2 + over/under odds from multiple books including closing odds) plus past World Cups/Euros; run the full match-layer pipeline (de-vig → lambda solve → Dixon-Coles → sims) over thousands of matches to give methods 1-3, 7 and 9 real statistical power; keep the fantasy layer validated on tournament player-match pools.
methods.evidence: This is how the World Cup forecasting literature achieves validity: Groll et al. (arXiv:1806.03208) train/evaluate pooling FOUR World Cups (2002-2014); Hvattum & Arntzen used ~8,000 matches; Wheatcroft's scoring-rule experiments use full league seasons. football-data.co.uk is the standard free source (Buchdahl's own analyses are built on it) with documented open/close odds for recent seasons. The engine's stdlib/cached-data design makes replaying trivially cheap. Caveat (marked): club-league calibration transfers imperfectly to international knockout football — neutral venues, extra time, weaker priors — so tournament-specific parameters (e.g. DC tau) still need tournament pooling.
methods.apply: New harness data-loader for football-data CSV schema (B365/PS open+close columns) mapped into the engine's cached-odds format; nightly-runnable offline. Immediately unblocks: Shin-vs-proportional bake-off at scale, PIT calibration curves with tight CIs, beta-calibration pre-fits for CS/AGS event families that method 7 then fine-tunes in-tournament, and honest MDEs for method 9. AIrsenal (Alan Turing Institute, MIT) is the closest open-source precedent of a DC-based fantasy pipeline validated on pooled seasons and is worth mining for harness design.

angle_summary: Fantasy-platform market microstructure is a genuinely scoreable channel this engine ignores: Holdet literally ranks managers by total team-value growth (games/holdet_gold/rules.md: "rank = total value"), and in FPL price rises compound budget worth ~£2-4m/season. The sweep found that (a) the FPL price rule has been empirically cracked to F1≈0.89 with a fixed ~200-240k cumulative net-transfer threshold plus a daily-flow gate, giving a proven recipe for reconstructing Holdet's rule from the cached stats_rN.json/players.json history; (b) Holdet growth is largely a deterministic function of match events already inside the 50k sims, so expected-growth and growth-variance can be emitted per player with almost no new machinery; (c) production solvers (FPL Review, sertalpbilal's open-source MILP) already monetize bank value (~0.10 pts/£1m) and time-decay (0.85), providing calibrated priors for adding price-delta and terminal-budget terms to the planner — with the LP budget dual as a principled exchange rate; (d) FIFA/UEFA matchday substitution+captain windows are a textbook two-stage stochastic program with recourse over day-conditioned sim slices, directly analogous to DFS late-swap practice and worth real points now; (e) deadline timing (buy early for the rise vs wait for confirmed XIs) is an optimal-stopping problem for which FPL Core's day-level hazard features (days_since_last_rise, rises-beget-rises momentum) supply the price side and the minutes domain's two-stage snap supplies the information side. The academic anchor is Matthews & Ramchurn (AAAI 2012), who hit top-percentile vs 2.5M humans by treating fantasy as a sequential belief-state decision problem — validating budget/price as state, not a per-round constant. Everything below is fittable offline from FPL bootstrap-static, Holdet feeds, and vaastav's archive within the stdlib constraint.

methods.name: Empirical reconstruction of the platform price-update rule (threshold-model identification)
methods.what: Reverse-engineer each platform's price-change function from telemetry, following the FPL Core methodology: hypothesis-test candidate rules (cumulative net-transfer thresholds, ownership scaling, daily-flow gates, counter resets after a change, unique-manager counting, chip-transfer exclusion) against observed round-over-round price deltas, and fit a day-level rise/fall classifier. For Holdet, first subtract the DETERMINISTIC component (the kr scoring table maps match events to growth, per games/holdet_gold/rules.md) and model the residual as the demand/popularity component.
methods.evidence: FPL Core's 7-part series (4 seasons + live 2025-26 data, 7.2M manager histories) found a fixed ~200,000-240,000 cumulative net-transfer threshold universal across players (price-level beta -0.005, i.e. negligible), a daily-flow gate of ~30-60k, counter reset on change, unique-manager counting (wildcard transfers only ~1.4% of pressure), and momentum ('rises beget rises': 2.01% day-1 post-rise hazard climbing to 6% by day 5; falls suppress rises to 0% day-1); final F1 0.89 on 2025-26 with days_since_last_rise as #1 feature; code public. LiveFPL self-reports 98-99% accuracy on rises and defines honest true-alarm metrics (~60-70% ceiling for falls). Holdet's own materials confirm prices change automatically after each round, driven by match actions plus popularity/trading. Holdet residual-demand share is unquantified — that part is speculative until fitted.
methods.apply: New core/market.py. Stage: a post-hoc fit, upstream of the MILP planner. Ingest cached stats_rN.json (event IDs already decoded per memory) + players.json price history; compute per-player realized kr growth from the scoring table, regress observed price delta = table_growth + f(ownership, net-trade proxy, price bracket) and identify f. For FPL next season, port the FPL Core threshold model onto bootstrap-static's transfers_in_event/transfers_out_event fields (poll once daily, cache to JSON — stays offline-runnable). Output: P(rise), P(fall), E[Δprice] per player per round, consumed by the planner (method 4) and deadline policy (method 7).

methods.name: Simulate Holdet kr-growth distributions inside the existing 50k Monte Carlo
methods.what: Treat team-value growth as a first-class simulated output, not a side effect. Because Holdet growth IS the kr scoring table applied to match events (goals, assists, cards, clean sheets, decisive goals), every one of the 50k sims already implies a per-player kr-growth realization. Emit E[growth], P85 growth, growth covariance across players, and captain-growth EV (captain = ×2 growth in Gold) exactly the way xPts is emitted today — then add the fitted residual-demand component from method 1 as a mean shift.
methods.evidence: Holdet rules confirmed: 'Spillere får værdi ud fra konkrete handlinger i kampene' — goals/assists positive, cards/goals-conceded negative, clean-sheet bonuses for GK/DEF, decisive-goal bonuses for forwards; prices update automatically after each round; rank = total value (confirmed in the repo's own games/holdet_gold/rules.md: 'Kroner-growth game... rank = total value', captain = ×2 growth). BetXpert's VM 2026 Manager expert strategy piece confirms winners compound value via low transfer fees + captain growth. The engine's cheap-boomer blindness (memory: holdet-price-prior-bias) was a symptom of scoring xPts while the game scores kr. Effect size on Holdet rank is structural (it's the objective), though no third-party benchmark exists — marked as reasoning, not measured benchmark.
methods.apply: Stage: per-player event simulation → scoring. In games/holdet_*/model.py, map each simulated event vector through the kr table (already encoded for expected growth) but PER SIM, retaining the full growth distribution alongside points. Adds ~one array per player; pure stdlib. Downstream: captain pick by E[growth] with variance-aware tiebreaks; trade rule upgraded from point-estimate 'delta > 1% × incoming price' to P(delta > fee) with covariance between the sold and bought player's growth (shared-fixture correlation comes free from the shared team-goal sims).

methods.name: Net-transfer demand model (predicting the crowd's flows with the Dirichlet-multinomial machinery)
methods.what: Predict each player's net transfers (and hence price pressure) for the coming days from: projected xPts rank, current ownership, price bracket, recent hauls (last-round points), fixture attractiveness, and price-move momentum features. Reuse the existing Dirichlet-multinomial ownership machinery: model the population's transfer-in shares as a Dirichlet-weighted softmax over a public-salience score, and transfer-out shares over negative signals (injury flags, blanks). Feed the outputs into method 1's threshold rule to get P(rise)/P(fall) horizons.
methods.evidence: Directional but strong practitioner evidence: LiveFPL and FPL Statistics achieve ~98-99% (rises) day-ahead accuracy purely from observed transfer velocity, proving flows are smooth/extrapolable at day horizon; FPL Core found behavioral autocorrelation (rises beget rises, day-5 hazard 6%) and that hauls/news drive step changes — i.e., flows are predictable from public signals days ahead, not just hours. No published academic model of FPL net-transfer prediction was found (the ML literature, e.g. OpenFPL and CNN forecasting papers, predicts points, and uses transfer_balance only as an input feature) — so multi-day-ahead accuracy achievable from xPts-rank/haul features is SPECULATIVE and must be validated on vaastav's per-GW transfers_balance history.
methods.apply: New core/demand.py, sitting between the projection output and core/market.py. Inputs it already has: engine xPts ranks, ownership snapshots (Holdet feeds carry ownership; FPL bootstrap-static has selected_by_percent + daily transfer counts), stats_rN hauls. Fit offline: for Holdet, regress observed residual price moves (method 1) on these features across cached rounds; for FPL, fit on vaastav's 6+ seasons of per-GW value/transfers_balance. Output: E[net transfers] → E[Δprice] with uncertainty, consumed by methods 4 and 7.

methods.name: Price-delta and terminal-budget terms in the MILP planner (with the budget dual as exchange rate)
methods.what: Extend the transfer-planning MILP objective with: (i) Σ_players E[Δprice_p] × hold_p × λ_budget (early-buy option value and hold-vs-sell), (ii) a terminal bank/team-value term converting end-of-horizon budget into future xPts, and (iii) time-decay on future-round points. Crucially, derive λ_budget (points per unit currency) from the LP relaxation's budget-constraint dual/shadow price at the current solve — the optimizer itself tells you what a marginal million buys in xPts — rather than hand-setting it.
methods.evidence: Production practice: FPL Review's solver exposes exactly these knobs — 'Bank Value per £1M' default 0.10 pts (recommended 0.00-0.20), time-decay default 0.85 (GW+3 ≈ 72% weight), FT value 1.75 pts — i.e., the strongest public FPL optimization stack already prices money and flexibility in points. sertalpbilal's open-source FPL-Optimization-Tools (multi_period.py, HiGHS) implements ITB value and decay and is the community-standard multi-period solver. Outcome evidence that value matters but is second-order: Full90FPL found team-value↔rank correlation 0.49 (top-25 global) to 0.7 (small league), top-25 averaging +£3.0m over casual managers, while cautioning causality and noting 80% of top-25 took zero early hits. The budget-dual calibration trick is my synthesis (standard LP duality) — no source implements it; speculative but low-risk.
methods.apply: Stage: the MILP planner (Holdet trade rule in games/holdet_*/model.py and the FIFA transfer planner). Replace the static trade rule 'growth delta > 1% × incoming price' with objective terms: E[Δprice] from methods 1-3, fee (1% incoming, Holdet) and 1% bank interest as explicit cash flows, decay ≈0.85 on future rounds, terminal value = bank × λ_budget where λ_budget = budget-constraint dual from a relaxed solve over the remaining horizon. Pure-stdlib feasible: the engine already solves selection; duals obtainable from a simple simplex or estimated by finite-differencing the budget (±0.5M resolve).

methods.name: Two-stage stochastic program for FIFA/UEFA matchday substitution and captain-switch windows
methods.what: Model each round as a stochastic program with recourse: Stage 1 (before Day 1) picks XI, bench order, and captain; Stage 2 (after Day 1 results, before Day 2 kickoffs) swaps not-yet-played players and moves the armband, subject to the platform's no-switch-back rules. Solve by consuming day-conditioned slices of the existing 50k sims: for each Day-1 scenario, the optimal Stage-2 recourse is a cheap deterministic re-solve over Day-2 players; Stage-1 choice maximizes E[stage1 + best recourse]. The captain choice becomes an exchange-option valuation: prefer a Day-1 captain because a bad draw can be re-optimized onto Day 2 — E[max(2×C_day1 kept, switch)] > naive max E[2×points].
methods.evidence: Rules confirmed: UEFA/FIFA fantasy allows subs and captain changes between matchdays; captain cannot move to a player who already played and cannot switch back (UEFA help center). Practitioner consensus codifies the option logic qualitatively: 'select a captain who will be playing on Tuesday... so you can switch to Wednesday if you need to' (UEFA rules article); Fantasy Football Scout and allaboutfpl publish the same day-ordering heuristics for WC 2026. Academic/DFS precedent for scenario-based lineup recourse: Newell's 'Optimizing daily fantasy sports contests through stochastic integer programming' and Hunter-Vielma-Zaman 'Picking Winners' (integer programming over correlated scenarios); commercial DFS late-swap re-optimizers (DraftEdge, SaberSim-class tools) do exactly this conditional re-solve in production. No public quantification of points gained from optimal (vs heuristic) window play — effect size speculative, but it is pure upside on scored money in the live FIFA game.
methods.apply: Stage: downstream of the 50k Monte Carlo, inside games/fifa/model.py. Tag each sim with per-match outcomes; partition each round's fixtures into Day-1/Day-2 sets from core/fixtures.py; for Stage-2, precompute conditional xPts of Day-2 players given Day-1 scenario buckets (coarse-grain Day-1 outcomes into ~50-200 buckets to keep it tractable); Stage-1 solved by enumerating captain/bench-order candidates against bucketed recourse values. Couples to the minutes domain's two-stage snap for Day-2 confirmed XIs. Output: 'captain now / plan-to-switch-if' policy card per round.

methods.name: Sell-price ledger and cash-flow-exact transfer accounting
methods.what: Make the planner's budget dynamics exact per platform. FPL: sell price = purchase price + floor(price rises since purchase / 2) in £0.1 steps (the 50% sell-on rule), so the optimizer must carry a per-player purchase-price ledger — future squads' budgets depend on WHEN each player was bought. Holdet: 1% fee on incoming player value, 1% interest per round on bank, round-1 fee exemption, contract limits (3 for Free, unlimited Gold) — model as explicit cash flows over the horizon rather than folding into a one-shot threshold.
methods.evidence: FPL sell-price mechanics are official (premierleague.com price-change explainer) and implemented in sertalpbilal's multi_period.py (sell-price/ITB handling), so this is settled practice among serious solvers, not speculation. Holdet: 1% transfer fee, 1% bank interest, and contract system confirmed by fantasyleague.gg's guide and Holdet's own blog/FAQ; the repo's rules.md already encodes the fee but not interest compounding or multi-round fee amortization (a knockout-phase winner profiled by BetXpert explicitly won on 'lav transfergebyr' — minimizing cumulative fees by holding through rounds). Effect: bounded but certain — fee/interest asymmetries of ~1-2% of a 50M budget per round, and FPL ledger errors compound over a season.
methods.apply: Stage: planner state. Add purchase_price to the per-player squad state in each games/*/state.json; budget-evolution constraints in the MILP become b_{t+1} = 1.01×(b_t + Σ sells×sell_price − Σ buys×(1.01×price)) for Holdet, and FPL's floor-divide sell rule as precomputed sell-price constants per candidate transfer week. Small, mechanical, and a prerequisite for methods 4 and 7 to be trustworthy.

methods.name: Deadline-timing policy as optimal stopping (price hazard vs confirmed-XI information value)
methods.what: A per-transfer 'execute now vs wait' policy: each day before the deadline, compare the expected cost of waiting (P(price rises tonight) × 0.1 × λ_budget, from methods 1-3's day-level hazard) against the expected value of information still to arrive (probability that press conferences / confirmed XIs flip the transfer decision × the xPts regret of a wrong early commit, from the minutes domain's two-stage snap). Execute early only when hazard-weighted price loss exceeds the option value of waiting; formally a finite-horizon optimal-stopping problem with 2-5 decision epochs (days).
methods.evidence: The trade-off is well documented qualitatively — 'Early transfers are a gamble; many managers prefer to accept a loss and wait until press conferences' (tipmaster explainer) — and both inputs are now quantifiable: FPL Core supplies day-level rise hazards conditioned on days_since_last_rise and flow (F1 0.89), and Full90's finding that 80% of top-25 finishers took ZERO early hits warns that the price side usually loses to the information side, i.e., the policy's main value is vetoing bad early buys with numbers instead of vibes. No published formal optimal-stopping treatment of fantasy transfer timing was found — the framing is novel/speculative; the inputs are not.
methods.apply: Stage: a thin decision layer above the planner, output as a line in the round research report: for each recommended transfer, print 'buy now' or 'wait until day X' with the two EV legs. Inputs: hazard from core/market.py + core/demand.py; info value = Δ(planner objective) between committing now vs re-solving under the minutes model's start-probability posterior after team news. For Holdet (prices move only between rounds) this reduces to which ROUND to book a transfer; for FPL (nightly moves) it is a genuine daily policy.

methods.name: Approximate-DP / belief-state MDP wrapper: budget and prices as state across the tournament
methods.what: Replace myopic round-by-round planning with a sequential decision process whose state is (squad, bank, current prices, beliefs about player rates), inspired by Matthews-Ramchurn-Chalkiadakis: they formalized season-long fantasy as a belief-state MDP over a multi-dimensional knapsack and solved it with tractable Bayesian Q-learning. Pragmatic version for this engine: approximate dynamic programming where the per-round MILP is the policy step and a learned/simulated value function V(bank, team_value, rounds_remaining) — fitted by rolling the engine forward on cached sims across remaining tournament brackets — replaces the terminal term of method 4.
methods.evidence: Matthews et al. (AAAI 2012) is the strongest academic datapoint in the entire domain: their sequential agent ranked around the top percentile against 2.5M human FPL managers over a full season — direct evidence that sequential optimization with budget-as-state beats repeated static solves at scale. The 2025 data-driven FPL framework (arXiv:2505.02170) confirms the field still mostly does rolling-horizon LP, i.e., the DP gap remains open. Caveat: their game had no knockout structure and the WC's 7-round horizon is short, so the marginal gain over method 4's terminal term on a 3-4 round knockout is unproven (speculative for this setting); payoff is larger for the full FPL season (38 GWs) next.
methods.apply: Stage: wraps the planner. Build V by backward induction over rounds: sample bracket continuations from the existing team-strength sims (who advances → which players exist next round), run the round-MILP under each, regress achieved future growth/xPts on (bank, team_value, contracts_left); use V as the terminal objective in today's solve. Pure stdlib (tabular/linear V, no ML deps). Fits the R32-plan memory: knockout rebuilds are exactly where a value function beats myopia.

methods.name: Offline market-telemetry corpus + price/backtest harness (vaastav archive + daily API snapshots)
methods.what: Stand up the data layer everything above fits on: (a) vaastav's Fantasy-Premier-League archive — per-gameweek player value, transfers_balance, selected(ownership), points for every player since 2016-17 — as the historical corpus for fitting the demand model and validating the price-rule reconstruction out-of-sample by season; (b) a once-daily cron snapshot of FPL bootstrap-static (transfers_in_event, transfers_out_event, cost_change_event, selected_by_percent) and the Holdet tournament feed, cached to versioned JSON so all fitting stays reproducible/offline per the stack constraint; (c) extend the nascent backtesting harness to score price predictions (Brier on rise/fall) and budget-augmented planner decisions (realized team value vs baseline planner) — the same audit style that caught the 2.3-pt xPts gap.
methods.evidence: vaastav's repo is the de-facto standard FPL research dataset (used by OpenFPL and most academic FPL papers as ground truth) and contains exactly the per-GW value/transfer fields needed; FPL Core demonstrated that multi-season telemetry suffices to identify the price rule (F1 0.89) — i.e., the corpus provably supports the fitting task. LiveFPL's published accuracy definitions (progress-at-change, true-alarm rate with a 60-70% realistic ceiling on falls) provide ready-made honest evaluation metrics for the harness. This is an enabler: its impact is realized through methods 1, 3, 4, 7.
methods.apply: Stage: data/caching layer beside stats_rN.json. Add a fetch-and-freeze script (stdlib urllib + json) writing dated snapshots; a loader normalizing vaastav CSVs to the engine's player schema keyed by stable IDs (respecting the fifaId-not-name reconciliation lesson from memory); and backtest entrypoints in tests/ scoring price-move predictions and planner-with-price-terms vs planner-without on past rounds/seasons. Do this FIRST — it de-risks every other method in this domain.

angle_summary: Awards (Holdet MOTM now, FPL 3/2/1 bonus next) are rank-order events inside a match — exactly the structure the engine's 50k joint sims already produce but never consume. The sweep found (a) a mature deterministic path for FPL bonus: compute the published Opta-fed BPS formula per simulated match from already-simulated events plus fitted count models for unsimulated volume stats (passes, tackles, CBIT/recoveries — which now also pay directly via FPL's 2025/26 defensive-contribution points), rank in-sim and award 3/2/1 with official tie rules — this is what commercial services (FPL Review) already do inside their 1,000-sim engine, and OpenFPL shows the hauler-category gap it closes; (b) a well-trodden statistical family for MOTM: conditional-logit / Plackett-Luce (exploded-logit) models over competitors within an event, proven since Bolton & Chapman's horse-racing work and recent rank-ordered-logit sports papers, trainable on cached Holdet event-513 history and on full within-match rating rankings from WhoScored/Sofascore archives (data-efficient via rank explosion); (c) a key forensic shortcut: many "MOTM" products (Betfair's Opta Player of the Match) are settled by a deterministic event-linear rating (Opta Points: goal ≈ up to 600, pass ≈ 10), so if Holdet's 513 mirrors a public rating provider, MOTM becomes a deterministic-function prediction like BPS, not a subjective award; and (d) bookmaker MOTM props exist as one more free odds anchor but carry documented goalscorer bias and inter-book disagreement, so they calibrate rather than define. Highest-upside items: in-sim BPS with match-state-conditional volume-stat draws, latent-rating (Gumbel/Plackett-Luce) MOTM simulated per draw so captain EV and P85 inherit award variance, and correlated residual-BPS to fix the same haulers-underprojected shape as the audited xPts-low bias.

methods.name: In-sim deterministic BPS computation with official rank/tie rules (bonus as a pure sim consumer)
methods.what: Inside each of the 50k simulated matches, compute every player's BPS from the published, deterministic Opta-fed BPS formula: event-driven components come straight from already-simulated events (goals by position, assists, clean sheets, saves, cards, minutes bands 1-60/60+), plus a drawn 'residual BPS' term for unsimulated components (pass volume, key passes, tackles, recoveries, being tackled/fouled). Rank all 22+ players within the simulated match and award 3/2/1 with FPL's official tie-breaking (ties at first give 3-3-1 etc.). Bonus xPts, bonus distribution, and captain-doubled bonus fall out for free.
methods.evidence: The BPS formula and tie rules are fully public (premierleague.com, updated for 2025/26). FPL Review — the commercial benchmark OpenFPL was measured against — explicitly simulates each match 1,000x per gameweek 'with players scoring goals, winning clean sheets, being substituted and even being awarded bonus points', i.e. bonus is awarded inside the sims, not added as an average. FPL Optimized's public scenario tool does the same downstream (3/2/1 within simulated matches). Effect size: bonus is ~10-15% of a premium attacker's season points (Haaland 2022-23 ~40 of 272) and doubles under captaincy; OpenFPL's category-stratified benchmark shows the accuracy battle is won/lost on 'haulers' (RMSE ~5.14-5.17), which is exactly where bonus concentrates. Per-match historical bps for fitting residuals is in the FPL API / vaastav open dataset (fpl-ai and similar repos already use per-match BPS as features).
methods.apply: New module core/awards.py consuming the existing per-sim event record right after per-player event simulation and before fantasy-table scoring — same pattern as the scenario-matrix export. Encode the BPS table as a stdlib dict; per sim: bps_i = event_bps(simulated events) + residual_bps_i (drawn); sort, apply tie rules, add bonus to that sim's player score. Residual-BPS per-player distributions are fit offline from cached historical per-match BPS minus event-attributable BPS (FPL API bootstrap-static + fixtures live data, cacheable). Nothing upstream changes; validation harness scores 'bonus' as a separate event stream.

methods.name: Match-state-conditional count models (negative binomial) for unsimulated volume stats: passes, tackles, CBIT/CBIRT
methods.what: Rather than a static positional prior, model each player's per-90 pass volume, tackles, clearances/blocks/interceptions and recoveries as negative-binomial counts whose means shift with the simulated match state: possession share implied by the (lambda_home, lambda_away) solve, winning/losing game state, and opponent style. Draw these counts per sim; they feed (a) the residual-BPS term in the bonus ranking and (b) FPL's new 2025/26 defensive-contribution points directly (2 pts for 10+ CBIT for defenders, 12+ CBIRT for mids/fwds, a threshold event that NEEDS a count distribution, not a mean).
methods.evidence: Negative binomial is the standard fix for overdispersed football count data (Reep et al. 1971 onward; Bayesian sports-modelling literature). Opta Analyst's own analysis of the new DC rule shows team possession share strongly predicts qualifying CBIT/CBIRT performances — i.e. the covariate the engine already implicitly has (relative lambdas) is the main driver. Effect size for the FPL port: Tarkowski would have earned 44 pts from DC in 2024/25 ('equivalent of 11 extra clean sheets'), and all top-10 DC earners were centre-backs — a whole scoring stream the engine currently cannot see, same omission shape as bonus. Threshold structure (10/12 cutoff, capped at 2 pts) makes the distribution's right tail, not the mean, the quantity that matters — Jensen's inequality bites hard here.
methods.apply: Extends the per-player event simulation stage: alongside goals/assists/SoT, draw NB counts per player per sim with mu = per90_rate * minutes/90 * f(team possession proxy from lambda ratio, simulated game state). Rates fit offline from cached FBref/Opta-derived per-match logs (or FPL API DC fields once the FPL port lands); stdlib NB sampling via Poisson-Gamma mixture. Consumers: residual BPS (method 1), DC points (FPL port), and MOTM features (methods 3-4). Replaces the 'cheap position/role priors' floor in the brief with a real conditional model.

methods.name: MOTM as Bolton-Chapman conditional logit over all players in a match, trained on cached Holdet 513 history
methods.what: Model P(player i wins MOTM | match) with a conditional (multinomial) logit where the choice set is the 22+ players in that match — the exact structure Bolton & Chapman used for horses within a race. Covariates per player per simulated draw: simulated goals/assists, winning-team indicator and margin, GK save count x losing/draw indicator (upset channel), position, minutes, penalty/set-piece roles, and a hierarchical player-quality intercept. At scoring time, evaluate the logit within each of the 50k sims on that sim's realized event lines and average — so MOTM probability is conditionally coherent with scorelines the engine already prices.
methods.evidence: Bolton & Chapman (1986, Management Science) is the canonical within-event multinomial logit and spawned a whole racing literature (Ali 1998, Lo & Bacon-Shone 1994, Johnson et al. 2010); rank-ordered logit remains state of practice for sports rank outcomes (2024 NHL-draft rank-ordered logit paper, ScienceDirect). Cricket MOTM ML studies confirm the award is dominated by a few interpretable drivers (top batsmen ~ goalscorers analogue; ODI studies find 'top three batsmen are hot candidates'). Training data exists in-house: event 513 decoded across cached Holdet rounds. Effect size: MOTM's kr value in Holdet is large relative to a goal per the user's own settlement data, and the engine currently projects it at exactly zero — pure signed bias on premium players, same shape as the audited ~2.3-pt-low xPts.
methods.apply: Offline fit: stdlib Newton/IRLS on the conditional-logit likelihood over cached (round, match, 513-winner) rows with features rebuilt from cached stats feeds — few dozen coefficients, no new dependencies. Online: a scorer that runs inside the existing per-sim loop after event simulation, adds E[MOTM points] per player, and exports MOTM probability alongside xPts/captain EV. Because Holdet history is thin (1 winner per match), regularize with the ratings-derived prior of method 4 and the hierarchical intercepts of method 6.

methods.name: Latent match-rating simulation with Gumbel noise (Plackett-Luce) — awards as argmax of a simulated rating, trained on FULL rating rankings via rank explosion
methods.what: The hardest, most-real version: give every player a latent per-sim match rating r_i = w·x_i + Gumbel noise, where x_i are that sim's event lines plus drawn volume stats. Argmax of Gumbel-perturbed scores IS Plackett-Luce/conditional logit (mathematically identical winner probabilities), but simulating the rating itself buys three things the pure logit cannot: (a) joint award outcomes correlated with everything else in the sim, so captain EV and P85 ceilings inherit award variance; (b) one model serving MOTM, any FIFA-game star-man mechanic, and future top-k awards; (c) training on FAR more data than winner-only history, because WhoScored/Sofascore archives give the full within-match ranking every match, and the Chapman-Staelin 'explosion' decomposes a ranking into independent choice sets — orders of magnitude more effective sample than one 513 winner per match.
methods.evidence: Plackett-Luce/Gumbel-max equivalence and Bayesian fitting are standard (Guiver & Snelson ICML 2009; generalized PL with ties, arXiv 2212.08543; truncated/time-weighted PL for multi-competitor sports, Bayesian Analysis 2018). The linear-in-events rating assumption is faithful to how the proxies are actually built: Opta Points is a transparent event-linear score (goal worth up to 600 points, a short own-half pass 10, foul -50; top score = Opta man-of-the-match), and WhoScored/Sofascore are deterministic event-weighted algorithms starting from 6.0/6.5 with goals/SoT/key passes carrying the highest weights (2025 Journal of Sports Sciences comparison of rating systems finds offensive metrics dominate). SPECULATIVE: no public benchmark of PL-on-ratings for MOTM hit-rate exists — this would be novel engineering, though each component is proven.
methods.apply: Same insertion point as method 3, but instead of evaluating a logit, draw g_i ~ Gumbel (stdlib: -log(-log(U))) and take argmax(w·x_i + g_i) per sim; the empirical winner frequency over 50k sims is the MOTM probability, and the winner identity is stored in the sim record so scenario-matrix exports, captain EV and P85 include award points natively. Fit w offline by exploded-logit MLE on scraped/cached WhoScored or Sofascore per-match rating rankings (public archives), then calibrate an offset on Holdet 513 winners so the argmax reproduces Holdet's settlement, not the raw rating.

methods.name: Holdet settlement forensics: identify the deterministic generator behind event 513 before modeling it as random
methods.what: Before fitting any probabilistic MOTM model, test whether Holdet's MOTM is settled by a deterministic public rating (the way Betfair's 'Opta Player of the Match' market is settled purely by the Opta Points algorithm, not by pundits). Cross-match every cached 513 winner against the top-rated player per match from WhoScored, Sofascore, FotMob and Opta Points archives. If one provider matches at 90%+, MOTM stops being a subjective award and becomes prediction of a deterministic event-linear function — the same problem class as BPS, with correspondingly higher achievable accuracy.
